**What is built, what is missing, and what it would take — the overworld, 2026-08-17.**

This is the companion to `audit.md`. **`audit.md` is what is *broken*; this is what is *absent*.**
Together they are the whole picture of the project's state at the end of milestone 29.

Thirteen independent agents produced it in one pass: ten read a domain of the code and researched
Bedrock's behaviour for the same domain, two hunted errors in the source nobody had ever read, and one
restructured `RESEARCH.md`. Nothing here was written from memory — every claim is a `file:line` or a
cited URL, and every fragment says plainly what it could not verify.

> **Part of it has since been acted on, and this file is annotated rather than rewritten.** A ✅ on a row
> or a heading means the gap closed on **2026-08-18** — the mining, block-drop, creature-drop and
> loot-table pass. Nothing is deleted, because the *reasoning* under a closed gap is the record of why it
> was built the way it was, and because a closure is a claim that deserves to be checkable against what
> it replaced. **Every ✅ in this file means "built, compiled clean at `/W4`, soaked clean for 45 seconds
> and reviewed"; not one of them means "played".**
>
> ⛔ **THAT LEGEND DOES NOT HOLD FOR ANY ✅ DATED 2026-08-19, AND THE EXCEPTION IS LARGER THAN IT SOUNDS
> — written 10:34.** A hardware throttle stopped all compilation partway through the evening, so
> today's closures were established by **reading, `static_assert` reduction by hand, and graded-control
> greps — never by a build**. Do not upgrade a ✅ to "compiled clean" on the strength of the legend above.
>
> **And the obvious workaround does not work either, which is the part worth knowing.** Comparing a
> source file's mtime against its `.obj` was proposed as a substitute and it is **too weak**: an object
> file proves that translation unit compiled *with its headers as they stood at the object's timestamp*.
> At least eleven headers — `Block.hpp`, `Item.hpp`, `Mining.hpp`, `Survival.hpp`, `Creature.hpp`,
> `WorldStore.hpp`, `Biome.hpp`, `Copper.hpp`, `Player.hpp`, `Inventory.hpp`, `FaceGeometry.hpp` — were
> rewritten after the newest object file in **either** preset, and between them they reach effectively
> every translation unit. **So none of the 122 TU compilations across both presets has evaluated the
> tree as it now stands.** The correct phrasing is *"this edit compiled at T"*, never *"this file is
> verified"* — and today, for the ✅s below, there is no such T.
>
> 🔬 **The object files are present — 122 of them, counted 2026-08-19 11:17** (per preset: 40 game +
> 21 engine = 61, ×2). *This figure read 124 until it was actually counted.* **If you meet a claim
> that the objects are gone, it is finding 9754 and it is refuted**: `Get-ChildItem <game.dir>
> -Filter *.obj` without `-Recurse` returns 0 because CMake nests objects under `game.dir\src\`.
> **Two agents got that zero independently and the agreement proved nothing, because both instruments
> shared the blind spot** — corroboration counts only when the instruments differ. The one-step
> control: run the query against a directory known to hold objects; it returns 0 there too, and **a
> detector that reports absence everywhere is reporting nothing.** The verdict above does not change,
> but its *cause* is newer headers, never missing objects.

> ⛔ **BEFORE YOU RENUMBER OR DELETE A SECTION ID IN THIS FILE — read this.** These `Gn.n` ids are

## How to use this file

**Do not read it end to end. It is ~700 KB and nobody needs all of it.**

1. Read **§0.3 The scoreboard** and **§0.5 The P0 list** below. That is ten minutes and it is the whole
   argument.
2. Pick the section for the area you are about to work on from the generated index above.
3. Inside a section, the ranked gap table comes first and the detail follows, keyed by **gap id**
   (`G7.4`, `G10.2`, …). **Gap ids are stable; line numbers are not — cite the id.**

Each section carries the same shape: what exists today (with `file:line`), a ranked gap table, per-gap
detail with Bedrock's real numbers and a source URL, errors noticed in passing, and sources.

**Effort:** XS (under one session) · S (one) · M (two to three) · L (about a week) · XL (multi-week).
**Priority:** P0 (a core thing is missing or unreachable) · P1 (notable, players expect it) · P2 (depth
and polish) · P3 (nice to have).

## 0.1 The scope this was researched under

Four rulings from the developer, current as of 2026-08-17. **They are why this document looks the way it
does**, and they narrow the work considerably.

- **The overworld only.** The Nether and The End are out of scope, are not on the timeline, and stay off
  it. No agent analysed them. Where an overworld system needs a Nether ingredient, it is noted in one
  line and dropped — that is why brewing, netherite/"Emberite" and a few enchantments carry an asterisk
  rather than a plan.
- **Mojang's assets are permanent.** The repository is private, the game is for personal use, and it will
  not be distributed for play. **The art problem recorded in `audit.md` §3 and §14 is retired** — 987
  textures, 53 skins, 57 sprites, a font, a HUD sheet and 497 sounds are no longer owed to anyone, and
  the friend authoring art is no longer a dependency, a blocker or a risk. **No agent was permitted to
  report missing art as a gap**, and none did. What remains from that analysis is the *packaging*
  question, answered in §0.6.
- **Ray tracing (M30) and global illumination (M32) are parked.** Nothing in this document needs them and
  nothing proposes them. Every visual item in §9 is achievable in the existing rasterised deferred
  pipeline.
- **Redstone signal logic is still not being built** — the player's own earlier decision, unchanged. The
  41-piece kit stays inert on purpose. The one place this genuinely costs something is rails, and §8.5
  proposes the smallest honest divergence rather than a signal engine.

## 0.2 The one-sentence answer

**The engine is finished and the game is half-built: nearly every system that makes a voxel sandbox a
*game* rather than a *world* is either absent, unreachable, or built but never wired to anything.**

The pattern repeats so often that it is the real finding of this pass. It is not that the code is bad —
it is unusually good, and every agent said so independently. It is that **the last wire is missing**, over
and over:

- Brewing is 53 recipes, a screen and a result preview — and the block is not in `isInteractive`, so none
  of it can be opened.
- Armour was 24 pieces with correct Bedrock defence and toughness and `armourDefence` had **zero call
  sites**. ✅ **Closed 2026-08-19, in two steps** — equipment slots, `Inventory::armourSet`,
  `armourDamageTaken` and wear landed at ~06:00, and the last wire landed before 09:57: `Main.cpp`'s
  `hurtPlayer` lambda now takes an `ArmourSet` **with no default**, which is what forces the compiler
  to name every damage site. Five of its six call sites pass `inventory.armourSet()`; the sixth passes
  `kNoArmour` deliberately, because a Harming potion is magic and armour does not touch it. See §0.5
  for the three smaller things still missing (no durability rows, no equip sound, no HUD bar).
- Three status effects have correct `constexpr` helpers — with **zero callers**, so Haste, Jump Boost and
  Slow Falling do nothing.
- Sixteen of 57 sound events are staged, loaded and **never triggered**.
- Fifteen sound recordings are unreachable *by construction* because `SoundMaterial::Coral` is never
  returned and `Ladder` is not an enumerator.
- Rails have all ten of the reference's shapes — and placement only ever emits two, so curves and slopes
  cannot be built.
- The random-tick sampler is exact to Bedrock's 204.8 s/cell — and filters to crops, so nothing else in
  the world ever ticks.

**Seven complete features are one predicate, one call site or one enumerator away from working.** That is
the cheapest work in the project and it is listed first in §0.5.

Cross-confirmation matters — these were found by agents that could not see each other's work.

| Finding | Found by | Where |

| **No experience system of any kind**, blocking enchanting, anvil, grindstone and Mending | **§1, §2, §7** + `Recipe.hpp`'s `repairResult` doc comment (line 116 as of 2026-08-19; the `:123` this replaced was past the end of a 120-line file) says so outright | absent. **Still absent**, and `Sounds.cpp` now files `LevelUp` as `SilentOnPurpose` for exactly this reason — the one event in the enum with no call site, on purpose. |
| ✅ **No loot tables**, so structures would be empty shells even once placed | §5, §6 | **Closed for villages, 2026-08-18** — `world/Loot.hpp`, **11 tables** (weaponsmith, toolsmith, house, mason, fletcher, shepherd, cartographer, armourer, butcher, tannery, temple). Every other structure still has none, and there is no other structure. |
| ✅ **Villager bed/job/bell claims are not saved** — villages die on reload | §4 + `audit.md` §13.3 | **Closed** — `SavedCreature` carries `bedCell`, `jobCell` and `meetCell` at player-record version 4 (`WorldStore.hpp`), and `WorldStore.cpp` records why: a villager that is employed but claims nothing can never work, and a restored village handed out a second armourer. |
| ✅ **Crops never grow at or above y=32** — chunk-local Y passed as world Y | `audit.md` §12.1 + verified directly | **Closed** — `World.cpp`'s random-tick sampler builds a world position on all three axes and says so in-line. |
| ✅ **The unit-mismatch bug shape struck again** — the altitude lapse rate is converted in one file and raw in the other, so snow-capped mountains get rained on | §11 | **Closed** — `Weather.hpp` is the one owner of `kWarmthBaseHeight`/`kWarmthPerBlock` and `Climate.cpp` derives `kLapseBase`/`kLapsePerBlock` from it. |
| ✅ **A table run was forgotten in a second function** — `harvestTier` misses runs 5–6, `blockHardness` misses run 6 | `audit.md` §13.5 + §11 | **Closed structurally, 2026-08-18** — `item/Mining.hpp` is one row per id sized by the enum, so there is no range test left to forget. It was worse than either agent measured: runs 1, 3, 4 and 7 had no `harvestTier` branch at all. |

The last two are the project's own recorded bug shapes #3 and #1 recurring — which is the strongest
available argument for the `selftest=1` startup pass proposed in `audit.md` §14.4.

> **And the fix for the second one is itself worth reading.** Sizing a table by the enum guarantees a row
> exists; it does **not** guarantee anyone chose it. An appended run came out perfectly self-consistent at
> hardness 1.0, no tool, hand tier — and passed all four of the sweep's original invariants. What turns
> that into a build error is a **sentinel** the fall-through returns and a fifth invariant that rejects it.
> That distinction was missed in the first implementation and caught by a reviewer.

## 0.5 The P0 list — what actually blocks the game being a game

Ordered by **value ÷ effort**, not by area. Every id links to its section's detail.

> ⚠️ **Before you pick anything off this list, read this — it is the failure mode of the list itself.**
>
> **The claims most likely to be wrong here are the ones saying something is missing**, and they rot in
> one direction only. A gap gets recorded, somebody closes it, and *nothing tells this document* — so
> entries decay from true to false silently, and always toward "absent" about something present.
> Measured twice on 2026-08-19: a briefing of eight persistence facts was **five wrong, all this way**,
> and six separate "absent" claims checked across the file were **six wrong, none in the other
> direction**. Nothing all session has claimed something exists when it did not. **So: check the entry
> in source before you build it.** One bare-name grep costs a minute; a duplicated feature costs a
> session, and there are eleven agents reading this page.
>
> **Search for the data, not for the accessor.** Powder snow read as "nothing places it" because
> `TerrainGenerator.cpp` and `Structures.cpp` both return **0** — the placement is two rows in the
> *biome table*. A sweep of the files where you expect the code to live is the sweep that confirms a
> stale claim. Likewise a bare substring lies: `ride` returns 25 hits in `Creature.cpp` and every one is
> `override` or `stride`, while `BeeNest` returns 0 because the id is built as `beeNestAtLevel`.
> **Use word boundaries, and ask how the value would look if it were computed rather than named.**
>
> 🔬 **And the rule that applies to *every entry in this file*, because every entry is an absence
> claim: an absence claim can never have a same-symbol *claim* control.** Its whole content is that
> there is nothing there to measure, so varying the subject cannot help. **It therefore takes four
> things — 2026-08-19:**
>
> - **⓪ Is this token the only way the concept could be spelled?** *No control can answer this*, and
>   it is where most wrong absence claims die. A `BeeNest` claim carried **two flawless controls** and
>   was still false, because the id is built by **`beeNestAtLevel`**. Also killed
>   `ChainmailHelmet + piece`, sixteen `CreatureKind` by index cast, seventeen `BiomeId` by
>   `static_cast`, and `familyRoughness` through a packed row. **Ask how the value would look if it
>   were *computed* rather than named.**
> - **① A same-symbol probe in a different file where the token is known to appear.** This is the
>   **strongest** evidence an absence claim can have, because it alone proves the detector sees *that
>   exact token*. (**An instrument control is defined by having a KNOWN EXPECTED ANSWER, not by using
>   a different symbol** — ① is same-symbol and an instrument control both.)
> - **② A different-symbol, same-file probe**, including a name invented on the spot that must
>   return 0, so a zero on the subject carries information.
> - **③ The probe count, computed from the results — never narrated.** A hardcoded
>   `Probes landed: 3 of 4` inside a demonstration of this very rule read 2 of 4 in reality.
> - **④ For a *behavioural* absence, follow the data, not just the name.** A control proves the
>   detector works; only tracing the gate proves the behaviour cannot occur.
>
> *Worked example, used to re-evidence the `VoidPearl` row: ⓪ case-insensitive `pearl` = **0** in all
> three producer files; ① `VoidPearl` = 1/1/1 in three known-positive files, **3 of 3 landed**;
> ② `Diamond` 3, `Bone` 14, invented name 0, **2 of 4 landed**; ④ the one computed `ItemId` in those
> files is `ChainmailHelmet + piece` with `piece` in `[0,3]`, pinned contiguous by an adjacent
> `static_assert`, so it **cannot** yield the subject.* **Two bare zeros are not evidence** — two
> agents lost 122 object files that way. **The one-question diagnostic: *if this control came out the
> other way, would the CLAIM be false, or the INSTRUMENT broken?*** — first means same-symbol, second
> means known-answer, **a control answering neither is vacuous however true its numbers**, and
> **its blind spot is ⓪, where the answer is *neither*: claim false, instrument perfect.**
>
> **The search term that beats "no caller": `"one call site short"` — this project's own name for the
> failure.** It works because **the author who fears a bug names it**, and anyone writing about an
> unwired feature in this codebase reaches for the house phrase. Sweep its neighbours too: `one call
> site`, `nothing reads`, `built but`, `dormant`, `unreachable`, `still empty`. *Run against these
> twelve documents on 2026-08-19 it returned 9 / 7 / 3 / 4 / 66 / 1.*
>
> **And the class no negative-word search can find: a spec written in the IMPERATIVE.** *"For each cell,
> read the block… write `beeHomeAtLevel(id, level + 1)`"* — every sentence true, nothing false, and it
> never says the requirement is unmet. **A spec in the imperative mood is a negative claim containing
> no negative words**, so *not / never / missing / TODO* cannot reach it. A reader honours it, and now
> two writers raise one honey level. Sweep for **instruction-shaped** text — *"write"*, *"add"*, *"the
> fix is"*, *"needs a"*, *"should call"* — and for each, **check whether it is already done.**
> *Measured 2026-08-19: this is a **header/comment** problem, not a documents problem — `GAPS.md`
> carries 307 negative-word claims against ~2 imperative specs, because a gap list states gaps as
> facts. Hunt the imperative in `.hpp` files, and the negative claim here.*
>
> **And when this list is wrong, the entry is often missing rather than stale — see G5.25.** The test
> that finds those: **ask it of a *property*, not a *feature*.** "If persistence were entirely absent,
> would this document say so, and under which heading?" **A feature always has a section; a property
> usually does not** — which is exactly how the worst data-loss bug in the tree went unrecorded until
> 2026-08-19.

## 0.6 The packaging and asset-location decision

The developer's ruling: *"i might as well have the textures accessible outside of the assets folder so the
game can be packaged or whatever when we first package it."* Here is the measurement that makes that easy.

Everything the game loads at runtime, measured today beside `build\release\bin`:

| Staged content | Files | Size |
|---|---|---|
| `blocks-reference/` (every block and item texture) | 1,354 | **0.40 MB** |
| `sounds-reference/` | 519 | **31.64 MB** |
| `spawn-eggs/` | 58 | 0.01 MB |
| `creatures-reference.png` · `hud-reference.png` · `font-reference.png` | 3 | 0.12 MB |
| `assets/` (our own, copied by CMake) | 133 | 0.07 MB |
| **Total the game actually needs to run** | **2,067** | **≈32.2 MB** |

**The textures are 0.5 MB. The whole runtime payload is 32 MB, and 98% of that is sound.** That is small
enough to stop treating reference art as a regenerable build artefact.

**The recommendation** (not implemented — this round is documentation only):

1. Promote the staged output to a tracked, first-class content directory — e.g. `content/` at the repo
   root, holding `blocks/`, `sounds/`, `spawn-eggs/`, `creatures.png`, `hud.png`, `font.png`.
2. Have CMake copy `content/` beside the executable exactly as it already copies `assets/`
   (`game/CMakeLists.txt:53`), so a build is self-contained.
3. `run.ps1` then stops regenerating six things on every launch, and the **662 MB `reference/` folder
   becomes optional** — needed only by `tools/check-models.ps1` and future extraction, not to play.
4. Packaging becomes "zip the `bin` folder", which is the whole of M35's asset story.

**Cost:** about 32 MB added to an 11 MB repository. **Benefit:** the game becomes runnable from a clone,
the art stops being able to go stale against the sheet it was composited from (a failure that has already
cost one session), and the layered `assets/` → reference fallback in `Main.cpp:1017` can eventually
collapse to one path.

> **Note on `audit.md`:** §3, §9.1, §14.1, §14.2 and §14.7 of that document argue at length about original
> art, the friend's schedule, and shipping legality. **Those sections are now obsolete** and are kept only
> so the reasoning is not lost. The `hud.png` "highest-risk file" warning and the packaging *gate* it
> proposed are retired with them. The loose PNGs in git history are no longer a distribution risk; they
> remain merely untidy.

## 0.8 What the consolidation pass found that was not in this document

**2026-08-18.** Six gaps that the original nineteen-section pass did not see, every one of them turned
up by *fixing* something else. That is the pattern worth naming: **five of the six were invisible from
the outside and became visible the moment a neighbouring wire was connected.** Wiring Night Vision is
what exposed Invisibility; wiring the effects made the absence of an effects display matter; building
the honeycomb shear is what showed that breaking the hive still leads nowhere. *(⚠️ 2026-08-19: that
third example was demoted at 09:59 — the shear branch existed but its guard could never be true — and
**reinstated at 10:23**, when `Main.cpp` gained the drain that fills a hive. The example survives and
is now stronger: the shear is what made the missing drain visible, which is exactly the claim. Both
the demotion and the reinstatement were correct at the minute they were written; see G6.17.)*

Each was re-verified against the tree before being written here. Line numbers are omitted on purpose —
cite the id.

### G7.23 · Invisibility brews, is drinkable, splashable, throwable and tippable — and nothing reads it

**Eight item ids** produce Invisibility (potion, extended potion, and the splash, lingering and arrow
forms of both), it is granted correctly through the one owner in `Main.cpp`, `Effects` stores it, and
**not one line of the game asks whether it is running.** It is the only *live* hole of its kind left:
Night Vision was the other and is now read by `setSunLighting`.

**The fix is not the one `Effects.hpp` describes.** Its note says Invisibility "skips drawing the
player and held item" — and there is no player model and no first-person hand in this game, so there
is nothing to skip. What is left is entirely `Creature.cpp`'s: it already shortens its notice range for
a crouched player, and invisibility is the same multiplier on the same number. **Effort XS.**

> **Four more effects are inert and are deliberately *not* on this list.** Nausea, Blindness, Health
> Boost and Saturation have no reader either — but they also have **no grant path anywhere**, no potion,
> no food row, no command. An effect nothing can produce is not a hole a player can fall into, and
> calling it one inflates the count. Nausea and Blindness want a post-process the renderer does not
> have; Health Boost and Saturation are `Survival.hpp` numbers. They become real the day something
> grants them, and the cheapest of those days is the pufferfish.

### G7.24 · There is no effects HUD, and the read side of the API has never had a caller

`Effects::all` and `Effects::count` — the pair a display would enumerate through — have **zero runtime
callers**, and `count` is kept honest only by a compile-time sweep at the foot of its own header.
`secondsLeft` has exactly one caller and it is not a display: `Player.cpp` reads it to decide whether an
absorption pool has been re-granted.

So a player can be running Strength, Regeneration, Fire Resistance and Slow Falling at once with **no
way to know it, no icon, no timer, and no cue when one expires.** Every potion in the game is drunk
blind. This is the single most-felt consequence of §2's 35%, and it belongs with the hunger and health
bars in `Main.cpp` rather than in `Effects.hpp` — which already says so in its own comment. **Effort S**,
and it is worth more per line than anything else in §7 now that armour is wired (2026-08-19) and only
its `hurtPlayer` argument is left.

### G6.16 · The void pearl has no source, so the throw path is dead code and the ender chest is uncraftable

`ItemId::VoidPearl` appears in exactly **four** places in `game/src`: its enumerator, a projectile
flight profile, a throw-and-teleport branch in `Main.cpp` gated behind a cooldown, and the ender chest
recipe. **Nothing drops it, no loot table contains it, no villager trades it and no recipe makes it.**
The whole teleport feature is reachable only by handing yourself one in creative.

**The root cause is a missing species, not a missing drop row.** `CreatureKind` has 58 entries and
**there is no analogue of the reference's tall black teleporting mob at all** — `Voidmite` is this
project's name for the *endermite*, which is a different creature that drops nothing. So this is not a
one-line table fix: it is a species, a rig, a skin, a teleport behaviour and a drop. **Effort L**, and
it is the reason a whole crafted block cannot be obtained.

### G6.17 · Breaking a bee hive angers no bees, because that needs Silk Touch, and there are no enchantments

⚠️ **This entry was corrected twice in twenty-four minutes on 2026-08-19, and the round trip is the
useful part — read both corrections before acting.**

**09:59 — first correction, and it was right at the time.** The entry's first sentence read
"Shearing a hive now yields three honeycomb, which closed the item's source gap." The *branch* exists
(`Main.cpp`, guarded by `beehiveHasHoney` and commented "the only source of honeycomb in the game"),
but its guard could never be true: natural nests generate at honey level 0 on purpose, bees queue
their home cell after pollinating, and `Creatures::takePollinated` had **no consumer anywhere** — so
no hive reached level 1, and honeycomb, every waxed copper form, every candle and the honeycomb
block were unobtainable in survival. Established with a graded control (`takeGrazed` and `takeVoices`
both reach `Main.cpp`; `takePollinated` did not; a fabricated name scored 0).

✅ **10:23 — second correction: the drain landed and the 09:59 paragraph is now history.**
`Main.cpp` iterates `creatures.takePollinated()`, re-reads each cell's id, skips anything that is no
longer a hive, skips full hives, and writes `beeHomeAtLevel(home, level + 1)`. **Honeycomb has a
source again**, and so do waxed copper, the seventeen candles and the honeycomb block.
> ⚠️ **Unverified by build, and the mtime shortcut does not rescue it** — `Main.cpp` source is
> 10:23:32 and the newest object file is 09:56:27 (debug, `Main.cpp.obj`) / **09:55:25** (release,
> `Creature.cpp.obj`), so this has never compiled. *(That release figure read 09:52:01 here until
> 2026-08-19 11:17, when it was re-measured; the objects were never in doubt — see below.)*
> **Nor would `src < obj` have proved anything if it had held:** an object file only
> proves its translation unit compiled with its headers *as they stood at the object's timestamp*,
> and `Creature.hpp`, `Block.hpp` and `Item.hpp` — all of which this code reaches — are newer than
> every object in either preset. Code-complete and unproven, **not absent**.
>
> 🔬 **The objects exist: 40 per preset, counted 2026-08-19 11:17. If you read anywhere that they are
> gone, that is finding 9754 and it is refuted.** Two agents independently reported zero because
> `Get-ChildItem <game.dir> -Filter *.obj` **without `-Recurse`** cannot see them — CMake nests them
> one level down under `game.dir\src\`, so the flat listing sees a lone directory and returns 0.
> **The agreement of those two zeros proved nothing, because both instruments shared one blind spot**
> — corroboration only counts when the instruments differ. *The control that settles it in one step:
> point the same query at a directory you know holds objects; it returns 0 there too, and a detector
> that reports absence everywhere is reporting nothing.* **The conclusion above is unchanged — nothing
> here is verified — but the reason is newer headers, not missing objects.**

> ⭐ **The lesson is not about bees.** A negative claim, correctly measured with a sound control, went
> stale in **thirty-two minutes** because seven agents were writing at once. `CLAUDE.md`'s rule —
> *date a negative claim and name what would make it false* — is what made this recoverable: the
> 09:59 stamp is the only reason anyone thought to re-measure. **Put a clock on every "nothing calls
> this", and re-check the clock before acting on one.** What would make *this* correction false in
> turn: the loop being removed, or the build failing on it.

**The entry's actual subject is still open**, and is unaffected by any of the above: breaking a hive
angers no bees, because that behaviour is gated on Silk Touch and there are no enchantments.

**Breaking** a hive is a separate half and is unchanged: in the reference, breaking a hive without
Silk Touch releases and angers every bee inside it, and breaking one *with* Silk Touch keeps them. With
no enchantment system the choice does not exist, so the outcome can only be "always angry" or "never
angry", and `Main.cpp` says so in-line and picks nothing. **This is an enchanting dependency, not a bee
bug** — filed here because it is the first concrete gameplay consequence of §7's "no experience
system", rather than a transitive one.

### G10.19 · Lava has no movement model, and unlike water it never seeks a hole

Two independent halves, both of them absences rather than bugs:

- **The player falls through lava at air speed.** `Player.cpp` reads `inLava` three times and every one
  of them is about damage or burning — the burn timer, the fire-resistance escape, the "already in it"
  exclusion. There is no buoyancy, no drag, no reduced swim speed and no slowed fall. Water has all
  four. Bedrock's lava is the slowest fluid in the game and ours is the fastest.
- **Flowing lava never searches for somewhere to fall.** `World::slopeDistance` exists, is correct, and
  is called only from the water update. `updateLava` picks its level from the neighbour supply and
  spreads evenly, so a lava pool one block from a shaft spreads *away* from it as readily as into it.

Filed together because they are the same shape as the project's own recorded bug #14 — *a rule that
exists, is correct, and is commented, in only one of the two places that need it* — and because lava's
spread, obsidian formation, ignition scan and cooling rules are otherwise complete and faithful.
**Effort S for the movement half, M for the slope search.**

### G5.23 · `World::saveAll` returns `void`, so a failed chunk write cannot reach the caller

`saveAll` is the shutdown flush, and it cannot report anything. A disk-full, a permission failure or a
locked file is retried on the next unload pass and then silently dropped, and `saveEverything` above it
has no way to know a chunk did not land — so the game exits reporting success on a world it did not
finish writing.

Everything under it is careful: one file per chunk, temp-and-rename, a retry queue, and a documented
last-go at `saveAll`. **It is only the return type that is missing**, which is why it is here rather
than in `audit.md` — nothing is broken, the failure signal was simply never given anywhere to go.
Persistence has no home section in this document; it is filed under §5 because a chunk file is what
fails. **Effort XS.**

### G5.25 · Gaps that are *missing* rather than *stale* — the structural bias in this document

**A stale entry gets refuted the next time somebody reads it. A missing entry is never evaluated.**
G5.24 existed as a bug for weeks and as an *entry* for minutes, and the reason is structural rather
than anybody's oversight: **this document is organised by what exists.** Every section takes a system
the game has and asks what is incomplete about it. **A thing that was never built has no system to be
filed under**, so it has no natural home, and the more completely something is absent the less likely
it is to appear here at all. That is exactly backwards, and naming it is worth more than any single
entry it explains.

**The tell is a section whose scope is a *file* or a *class* rather than a *player-visible outcome*.**
`G5.23` names it out loud — *"Persistence has no home section in this document"* — and it was filed
under §5 only because a chunk file is what fails. Persistence is not a system the game has; it is a
property every system needs. **Categories like that are where missing entries hide.**

**The check that finds them, and it is cheap:** take a major system and ask **"if this were entirely
absent, would this document say so, and under which heading?"** If the answer is "nowhere obvious",
that heading is missing, not the feature. Ask it of properties rather than of features — persistence,
failure reporting, cross-screen consistency, what happens on a torn file — because a *feature* always
has a section and a *property* usually does not.

**The dormant categories, collected here because no single section owns them.** Each is a block of
content that exists in the tables and cannot be reached in play, and each is dormant for a *decided*
reason rather than an unfinished one — so none of them is a gap, and all of them look like one to a
grep:

| Category | Size | Why it is dormant, and whether that can change |
|---|---|---|
| **Redstone ids** | ~400 | There is no redstone signal engine, by decision (`DECISIONS.md`). Not a gap. |
| **Silk-Touch-only blocks** | 39 | No enchanting, so no Silk Touch. Unblocks if enchanting lands. |
| **XP-gated content** | — | No XP system; `SoundEvent::LevelUp` is the one staged event with no trigger, for this reason. |
| **`ChorusPlant`, `PoppedChorusFruit`, and the End/Nether item run** | — | **Permanently unreachable by direct user ruling** — the overworld is the whole game and the End and Nether are deliberately absent from `TIMELINE.md`. **This will not change**, so do not file these as gaps, plan a portal, or add a "general" dimension stack. |

**Why this table matters more than it looks:** every one of these will read as "built but unreachable"
to the bare-name sweep that correctly finds real instances of `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #15. **Without a
list of the deliberate ones, every audit re-discovers them and re-files them**, and the real
one-call-site-short bugs get harder to see for the noise. *Compiled 2026-08-19; the chorus ruling is
the user's own and is not subject to re-litigation by a later audit.*

> ⏳ **Every row above except the chorus one is a measurement with a timestamp, not a property of the

### G5.26 · The persistence register — everything that must survive a quit, in one place

**This is the home section `G5.23` says does not exist.** Its absence is why G5.24 could go unrecorded:
a document organised by *what exists* has nowhere to file *what was never built*, so a whole category
of gap has no natural home and is invisible until someone trips over it. **Every row below was read
out of the source on 2026-08-19; none was taken from a briefing** — see the warning at the end, which
is the most useful thing on this page.

| What | State | Where it lives | Falsifier |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Chunk blocks** | ✅ Saved | one file per chunk, temp-and-rename, retry queue; `kChunkFormatVersion = 8` | version ≠ 8 |
| **Player position, health, hunger, XP** | ✅ Saved | `SavedPlayer`, `player.dat` | — |
| **Inventory, including the cursor stack and the crafting grid** | ✅ Saved | folded into a `carried` copy, then `saved.inventory[i] = carried.slot(i)` | that assignment reading `inventory` instead of `carried` |
| **Worn armour** | ✅ Saved | `SavedPlayer::armour`, read from `inventory` **not** `carried` (deliberate — armour is a separate array with a separate restore) | — |
| **Status effects and absorption** | ✅ Saved | `SavedEffect`, proved on hand-built bytes | — |
| **Respawn point** | ✅ Saved | `SavedPlayer::respawnBed` | — |
| **Time of day** | ✅ Saved | `SavedPlayer::timeOfDay`; save and load both present | either call site disappearing |
| **Weather** | ✅ Saved — 🔴 **but see the join defect below** | four fields — `weatherRaining`, `weatherThundering`, and the two `…Seconds`; **exactly the four `Weather` cannot recompute** | a fifth weather field appearing |
| **Creatures** | ✅ Saved | `SavedCreature`; markers relocated after the header so a tear no longer re-breeds the world | — |
| **Dropped items** | ✅ **Saved — closed 2026-08-19** | `SavedItem`; `world.store().loadDrops()` restore loop and `wrote(world.store().saveDrops(savedDrops), "drops")`, both gated `if (!settings.dropShowcase)` | either name *disappearing* from `Main.cpp`, or a second writer of `drops.dat` — see **G5.24** |
| **Furnace contents** | ✅ Saved | `PlacedFurnace` | — |
| **Failure reporting** | ⛔ Partial | `World::saveAll` returns `void` — see **G5.23** | the return type changing |

**Two design rulings worth not re-litigating**, both argued at length in `WorldStore.hpp`:

- **World state rides in `player.dat` and there is deliberately no `level.dat`.** Time of day and weather
  are world state filed under the player, on the reasoning that the split exists because N players share
  one world — and **multiplayer is permanently cut (`CLAUDE.md`), so N is 1 forever.** The header names its
  own revisit trigger: *the second* piece of true world state (a game-rule table, a difficulty, a world
  border), at which point `level.dat` earns its keep and the fields move — a migration the rung machinery
  already handles. **Do not add a `level.dat` for a single float.**
- **Ramps are not saved, flags are.** `Weather` keeps eleven members; five are presentation ramps that chase
  the flags at 0.2/s. Saving one would freeze a presentation detail into the format and give the next reader
  **two sources for one fact** (bug shape #1). Not saving costs a five-second fade-in on load, once.

**The version ladder is self-defending.** `SavedPlayer` runs **2…8 contiguous**, and a `static_assert` chain
pins every rung to its predecessor *and* the newest to `kFormatVersion`, so **bumping the version fails to
build until the next rung constant is declared.** That is the pattern to copy: it makes the *format bump*,
not the reader's diligence, the thing that cannot be forgotten.

> ⚠️ **The methodological warning, and it is the reason this table is written the way it is.** This section
> was commissioned from a briefing listing eight persistence facts. **Five of the eight were stale, all in
> the same direction — describing as absent things that now exist**: time of day, weather, the cursor stack
> at quit, worn armour, and the chunk format version (said to be "about to go 7→8"; it was already 8). The
> ladder was described as v7; it is v8. **Had the briefing been transcribed, this page would have been born
> with five brand-new false "absent" claims in the one document agents read to pick work** — the exact
> failure this file exists to prevent, manufactured by the act of documenting. Only **one** briefing item —
> dropped items — survived checking, and it is the one row here marked ⛔.
>
> **So: a persistence claim is cheap to check and expensive to guess.** Every row above names the falsifier
> that would refute it. **Re-read the source, never a summary of it — including this one.** *Register
> compiled 2026-08-19 10:52 and unverified by any build; no compilation tonight has evaluated the tree as
> it stands.*

## 1. Crafting, smelting and workstations

**Scope:** Overworld crafting grids, the recipe table, smelting (furnace / blast furnace / smoker / campfire) and every workstation block that is not a pure container — measured against Bedrock Edition.

**Headline verdict:** The *matcher* is finished and correct; the *content* around it is not. 1,152 recipes sounds close to complete, but roughly 900 of them are generated repetitions of about eight patterns (240 cut shapes, 256 stowbox re-dyes, ~190 colour recipes, ~154 per-wood, 70 tools) — the number of distinct hand-written recipe *ideas* is nearer 130, and whole categories that Bedrock has are absent: no bread, no boats, no minecarts, no cake, no item frame, no painting, no armour stand, and no recipe for eleven of the workstation blocks that already exist as placeable blocks. Smelting is a single 10-second timer, a 22-row recipe table and a three-row fuel table, with no XP and no input restriction on the smoker or blast furnace. Of sixteen Bedrock overworld workstations, seven do something, one (the brewing stand) has a complete 53-row implementation that **cannot be reached because `isInteractive` does not list the block**, and eight are inert scenery. The anvil and grindstone share one function — combine two damaged items — which is about a fifth of what either does in Bedrock, and the rest of both is blocked on there being no experience system anywhere in the game.

**Completeness estimate:** Roughly **55%** of Bedrock's overworld crafting, smelting and workstation behaviour. Split: crafting grid mechanics ~90%, recipe breadth ~65%, smelting ~45%, workstations ~30%.

---

### 1.1 What exists today

| Feature | State | Where it lives (file:line) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2×2 and 3×3 grids, one matcher | **Full** | `Recipe.hpp:14`, `Recipe.cpp:1116` | Pattern stored at its own size; matcher compares against the bounding box of filled cells, so a 1×2 recipe works in any column. Grid size is an argument, so a table is a layout change only. |
| Shaped matching | **Full** | `Recipe.cpp:1070-1081` | Does **not** mirror. Stairs compensate by declaring both hands (`Recipe.cpp:783-796`). |
| Shapeless matching | **Full** | `Recipe.cpp:1083-1113` | Counts leftovers, so an extra item in the grid refuses rather than being eaten. |
| Recipe table (1,152; 521 fit 2×2) | **Partial** | `Recipe.cpp:239-1030` | Mostly loop-generated. See §1.2 for what is missing. |
| "Craftable now?" query | **Full** | `Recipe.cpp:1156-1213` | Greedy count, correct only while no ingredient names a set — documented in place. |
| Recipe book / catalogue | **Stub** | `InventoryScreen.cpp:729-741`, `Main.cpp:3714-3746` | Shows every item, tints craftable green / uncraftable red. **In survival, clicking does nothing** — the whole handler is gated on `creative`. No unlocking, no toasts, no fill-the-grid. |
| Furnace | **Partial** | `Furnace.cpp:31-71`, `Smelting.hpp:9` | Flat `kSmeltSeconds = 10.0f` for every recipe. Fuel lit only when there is work. Progress rewinds at 2× when starved. Persists to `furnaces.dat`. **No XP.** |
| Smelting recipe table | **Partial** | `Smelting.cpp:15-40` | 22 explicit rows, plus generated raw-food→cooked (`Item.hpp:1095`) and 16 terracotta→glazed (`Smelting.cpp:70-80`). Six of the 22 rows are Nether-only content that never generates. |
| Fuel table | **Stub** | `Smelting.cpp:55-58, 90-104` | Three rows (coal 80 s, charcoal 80 s, stick 5 s) plus one blanket rule: any log, planks or flammable cut shape = 15 s. |

### 1.3 Gap detail

#### G1.1 — Brewing stand is placeable but cannot be opened · XS · P0
- **Bedrock behaviour:** right-clicking a brewing stand opens a three-bottle, one-ingredient, one-fuel screen; brewing takes 400 ticks (20 s) per operation and burns one of a blaze powder's 20 charges. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Brewing]
- **What we have:** the whole brewing *table* is built and correct — `kBrews` is 53 rows transcribed from Mojang's `brew_*.json` (`Recipe.cpp:1232-1343`), plus the gunpowder→splash and dragon's-breath→lingering rules, and 41 potions × 4 forms in `Item.hpp`. `Main.cpp:4409-4417` has a branch that would set `openScreen = Kind::SmithingTable` with `openBench = BrewingStand`, and `Main.cpp:2919-2925` and `3493-3502` both already route that bench to `brewingResult`. **But the entire if-chain is guarded by `game::isInteractive(...)` at `Main.cpp:4375`, and `isInteractive` (`Block.hpp:2825-2831`) lists CraftingTable, SmithingTable, furnaces, chests, hoppers, Grindstone, Anvil, Stonecutter, ChippedAnvil and DamagedAnvil — and not BrewingStand.** The branch is unreachable.
- **What must be built:** add `|| id == BlockId::BrewingStand` to `isInteractive`. That is the whole fix for reachability. Then, separately: three bottle slots instead of one (the shared bench screen has two input slots), and a decision on whether to keep the named divergence of instant brewing (documented at `Recipe.hpp:110-118` and `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` "Effects, potions and brewing").
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock brew time 400 ticks = 20 s. Blaze powder = 20 brewing charges. Overworld-only potions are **Weakness** (water + fermented spider eye) and the **Mundane** junk base; awkward potion needs nether wart, so every effect potion is Nether-gated in Bedrock — ours is not, because the reagents are simply items here.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` currently asserts "The stand borrows the smithing screen, because both are two inputs and a previewed result" — that documents intent, not the shipped build. Verify by placing one before and after.

#### G1.2 — The basic food chain has no recipes and no sources · S · P0
- **Bedrock behaviour:** bread = 3 wheat (shaped row, 1 output); cookie = 2 wheat + 1 cocoa beans → 8; pumpkin pie = pumpkin + sugar + egg → 1; golden apple = 8 gold ingots around 1 apple; cake = 3 milk + 2 sugar + 1 egg + 3 wheat; honey bottle = 4 glass bottles on a full beehive. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Crafting]
- **What we have:** `ItemId::Bread`, `GoldenApple`, `PumpkinPie`, `EnchantedGoldenApple`, `HoneyBottle` and `Egg` all exist and all carry hunger/saturation values (`Survival.hpp:166-226`). **None of Bread, GoldenApple or PumpkinPie appears anywhere in `Recipe.cpp`, in a loot table, or in a mob drop.** Grep across `game/src` finds `ItemId::Bread` only in `Item.hpp`, `Farming.hpp` (compost chance) and `Survival.hpp` (food value). The cookie recipe *does* exist (`Recipe.cpp:944-947`) but needs `ItemId::CocoaBeans`, which has no source either. `BlockId::Cake` does not exist at all.
- **What must be built:** four one-line recipes (bread, golden apple, pumpkin pie, honey bottle) plus a cocoa-bean source (jungle-log cocoa pods, or accept the existing brown-mushroom stand-in for dye and give cocoa a loot source). Cake needs a new block with 7 bite states and a milk bucket item.
- **Numbers that matter:** bread 3 wheat → 1; cookie 2 wheat + 1 cocoa → **8**; golden apple **8 ingots** (not nuggets) → 1; glistering melon **8 nuggets** → 1 (this one is already correct at `Recipe.cpp:522`); pumpkin pie 1 pumpkin + 1 sugar + 1 egg → 1.
- **Risks / dependencies:** bread is a compostable at 85% (`Farming.hpp:159`) and a food at `Survival.hpp:166`, so the item is fully wired — only the recipe row is missing. This is the cheapest P0 in the list.

#### G1.3 — Eleven workstations and ~25 utility items have no recipe · M · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour / recipes:** blast furnace = 5 iron + furnace + 3 **smooth stone**; loom = 2 string over 2 planks; cartography table = 2 paper over 4 planks; fletching table = 2 flint over 4 planks; anvil = 3 iron blocks + 4 ingots (**31 iron**); campfire = 3 sticks + 1 coal/charcoal + 3 logs; enchanting table = 1 book + 2 diamonds + 4 obsidian; beacon = 5 glass + nether star + 3 obsidian [Nether dependency, one line]; conduit = 8 nautilus shells + 1 heart of the sea; chiselled bookshelf = 6 planks + 3 wooden slabs; flower pot = 3 bricks. Transport: boat = 5 planks → 1; chest boat = boat + chest; minecart = 5 iron; chest/furnace/hopper/TNT minecart = minecart + the block. Utility: item frame = 8 sticks + 1 leather; painting = 8 sticks + 1 wool; armour stand = 6 sticks + 1 smooth stone slab; target = 4 redstone + 1 hay bale; scaffolding = 6 bamboo + 1 string → 6; tinted glass = 4 amethyst shards + 1 glass → 2; packed mud = mud + wheat; mud bricks = 4 packed mud. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Crafting]
- **What we have:** every one of those blocks except Cake, DecoratedPot and Crafter already exists as a `BlockId` with textures, hardness, blast resistance and a catalogue entry — `BlastFurnace` at `Block.hpp:832`, `Loom` 833, `CartographyTable` 829, `FletchingTable` 830, `Anvil` 840, `Campfire` 896, `EnchantingTable` 827, `Beacon` 929, `Conduit` 930, `ChiseledBookshelf` 828, `FlowerPot` 844, `Scaffolding` 843, `TintedGlass` 928, `Target` 576, `PackedMud` 364, `MudBricks` 365. A grep for each of those names in `Recipe.cpp` returns **zero hits**. There are no boat, minecart, item frame, painting or armour stand items in `Item.hpp` at all.
- **What must be built:** roughly 20 recipe rows for the blocks that already exist (cheap), plus new items for boats (11 wood families ×2 with chest boats = 22 items), minecarts (5), item frame, glow item frame, painting and armour stand — each of which needs an entity or a placeable, not just an icon.
- **Numbers that matter:** blast furnace needs smooth stone, which we can already smelt (`Smelting.cpp:19`). Anvil is 31 iron. Boat yield 1 from 5 planks; **bamboo raft** rather than a boat for the bamboo family; bamboo planks are **2** per block of bamboo, not 4.
- **Risks / dependencies:** boats and minecarts are entities and belong with the transport/entity section; the *recipes* are trivial once the items exist. Do the eleven block recipes first — they are one afternoon and they turn eleven pieces of scenery into obtainable blocks.

#### G1.4 — Fuel table is three rows plus one blanket rule · XS · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Smelting#Fuel] — lava bucket 20 000 ticks (100 items), block of coal 16 000 (80), dried kelp block 4 000 (20), coal/charcoal 1 600 (8), any boat 1 200 (6), logs/wood/planks/stairs/slabs/fences/gates/pressure plates/trapdoors/ladders/crafting table/chest/barrel/bookshelf/lectern/composter/loom/cartography/fletching/smithing table/jukebox/note block/daylight detector/banner/fishing rod 300 (1.5), bow/crossbow/doors/signs/hanging signs/wooden tools/bowl 200 (1), wooden buttons/saplings/sticks/dead bush/azalea 100 (0.5), bamboo/scaffolding 50 (0.25). **Wool and wool carpet are NOT fuel in Bedrock** (Java-only).
- **What we have:** `kFuels` (`Smelting.cpp:55-58`) is exactly three rows — coal 80 s, charcoal 80 s, stick 5 s — and `fuelBurnSeconds` (`Smelting.cpp:90-104`) falls back to a flat **15 s for any log, planks, or shaped block that answers `isFlammable`**.
- **What must be built:** a real fuel table with the four tiers (15 s / 10 s / 5 s / 2.5 s) plus the four big-ticket entries. Keep the shape-driven fallback for the 15-second tier — it is the right design and covers ~600 cut shapes — but add explicit rows above and below it.
- **Numbers that matter:** at `kSmeltSeconds = 10.0f`, one item = 10 s, so seconds map to items 1:10. Lava bucket 1 000 s, coal block 800 s, dried kelp block 200 s, boat 60 s, log/planks 15 s ✓ (ours is already right), door/sign/bow/bowl/wooden tool 10 s, button/sapling/stick/dead bush 5 s ✓ (stick is right), bamboo/scaffolding 2.5 s.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the fallback currently makes **wool carpets fuel** (they are `isShapedBlock` and their parent wool is `isFlammable`), which Bedrock does not. It also makes wooden buttons and pressure plates burn 3× too long and doors 1.5× too long. Wooden tools burn for 0 s because they are not block items and are not listed.

#### G1.6 — Smoker and blast furnace accept every smeltable · XS · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** blast furnace takes raw metals, ore blocks, and iron/gold/copper/chainmail tools and armour — and nothing else. Smoker takes food only (including potato and kelp). Both run at 100 ticks per item and burn fuel 2× fast, so items-per-fuel is unchanged. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Blast_Furnace] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Smoker]
- **What we have:** `cookSpeed` (`Block.hpp:2806-2809`) returns 2.0 for both and 1.0 otherwise, applied to the whole tick (`Main.cpp:5850`) — that half is exactly right and well reasoned. But `tickFurnace` (`Furnace.cpp:31`) calls `canCook` → `smeltResult(input)` with no knowledge of which cooker it is in, so **any smeltable works in any of the three**.
- **What must be built:** pass the cooker's `BlockId` into `tickFurnace` (or a small enum), and gate `canCook` on a `acceptsInput(cooker, item)` predicate. `isRawFood` and `isFood` already exist for the smoker half; the blast furnace half needs an `isSmeltableMetal(item)` predicate.
- **Numbers that matter:** 100 ticks = 5 s per item in both. Our 10 s ÷ 2 = 5 s ✓.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the same predicate has to be asked by the screen's shift-click target, or shift-clicking cobblestone into a smoker will still put it in the input slot where it sits forever.

#### G1.7 — No smelting XP · S · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** the furnace keeps a hidden accumulating XP counter. XP is awarded **only when a player manually removes items from the output slot**, and the counter then resets; a hopper extracting still banks it; breaking the furnace drops all banked XP. Fractional XP: `total = value × items_removed`, integer part awarded, the fraction is the probability of one more, remainder stays in the block. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Smelting#Recipes]
- **What we have:** nothing. There is no experience anywhere in the codebase — a grep of `Main.cpp` for `experience`, `xp` or `enchant` returns only texture filenames.
- **What must be built:** an XP system belongs to the survival-systems section and should be scoped there. Within this section the work is: an `xpFor(ItemId input)` table (the values in G1.5's table above), a `float bankedXp` field on `Furnace`, awarding it in the output-slot take path (`Main.cpp:3480+`), dropping it on break, and a `static_assert` that every smeltable has an XP value.
- **Numbers that matter:** iron/copper/redstone 0.7; gold/diamond/emerald 1.0; lapis 0.2; coal 0.1; food 0.35 (**kelp 0.1**); clay ball 0.3; clay block 0.35; wet sponge 0.15; charcoal 0.15; cactus/sea pickle 0.2 [BE]; everything stone-family 0.1; gear recycling 0.1.
- **Risks / dependencies:** blocked on XP existing. Do not build a furnace-local XP counter first — it will be the second owner of the number.

#### G1.8 — The anvil is a two-item repair and nothing else · M · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Anvil_mechanics]
  - Prior-work penalty `2^c − 1` → 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 31…; on combine the new penalty is `2n+1` where n is the **larger** of the two.
  - **Unit repair: 25% of max durability per unit of material, 1 level per unit** (max 4 units for a full repair) + prior work.
  - **Combining two items: result durability = durability(sacrifice) + 12% of max**, capped; repair portion costs 2 levels.
  - Rename +1 level; rename does not raise the prior-work penalty; **[BE] has no rename clamp**, so a rename can hit "Too Expensive".
  - **"Too Expensive!" is ≤ 39 levels — 40+ is refused.** No cap in Creative.
  - **12% degrade chance per use**, three states (Anvil → Chipped → Damaged → destroyed). Falling anvil: 2 HP per block after the first, capped at 40.
  - Bedrock's enchantment-combine cost is `(final_level − initial_level_on_target) × multiplier`, which is dramatically cheaper than Java's `final_level × multiplier`.
- **What we have:** `repairResult` (`Recipe.cpp:1365-1382`) — two items of the same kind, `remaining = (max − dmgA) + (max − dmgB) + max/20`, capped at max. That is the **grindstone / crafting-grid** formula (5%), not the anvil's combine formula (12% of max added to the sacrifice's durability). The anvil, the chipped anvil, the damaged anvil and the grindstone all route to the same call (`Main.cpp:3495-3501`).
- **What must be built:** a real anvil path: a `prior work` field on `ItemStack` (or a side table), the material-repair branch, a rename text field, the level cost, the 39-level refusal, and the 12% degrade roll that swaps `Anvil → ChippedAnvil → DamagedAnvil → Air`. All three anvil ids already exist (`Block.hpp:840-842`, `isAnvil` at `Block.hpp:2947`).
- **Numbers that matter:** 25% per unit, 12% combine bonus, 5% grindstone bonus, 39-level cap, 12% degrade, `2^c − 1` prior work.
- **Risks / dependencies:** XP (G1.7's dependency). The repair-only half can ship without XP if you accept a free repair as a named divergence, but the cost formula is the point of the block.

#### G1.9 — Enchanting table is inert · XL · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Enchanting_Table] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Enchanting_table_mechanics] — 1 book + 2 diamonds + 4 obsidian. Lapis cost 1–3; the level charged is the lapis number, but you must *have* the displayed requirement. Max 15 bookshelves; 15 = guaranteed level-30 bottom slot. **Bedrock placement rule differs from Java:** the bookshelf must be exactly 2 blocks away along one horizontal axis and up to 2 along the other, at table height or 1 higher, and **the entire 2-high gap must be air** — a torch, a snow layer or a carpet blocks it. Java only requires the block at bookshelf height to be an `enchantment_power_transmitter`.
- **What we have:** the block, its 12/16-tall model, its light and its blast resistance. Nothing else.
- **What must be built:** enchantment storage on `ItemStack` (there is no field — `damage` is already carrying stowbox handles, `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` "The stowbox"), the ~35 enchantment table with levels and incompatibility groups, the three-offer UI, the bookshelf scan and the XP cost.
- **Numbers that matter:** `xpBase = 1 + rand(7) + floor(min(15,B)/2) + rand(min(15,B))`; `top = floor(max(1, xpBase/3))`; `middle = floor(2·xpBase/3) + 1`; `bottom = floor(max(xpBase, 2·B))`. Enchantability: gold armour 25, gold tools 22, leather/wood 15, iron tools 14, chainmail 12, diamond 10, iron armour & turtle shell 9, stone 5, book/bow/crossbow/fishing rod 1.
- **Risks / dependencies:** XP; a per-stack enchantment payload that has to survive `player.dat`, `chests.dat` and the item entity. This is a milestone, not a task.

#### G1.10 — The recipe book does not fill the grid and nothing unlocks · S · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Recipe_book] — Bedrock's recipe book **opens by default** with the inventory in survival. Tabs mirror the creative tabs (Construction, Equipment, Items, Nature, All) plus search; the furnace book has Food / Blocks / Items / All. There is an **All ↔ Craftable** toggle. **Left-click auto-fills the grid with available materials; right-click crafts it immediately; shift crafts as many as materials allow.** Recipes unlock on **obtaining the relevant ingredient**, with two odd exceptions — boats unlock on touching water, chests after filling 10 inventory slots — and a toast appears. You do not need a recipe unlocked to hand-craft it.
- **What we have:** the catalogue card is already the right shape — four category tabs matching the four `ItemCategory` values plus a search tab (`InventoryScreen.hpp:118-127`), and cells tinted `Craftable` / `Uncraftable` from `craftableItems(inventory, craftSize(kind))` (`InventoryScreen.cpp:729-741`). But **`Main.cpp:3721` gates the entire click handler on `creative`**, and the comment there says so outright: *"Survival gets nothing from it yet — there it is a recipe book, and clicking a recipe fills the grid rather than conjuring the item."*
- **What must be built:** in survival, a click on a craftable catalogue entry should look up the first recipe producing that item, and lay its pattern into `craftSlots` from the inventory. Add the All ↔ Craftable toggle. Unlocking is optional — Bedrock does not gate hand-crafting on it — but the toast is cheap and is a real progression signal.
- **Numbers that matter:** `craftableItems` is a greedy count over all 1,152 recipes (`Recipe.cpp:1156-1213`) and runs every frame a screen is open; the fill path needs `findMatch` in reverse, which does not exist yet.
- **Risks / dependencies:** an item with several recipes (torch from coal or charcoal; brown dye from cocoa or mushroom) needs a rule for which one to lay out — Bedrock cycles.

#### G1.11 — Loom is inert; banners have no patterns · L · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Loom] loom = 2 string over 2 planks. Three slots: banner, **dye (consumed, one per pattern)**, and an optional **banner pattern item that is not consumed**. **42 loom patterns**, of which 10 require a pattern item (Flower Charge, Creeper Charge, Skull Charge, Thing, Snout, Globe, Field Masoned, Bordure Indented, Flow, Guster). **Max 6 layers in both editions** — Java's "16" is a command-only display artefact. Bedrock additionally lets most patterns be applied by *crafting* (banner + dyes in the 3×3, a **fixed**, non-mirrorable recipe — the only fixed recipes in vanilla, and Bedrock-only). Banner copy: patterned + blank same colour → 2 identical; **[BE] the patterned banner must be left of or above the blank one**.
- **What we have:** sixteen banners, one per wool colour, made from 6 wool + 1 stick (`Recipe.cpp:765-774`), living in the sign family (`signAt(2, colour, …)`). The loom block exists and does nothing.
- **What must be built:** a per-banner layer list (up to 6 entries of pattern + colour) that has to ride on the item and the block entity; a loom screen; 42 pattern textures composited at draw time; the copy recipe.
- **Numbers that matter:** 42 patterns, 10 needing a pattern item, 6 layers max, 1 dye per layer.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the layer list is the expensive part — `ItemStack::damage` is already spoken for by the stowbox, so this needs a second side table with the same save/restore discipline (`stowboxes.dat` is the pattern to copy).

#### G1.12 — Campfire is inert · S · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Campfire] 3 sticks + 1 coal/charcoal + 3 logs. Cooks **4 items at once**, **600 ticks (30 s) each**, **no fuel required**, **no XP**, and the finished items **pop off onto the ground** — there is no output inventory, so a hopper cannot load one but a hopper below collects the drops. Cooks the same 9 items a smoker does (the 8 raw meats/fish plus potato and kelp). Light 15. Damages entities standing in it. Smoke rises 10 blocks, or 24 with a hay bale below.
- **What we have:** the block, its four-log model, its light and its particle. No cooking, no recipe.
- **What must be built:** a block entity holding 4 (item, elapsed) pairs; a right-click that puts one raw food on it; a tick that spawns the cooked drop at 30 s; drop-all-on-break. It is a simpler furnace with no fuel and no output slot.
- **Numbers that matter:** 4 slots, 600 ticks = 30 s, no fuel, no XP. Signal fire smoke 24 blocks with hay below.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `ItemEntities::spawn` already exists and already carries a damage value, so the drop half is free.

#### G1.13 — Stonecutter offers three cuts and no cascades · M · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Stonecutter] every stonecutter recipe is 1→1 **except slabs, which are 1→2**, and copper, which is a genuine material multiplier: a block of copper (any oxidation, waxed or not) gives **×4** cut copper / copper grate / chiselled copper / cut copper stairs, and **×8** cut copper slabs. The families cascade: **stone → cobblestone** (stonecutter-exclusive), stone bricks, chiselled stone bricks; **[BE] only** cobblestone → stone bricks and their stairs/slab/wall; granite/diorite/andesite → polished + polished stairs/slab; deepslate → cobbled/chiselled/polished/bricks/tiles each with their own downstream cuts; tuff → chiselled/polished/bricks/chiselled bricks; sandstone and red sandstone → chiselled/cut/smooth; smooth stone → smooth stone slab ×2 only. Stairs are 33% cheaper than crafting (1 block → 1 stair vs 6 → 4); slabs are the same value.
- **What we have:** `kStonecutterOptions = 3` (`Block.hpp:3688`) and `stonecutterOption(parent, n)` (`Block.hpp:3696-3722`), a reverse lookup over `kStairFamilies`, `kSlabFamilies` and `kWallFamilies` — which is the right design and is *why* it covers 52 materials for free. Yields are correct (`stonecutterYield`, `Block.hpp:3726`: slab 2, everything else 1).
- **What must be built:** widen `kStonecutterOptions` and add a small **cut table** naming parent → derived block for the non-family cuts (polished, brick, chiselled, cobblestone-from-stone) with a per-option yield. Keep the reverse lookup for the three shape families.
- **Numbers that matter:** slab ×2, copper block → cut copper ×4 and cut copper slab ×8, everything else ×1.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the screen shows exactly 3 result slots (`resultSlotCount(kind)`, `InventoryScreen`), so widening the options means widening the layout — and Bedrock's stonecutter shows a scrollable grid, not a row.

#### G1.14 — Cauldron is water-only · M · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cauldron] Bedrock has **0–6 levels** (Java 0–3) and a bottle is **±2 levels**; you cannot retrieve below 2. **Dyeing water is a Bedrock exclusive** — use a dye on the cauldron at any fill level, dye consumed, and mixing follows `c_next = floor((c_current + c_dye)/2)` per ARGB channel; leather armour, leather horse armour and wolf armour are then dyed by using them on the dyed cauldron at **−2 levels each**. **Potion storage is also Bedrock-exclusive** — a potion in is +2 levels, a glass bottle out is −2. Tipped arrows from a potion cauldron are Bedrock-only: 1–16 arrows = −1 level, 17–32 = −4, 33–64 = −6. Undyed water washes dye off leather armour and shulker boxes and removes **the topmost banner layer**, −1 level each. Fills from rain at 5% of the snow rate, or instantly if a water block touches the top; fills from a pointed dripstone up to 10 blocks above. Comparator reads 0–3, and a lava cauldron reads 3.
- **What we have:** `Main.cpp:5107-5161` — a water bucket fills to 6, an empty bucket at 6 empties it, a glass bottle at ≥2 takes 2, a water bottle at ≤4 adds 2. Correct and Bedrock-shaped as far as it goes. `isCauldron`/`cauldronLevel`/`cauldronAt` at `Block.hpp:2274-2290`.
- **What must be built:** dyed-water state (a colour per cauldron — a block entity, since 16 colours × 7 levels is 112 ids), potion state, the washing branch, rain and dripstone filling, and lava/powder-snow variants.
- **Numbers that matter:** 0–6 levels, ±2 per bottle, −1 per wash, −2 per dyed item, rain fill at 5% of snow accumulation, dripstone reach 10 blocks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** dyeing leather armour has no other path in Bedrock, so armour colour is blocked on this. Potion storage is blocked on G1.1.

#### G1.15 — Grindstone duplicates the anvil exactly · S · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Grindstone] 2 sticks + 1 **stone slab** + 2 planks. Removes **all non-curse enchantments** and returns XP; curses are not removed and the custom name is not removed. **Resets the prior-work penalty to 0.** Two-item repair = `dur(A) + dur(B) + floor(5% of max)`, capped, output unenchanted. An enchanted book becomes a plain book. XP returned is a uniform random **50–100% (rounded up)** of the sum of each non-curse enchantment's minimum modified level. **[BE] quirk: a grindstone breaks if unsupported or placed in water**; Java needs no support.
- **What we have:** the same `repairResult` the anvil uses (`Recipe.cpp:1365`) — and its 5% figure is **correct for the grindstone**, which is the one place it belongs.
- **What must be built:** the disenchant half, the prior-work reset, and the XP return. All blocked on G1.9.
- **Numbers that matter:** 5% of max as the repair bonus; XP return 50–100% of summed minimum modified levels.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the grindstone's own recipe (`Recipe.cpp:585-589`) is currently 2×3 of planks/sticks/planks and uses hard-coded **oak** planks — see §1.4.

#### G1.16 — Seven recipes need an ingredient with no source in the world · S · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** n/a — this is a self-consistency gap.
- **What we have:** a grep across `game/src` for each ingredient shows the following appear **only** in `Item.hpp` (the enum) and `Recipe.cpp` (as an ingredient) — no worldgen row, no mob drop, no loot table, no block drop:

| Ingredient | Recipes it blocks | File |
|---|---|---|
| `ItemId::CocoaBeans` | Cookie (`Recipe.cpp:946`), brown dye (`:944`) | brown-mushroom dye path still works |
| `ItemId::GlowstoneDust` | Glowstone block (`:971`), redstone lamp (`:746`), sea lantern (`:267`), and every "glowstone strengthens" brew (`:1269-1277`) | `BlockId::Glowstone` does not generate |
| `ItemId::Quartz` | Comparator (`:735`), observer (`:730`), daylight detector (`:685`), quartz block (`:874`) | Nether-gated in Bedrock too — one line |
| `ItemId::VoidPearl` | Ender chest (`:557`) | thrown in `Projectile.cpp:64` but nothing drops one |
| `ItemId::RabbitFoot` | Leaping brew (`:1238`) | rabbits exist; no drop row |
| `ItemId::PhantomMembrane` | Slow-falling brew (`:1250`) | no phantom drop |
| `BlockId::SoulSand` | Soul torch (`:928-930`), soul lantern (`:927`) | Nether — one line |
| `ItemId::CinderRod`, `PoppedChorusFruit`, `NetherBrickItem` | End rod (`:934`), purpur, nether bricks, nether brick fence | Nether/End — one line |

- **What must be built:** either give the overworld ones a source (cocoa pods on jungle logs; rabbit's foot and phantom membrane as mob drops) or remove the recipe so the catalogue stops promising it. **Cocoa beans, rabbit's foot and phantom membrane are the three genuinely-overworld ones.**
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock rabbit's foot drop chance 10% (0/1, +3% per Looting level); phantom membrane 1–2 per phantom.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `craftableItems` will keep tinting these red forever, which reads as "you don't have the materials" rather than "this is impossible".

#### G1.17 — Cartography table inert; maps do not exist · M · P3
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cartography_Table] 2 paper over 4 planks. Map + paper = zoom out one level; map + empty map = clone into two; map + glass pane = locked map. **Bedrock-only extras:** paper alone → empty map, paper + compass → empty locator map, map + compass → locator upgrade, and a **free rename field with no XP cost**.
- **What we have:** `ItemId::EmptyMap` (9 paper, `Recipe.cpp:389`) and `ItemId::FilledMap` exist and do nothing. The block is inert.
- **What must be built:** the whole map feature — a per-map raster of explored terrain, a render path for the held item, and the four table operations.
- **Numbers that matter:** 5 zoom levels (1:1 to 1:16), 128×128 pixels per map.
- **Risks / dependencies:** this is really a map feature with a table attached; scope it as one.

#### G1.18 — Smithing templates and armour trims · L · P3
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Smithing_Template] since 1.20 the netherite upgrade needs a **Netherite Upgrade template** [Nether — one line]. **18 trim templates**, of which 13 are overworld-obtainable (Sentry/pillager outpost, Vex/woodland mansion, Coast/shipwreck, Wild/jungle temple, Dune/desert pyramid, Wayfinder+Raiser+Shaper+Host/trail ruins, Ward+Silence/ancient city, Tide/elder guardian 20%, Bolt+Flow/trial chambers). Duplication is 7 diamonds + the template + its material → 2. **10 trim materials**: amethyst shard, copper ingot, diamond, emerald, gold ingot, iron ingot, lapis lazuli, redstone dust, plus quartz and netherite [Nether]. Trimming costs **0 XP** and preserves durability, enchantments and name.
- **What we have:** `smithingResult` (`Recipe.cpp:1345-1362`) — diamond tool/armour + Emberite ingot → Emberite, using contiguous-run arithmetic. No template slot (the shared bench screen has two slots, not three).
- **What must be built:** a third input slot on the bench screen, a per-item trim payload (pattern + material) and a trim overlay layer on every armour icon and model.
- **Numbers that matter:** 18 templates, 10 materials, 0 XP, 7 diamonds to duplicate.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the same per-stack payload problem as enchantments and banner layers. Solve that once.

#### G1.19 — Dye chain and dyeable-target gaps · XS · P3
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Dye] — the two-tall flowers give **2** dye (sunflower→yellow, lilac→magenta, rose bush→red, peony→pink); beetroot→red (1); wither rose→black (1); pink petals→pink; torchflower→orange; pitcher plant→cyan (2). Multi-dye paths exist: light gray = black+white+white (3), magenta = white+blue+red+red (4) or pink+blue+red (3). Application: wool ×1, carpet ×1, terracotta 8+1→8, concrete powder 4 sand + 4 gravel + 1 dye → 8, glass and panes 8+1→8, **bed ×1 (an existing bed can be re-dyed)**, candle ×1, bundle ×1, shulker box ×1. **[BE] substitution rule:** bone meal ↔ white dye, ink sac ↔ black dye, lapis ↔ blue dye, cocoa ↔ brown dye are interchangeable in *any* recipe, but the substitution must be total. **[BE] leather armour is dyed at a cauldron only, never directly.**
- **What we have:** 12 flower dyes (`Recipe.cpp:143-157`), bone→bone meal→white, ink→black, lapis→blue, mushroom→brown, cocoa→brown, cactus→green (smelted), and the 9 mixes at yield 2 (`Recipe.cpp:165-175`). Wool, terracotta, concrete powder, stained glass, panes, candles, stowboxes and beds are all dyeable. **A bed's colour comes from its wool at craft time — an existing bed cannot be re-dyed.**
- **What must be built:** the four ×2 tall-flower recipes, beetroot→red, wither rose→black, the bed re-dye loop (copy the stowbox pattern at `Recipe.cpp:455-468`), and the four-way substitution rule.
- **Numbers that matter:** tall flowers yield **2**; mixes yield 2; terracotta/glass/concrete 8+1→8 ✓ already correct.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the substitution rule needs an ingredient that names a set, which is exactly what `craftableItems` says it cannot have — see G1.20.

#### G1.20 — No item-tag ingredients: recipes cannot mix woods · M · P3
- **Bedrock behaviour:** planks, logs, wooden slabs, coals and dyes are matched by item **tag**, so two oak and two spruce planks make a crafting table.
- **What we have:** `Recipe::pattern` is an array of plain `ItemId`s (`Recipe.hpp:29`), so shared wooden recipes are **generated once per wood** (`Recipe.cpp:97-110`, then the loops at `:599-648` and `:657-702`). This is the biggest single reason the table is 1,152 rows.
- **What must be built:** an ingredient that names a set, and — the comment at `Recipe.cpp:1188-1204` spells this out in detail — `craftableItems` then has to become **Kuhn's algorithm** rather than a greedy count, because "do I have the materials?" becomes bipartite matching. The comment is explicit that nobody will connect the two unless it is written down, which it is.
- **Numbers that matter:** 11 woods × ~14 shared recipes = ~154 rows that would collapse to ~14.
- **Risks / dependencies:** this is a documented, deliberate divergence (`Recipe.cpp:89-95`), not an oversight. Only worth doing if the tag mechanism buys something else too — the dye substitution rule in G1.19 would be the second customer.

#### G1.21 — No crafter (1.21) · M · P3
- **Bedrock behaviour:** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Crafter] 5 iron + crafting table + dropper + 2 redstone. Nine slots, each empty one click-toggleable to disabled. Fires **4 game ticks (2 redstone ticks)** after receiving power, ejects one crafted item from the front or inserts it into a facing container. Fill order is reading order across enabled slots; when all are full it adds to the smallest matching stack. Comparator output = the number of slots that are **disabled or occupied** (0–9), stack size irrelevant.
- **What we have:** nothing — there is no `BlockId::Crafter`.
- **What must be built:** the block, the 9-slot screen with per-slot disable, and the trigger.
- **Numbers that matter:** 4-tick delay, comparator 0–9.
- **Risks / dependencies:** **there is no redstone signal engine in this game by decision** (`DECISIONS.md`), so a crafter would have no trigger. Park this until that decision changes.

## 2. User interface, screens and menus

**Scope:** every pixel the player reads — the HUD, the inventory and container screens, tooltips, text rendering, and the menus that should exist outside the world (main, world select, pause, settings, death). Overworld only; Nether/End screens are out of scope by project rule.

**Headline verdict:** What exists is unusually good and unusually narrow. The inventory family is genuinely close to Bedrock — eight screen kinds, a real recipe-book/catalogue card with five tabs, scrolling, search, craftable colouring, hover tooltips, a scissor-clipped last row, full click/right-click/shift-click/double-click/drag semantics, and a gamepad that drives all of it through a virtual pointer rather than a second interaction model. Outside that one screen there is almost nothing: **there is no main menu, no world selection, no world creation, no pause menu, no settings screen and no death screen.** The game boots straight into a single hardcoded world (`kWorldSeed = 1337u`, `Main.cpp:171`), 44 options are reachable only by editing `settings.cfg` in a text editor, 12 more only by pressing an undocumented function key, and dying silently teleports you 1.6 seconds later with no screen and no button. The HUD is three bars, a hotbar, a crosshair and a developer overlay that — remarkably — does not print your coordinates.

**Completeness estimate:** roughly **35 % of Bedrock's overworld UI surface**. Broken down: the in-world container/inventory screens are ~65 % there, the HUD ~40 %, item presentation (tooltips, durability, stack labels) ~35 %, and everything outside the world (main menu, world select/create, pause, settings, death, chat) is **0 %**.
