### 2.3 Gap detail

#### G2.1 — Main menu, world select and world creation · XL · P0
- **Bedrock behaviour:** the game opens on a title screen (Play / Settings / Marketplace / Profile), and "Play" leads to a Worlds list with Create New World. World creation exposes world name, default game mode, difficulty, seed, flat-world toggle, starting map, bonus chest, cheats, and every world-rule toggle — "Seed: *A mysterious series of numbers used to create your world*", "Show coordinates: *Display your current position at all times*". [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tutorial:Menu_screen_(Bedrock_Edition)]
- **What we have:** nothing. `main()` calls `loadSettings` (`Main.cpp:981`), constructs `World world(kWorldSeed, executableDirectory()/"saves", …)` (`Main.cpp:1896`) and captures the cursor (`Main.cpp:1893`) before the first frame. The seed is `constexpr std::uint32_t kWorldSeed = 1337u` (`Main.cpp:171`) with the comment "Change this and the entire world changes, reproducibly" — i.e. it is a recompile. `settings.cfg` has **no** `seed` key (`core/Settings.cpp:127-137`); it has `spawn_x`/`spawn_z` instead.
- **What must be built:** (1) promote the seed from a compile-time constant to a value read from a per-world file, and write it into the save alongside `kChunkFormatVersion`; (2) give `WorldStore` a world *directory* rather than one `saves/`; (3) a screen stack in `main()` — today `openScreen` is a single `std::optional<Kind>` (`Main.cpp:2562`) and the whole frame is gated on it, so a menu that runs *without a world* needs the frame loop split into "menu state" and "playing state"; (4) three screens: title, world list, create-world; (5) list rendering with scrolling — the catalogue card already proves scroll + scissor + click resolution, so reuse `catalogueListBounds`/`setClippedScreenMesh` rather than inventing a widget system.
- **Numbers that matter:** the panel art pipeline is 185 × 1687 px today and grows per panel (`hud/HudPrimitives.hpp:24`); a menu built from the existing 6-grey visual language needs one new panel row per screen in **both** `tools/make-hud-sheet.ps1` and `tools/make-reference-hud.ps1` (the game prefers the second — `INTERFACE.md §1.5`). Text is 8 px cells; a menu button reads well at 8–10 art pixels of text height.
- **Risks / dependencies:** this is the one gap that changes the shape of `main()`. Doing it badly means a second copy of the input handling. The cheapest honest version is a **world-select screen only** (list the directories under `saves/`, plus "New World" with a seed field reusing the search field's text input) and leave the title screen for later.

#### G2.2 — Pause menu and the settings screen · L · P0
- **Bedrock behaviour:** the pause menu carries Resume, Settings, Marketplace, Save & Quit, plus achievements and the player doll; it genuinely pauses single-player. Settings is split into **General / Video / Audio / Controls (Keyboard & Mouse, Controller, Touch) / Accessibility**, with Video carrying brightness, render distance, FOV, GUI scale, UI profile (Classic/Pocket), fancy graphics, view bobbing, camera shake, hide hand and screen safe area. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Heads-up_display]
- **What we have (counted, read in the code):** `settings.cfg` parses **44 keys** — 11 unsigned (`worker_threads`, `render_distance`, `detail_distance`, `frame_cap`, `day_length_seconds`, `tone_map`, `shadows`, `clouds`, `rain_distance`, `start_weather`, `input_mode`), 2 int (`spawn_x`, `spawn_z`), 21 float (volumes, exposure, bloom strength, handheld light, cloud coverage/shadow, shadow darkness, five water sliders, foliage sway, anti-alias, render scale, contact shadows, four `controller_*`), and 10 bool/int (`controller_invert_y`, `bloom`, `weather`, `particles`, `spawn_underground`, `creature_showcase`, `drop_showcase`, `creative_mode`, `worldgen_probe`, `block_probe`) — `core/Settings.cpp:127-219`. **None** is editable in game. Live hotkeys number **12 actions across 16 keys**: F1/F2 frame cap, F3/F4 FOV, F5 overlay, F6/F7 render distance, F8/F9 spawn a hostile, F10 tone mapper, F11 bloom, F12 renderer debug view, G shadows, C clouds, F input mode, V weather (`Main.cpp:3245-3371`). So: **38 player-facing options behind a text editor, 12 behind an undocumented key, and 0 behind a screen.**
- **What must be built:** a pause state (`Escape` when nothing else is open) with Resume / Settings / Save & Quit; a tabbed settings screen with Video, Audio, Controls and Accessibility; three widget kinds only — toggle, slider, and cycler — which covers 42 of the 44 keys; and `saveSettings` on every change (five hotkeys already do this, three do not — §2.4). Retiring F1–F7 is the milestone's stated goal (`TIMELINE.md:1938`: *"a `Video` tab exposing quality levels, clouds, ray tracing, resolution, render distance and frame cap (retiring the temporary `F1`–`F7` bindings), plus key rebinding, audio and accessibility options"*).
- **Numbers that matter:** `Settings.hpp` already provides the bounds a slider needs — `kMaxWorkerThreads = 64`, `kMaxRenderDistance = 32`, `kToneMapperCount = 4`, `kShadowQualityCount = 4`, `kCloudQualityCount = 3`, `kInputModeCount = 3` — and the clamps at `Settings.cpp:222-250` give every float its range. Nothing new has to be decided.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `Settings.hpp:15-22` states everything is read **once at startup** and `workerThreads` needs a restart. A settings screen must mark which rows are live and which need a relaunch, or it will silently lie. Two keys are dev-only (`worldgen_probe`, `block_probe`) and must not appear.

#### G2.3 — Death screen and respawn flow · S · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** a "You died!" screen with the cause of death, a Respawn button and a Title Screen button; the hotbar stays visible; the `immediateRespawn` world option skips it. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings]
- **What we have:** `Main.cpp:4284-4321`. `player.deathSeconds` accumulates (`world/Player.cpp:163-165`), and at `kRespawnSeconds = 1.6f` (`world/Survival.hpp:142`) the inventory is spilled as drops, the screen closed and `respawnPlayer` called. `hudDirty = true` fires every frame while dead but nothing new is drawn — the world simply keeps rendering. Rumble plays once. Bed respawn already works, and a missing bed logs `"Your bed was missing or blocked."` to the **console**, where the player cannot see it.
- **What must be built:** a `Kind`-like death state that suppresses movement input, dims the world (the 55 %-alpha dim quad already exists, `InventoryScreen.cpp:45`), draws a centred title and two buttons, and holds until Respawn is pressed. The 1.6 s auto-respawn becomes the *`immediateRespawn` = on* path rather than the only path. Carry the bed-missing message onto the screen.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's death delay before the screen is immediate; the 1.6 s here is ours and should stay as the "settle the body" animation *before* the screen appears, not instead of it.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the inventory spill currently happens at the 1.6 s mark. If respawn becomes player-driven, decide deliberately whether the drop happens on death or on respawn — Bedrock drops on death, and drops despawn on a timer, so holding the screen open indefinitely must not extend the drop's life.

#### G2.4 — ~~Armour slots~~ and an offhand · S · P2 — **armour half closed 2026-08-19**
- **Bedrock behaviour:** "The inventory consists of 4 armor slots, 27 storage slots, 9 hotbar slots, and an off-hand slot… Armor is considered equipped only when it is in an armor slot." [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Inventory]
- **What we have, re-measured 2026-08-19 09:57:** ✅ **the armour column is finished.** `Inventory` carries `kArmourSlots = 4` beside its 36 (`item/Inventory.hpp`, `armourAt`/`armourSet`/`equipArmour`), `InventoryScreen.cpp` `slotAt` produces `SlotHit{Region::Armour, i}` gated through `armourSlotCount(kind)`, `build` draws the column, `armourSlot(item)` is the single owner of which piece goes where so a boot cannot reach a head, `Inventory::armourSet` refuses a piece sitting in the wrong slot, and the worn set is persisted as `SavedPlayer::armour` at **player format version 7**. The reduction itself belongs to §7 and is also done. ❌ **The offhand is still dead code, and is now the last one:** `Region::Offhand` exists as an enumerator and as `case` labels in `InventoryScreen.cpp`, and **nothing anywhere constructs a `SlotHit` for it** — same shape as the armour column was, one cell smaller. So the shield and the elytra remain unwearable. *Superseded text, kept because it names what changed: "24 armour pieces, a shield and an elytra exist as items and cannot be worn"; "`armourPoints` has no callers, so armour reduces no damage today" (the function is `armourDefence`, and it now has real callers).*
- **What must be built:** one offhand slot — storage on `Inventory`, a `SlotHit{Region::Offhand, 0}` production site in `slotAt`, a draw, and a rule for what may go in it. **The `player.dat` bump this row used to be blocked on has already been spent** (v7 added the four armour stacks), so an offhand costs a v8 rather than a first migration. Shift-click-to-equip already routes through `quickMoveTargets` for armour; extend it, do not copy it.
- **Numbers that matter:** four armour slots stacked vertically on the 18 px pitch, offhand one slot below/beside them; Bedrock's armour bar is 10 icons on the same 10-px pitch as hearts (`StatusBars.hpp` already has `kIconsPerRow = 10`); armour caps at 20 points = 10 icons. The HUD bar itself is **still absent and no longer blocked** — see §2's HUD table.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none left for armour. For the offhand, `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #8 applies to the v8 migration — read the bytes on disk after it.

#### G2.5 — Coordinates and a real debug screen · XS · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** "Show coordinates — *Display your current position at all times*" is a world option that puts a plain XYZ line on the HUD; a fuller debug overlay adds chunk position, biome, light and facing. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings]
- **What we have:** `OverlayStats` (`hud/DebugOverlay.hpp:12-52`) carries 22 fields and **no position**. The 19 rows at `hud/DebugOverlay.cpp:90-117` are engine diagnostics. The player's biome is printed once at startup (`Main.cpp:2244-2249`) and lives in the overlay as `stats.biome`, but XYZ appears nowhere on screen.
- **What must be built:** three fields on `OverlayStats` (position, facing, chunk) and three rows. That is the whole change; the row table is a plain array. Optionally a standalone one-line coordinate readout independent of F5, which is the Bedrock-shaped version.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock prints coordinates without decimals. Facing is the eight-point compass plus the yaw in degrees.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none. This is the cheapest P1 in the document.

#### G2.6 — Durability bars and richer tooltips · S · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** a used item shows a coloured bar under its icon in the inventory *and* the hotbar, green→red as it wears; an unused item shows none. Tooltips show name, enchantments and (Bedrock) the item's category. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tooltip] [https://minecraft.fandom.com/wiki/Durability]
- **What we have:** `ItemStack` carries `int damage` (`item/Item.hpp:1583`) and the tool table knows every item's maximum. `appendStack` (`hud/HudPrimitives.cpp:307-326`) draws the icon and, when `count > 1`, the number — **and nothing else**. The tooltip (`HudPrimitives.cpp:329`, called `InventoryScreen.cpp:831`) draws `displayNameOf(item)` and nothing else.
- **What must be built:** in `appendStack`, when `damage > 0`, two quads at the bottom of the slot — a dark backing and a coloured fill of width `1 - damage/max` — using the existing white-texture layer, at a depth between icon and count. Because `appendStack` is the single owner used by the hotbar, the inventory, the chest and the catalogue, one change covers every place a stack is drawn. Then widen `appendTooltip` to take multiple lines so it can carry name + category (+ later, enchantments).
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's bar is 13 × 2 px inside an 18 px slot, offset 2 px from the left and 2 px up from the bottom; hue runs from `hsv(0.33)` at full to `hsv(0.0)` at empty.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `appendTooltip` currently sizes its panel from one string (`HudPrimitives.cpp:338-341`); multi-line needs the widest line and a per-line advance. Low risk. Note `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #13 — the icon path, the drop path and the mesher path all draw items differently; only `appendStack` needs the bar, but check that the dropped-item entity is not expected to show one (it is not, in the reference).

#### G2.7 — Recipe book slice 8: click a recipe to fill the grid · M · P1
- **Bedrock behaviour:** on a recipe-book entry, **left click fills the grid** with available materials, **right click crafts one**, **shift crafts as many as materials allow** — the direct design, unlike Java's ghost items. [quoted from `INTERFACE.md §4.5`, sourced from `Mojang/bedrock-samples` and minecraft.wiki]
- **What we have:** in survival the catalogue is browse-only. Clicking an entry is gated on `creative` (`Main.cpp:3722`), where it is a source. `INTERFACE.md §7` lists slice 8 as unbuilt and names it *"The payoff. Needs 2 and 5."*
- **What must be built:** the five-step auto-fill algorithm `INTERFACE.md §4.5` already specifies — (1) if the grid already holds this recipe, do nothing; (2) **empty the grid back into the inventory first, and abort the whole operation if it will not fit** rather than partially filling; (3) build the item→count map; (4) craft count = 1, or for craft-all `min(possible crafts, smallest ingredient's stack limit, result stack limit)`; (5) fill each cell from the first matching stack in a linear scan. Plus the red output slot when the selected recipe is unaffordable (`INTERFACE.md §3.1b`: catalogue red `243,74,63`, output-slot red `239,92,70` — "one shared state meaning *this is not going to happen*, used in two places").
- **Numbers that matter:** 1,152 recipes today, of which the 2×2-capable subset is what the inventory screen's book may offer (`fitsInTwoByTwo`, already computed per recipe). `INTERFACE.md` recorded 1029 items / 1019 recipes / 460 two-by-two at the time it was written — re-derive rather than trusting those.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the matcher must tell the placer **which concrete item it chose** (`INTERFACE.md §4.5`); letting the placer re-decide gets stuck. Greedy affordability is still correct only while no ingredient is a set — the counter-example is written at the call site and must stay there.

#### G2.8 — Hover highlight, panel titles, held-item name popup · XS · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** the slot under the cursor lightens; container screens are titled; switching hotbar slot shows the item's name above the bar for a few seconds, on a black background whose opacity is an accessibility setting. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Heads-up_display]
- **What we have:** only catalogue cells have a hovered state (`InventoryScreen.cpp:515-519`, mixing toward white by 0.45). No panel carries a title. Switching hotbar slot writes `"Holding: <name> x<n>"` to the **console** (`Main.cpp:4069-4075`).
- **What must be built:** a pale quad at `kCellDepth` over whichever slot `slotAt` answers; one `appendText` call per screen kind for the title (the art already leaves the row); and a fading name label above the hotbar driven by a timer, replacing the console line.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's slot highlight is white at ~40 % alpha over the full 18 × 18 cell. The hotbar name label sits just above `kHotbarTopY` (`hud/Hotbar.hpp:29`) and fades over ~2 s.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none, but see §2.4 — the console line is currently emitted once per *keystroke* while typing in the search field, so removing it fixes a live annoyance too.

#### G2.11 — GUI scale and narrow-aspect safety · S · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour:** a GUI Scale slider in Video settings, plus a UI Profile switch (Classic/Pocket) that re-lays the whole HUD; on mobile the bars move to the screen corners. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Heads-up_display]
- **What we have:** every UI dimension is a fixed fraction of window **height** — `kPanelHeight = 1.30` on a 2.0-tall screen, so the panel is always 65 % of the window height and `kPixel = kPanelHeight / 166` (`InventoryScreen.cpp:146-154`). That is scale-independent, which is good, but it is also unadjustable, and on a 4K display the 8 px font is rendered at 8/166 × height ≈ 104 device pixels tall — fine — while on a 720p window it is ~35, which is legible but not chooseable.
- **What must be built:** one multiplier applied to `kPanelHeight` (and therefore to `kPixel`, and therefore to everything, since every position goes through `toScreen`) plus the same for the hotbar's `kHotbarSlotSize`. Because `INTERFACE.md §6.1` is right that *"every position comes from one function"*, this is genuinely a one-constant change — but it must become a runtime value, so the `constexpr` layout table has to take it as a parameter.
- **Numbers that matter:** the two cards are `146 + 4 + 176 = 326` art pixels wide (`InventoryScreen.cpp:184-185`), which at `kPixel = 1.30/166 = 0.007831` is **2.553 screen units**, i.e. half-width 1.2765. The window is `2 × aspect` wide. **So the layout needs aspect ≥ 1.277.** 16:9 (1.778) and 4:3 (1.333) are safe; **5:4 (1.25), 1:1 and any portrait window clip both cards**, and a GUI-scale slider makes that reachable at 16:9 too. Add a clamp.
- **Risks / dependencies:** making `kPixel` runtime turns a pile of `constexpr` layout constants into functions. Do it in one commit or the hit tests and the drawing will disagree — which is precisely the failure `toScreen` exists to prevent.

#### G2.12 — The container screens that are missing or wrong · L · P2
- **Bedrock behaviour, slot counts:** brewing stand **5** (3 bottles + 1 ingredient + 1 blaze-powder fuel); anvil **2 in + 1 out + a rename text field**; grindstone 2 + 1; smithing table 3 (template + base + addition) + 1 out; enchanting table 1 item + 1 lapis + 3 option rows; beacon 1 payment slot + a pyramid/effect picker; loom 3 + 1; cartography table 2 + 1; dispenser/dropper **3 × 3**; horse 1 saddle + 1 armour, donkey/mule + **15** chest slots; villager trading is a scrolling offer list on the left with 2 in + 1 out on the right. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Inventory]
- **What we have:** `isInteractive` (`world/Block.hpp:2824-2828`) admits exactly crafting table, smithing table, furnace family, chest family, hopper, grindstone, the three anvils and the stonecutter. Everything else on that list — including the enchanting table, which **exists as a block** (`world/Block.hpp:827`, name row `world/Block.hpp:7138`) — cannot be opened at all. Brewing is the sharp case: `Main.cpp:4413` and `Main.cpp:2924` handle `BlockId::BrewingStand` and `brewingResult()` is implemented at `Recipe.cpp:1308`, but `isInteractive` omits it, so the branch is unreachable (§2.4). The anvil opens a 2-input screen with **no rename field**, despite text input existing.
- **What must be built, cheapest first:** (1) add `BrewingStand` to `isInteractive` and give it a proper 5-slot layout rather than borrowing the smithing pair — this alone makes an implemented system reachable; (2) the anvil's rename field, which is the search field with a different owner (`insideSearchField` and the caret code generalise directly); (3) dispenser/dropper as a 9-slot container — it borrows `Region::Chest` exactly as the hopper does, so it is a panel and two constants; (4) loom and cartography as smithing-shaped 2-in/1-out screens; (5) enchanting, beacon, trading and horse only once their systems exist.
- **Numbers that matter:** the hopper precedent (`INTERFACE.md §1.5`) says a new container is a panel row in **two** sprite scripts plus `chestSlotCount`/`isContainer`; a 3 × 3 dispenser at the 18 px pitch is 54 × 54 art pixels.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `craftSize`'s `default: return 2` (§2.4) means every new `Kind` silently gets a 2 × 2 grid and four writable-but-invisible slots — fix that *before* adding kinds, not after. The furnace's borrowed-buffer duplication bug (`INTERFACE.md §1.5`) is the shape this repeats.

---

### 2.4 Errors and inconsistencies noticed while reading

- **`game/src/Main.cpp:4413` + `game/src/world/Block.hpp:2824-2828` · the brewing stand screen is unreachable.** `isInteractive()` gates the entire interact-to-open path at `Main.cpp:4374`, and it lists crafting table, smithing table, `isFurnace`, `isChest`, `isHopper`, grindstone, the three anvils and the stonecutter — **not `BrewingStand`**, and none of the family predicates covers it (`isFurnace` is furnace/smoker/blast furnace, `Block.hpp:2715-2719`). So the `opened == BlockId::BrewingStand` test at `Main.cpp:4413` can never be true, the `brewingResult` branch at `Main.cpp:2924` and `Main.cpp:3498` is dead, and every brewing recipe in `Recipe.cpp:1308-1343` is unreachable in play. · confidence: **certain**
- **`game/src/hud/InventoryScreen.hpp:66-79` · `craftSize` has a `default:` that returns a real grid size.** Already logged as `audit.md §4.6`; repeated here because it is now load-bearing for §2.3 G2.12. Every kind but `Inventory` is listed explicitly and `default: return 2` catches the one that is not — so a tenth `Kind` silently gets a 2 × 2 grid, four writable slots nobody draws, and a give-back loop in `closeScreen` that hands the player items from a screen that never had a grid. Bug shape #10. Naming `Kind::Inventory` and deleting the `default:` lets `-Wswitch` do the work. · confidence: **worth checking** (latent, not currently reachable)
- **`game/src/Main.cpp:3178` + `game/src/Main.cpp:4066-4075` · typing in the search field spams the console.** Every accepted character sets `hudDirty = true`, and `hudDirty` also triggers `logInfo("Holding: …")`. `INTERFACE.md §6.3` predicted exactly this — *"`hudDirty` doubles as a console-log trigger — typing in a search box would spam the log until that is separated"* — and slice 7 shipped without separating it. One log line per keystroke, up to the 22-character cap, every time the player searches. · confidence: **certain**
- **`game/src/hud/InventoryScreen.cpp:146-158` vs `:207-210` · the comment and the code disagree about how a tall panel grows.** `kPixel`'s comment says *"A taller screen grows downward at the same slot size"*, but `toScreen` subtracts `panelPixelHeight(kind) * 0.5f`, which centres the panel — so the double chest grows **both** ways, 27 art pixels up and 27 down. Harmless today (220 px × `kPixel` = 1.723 of 2.0, so it fits), but the comment is what a future session will trust when adding a taller screen. · confidence: **certain** (documentation, not behaviour)
- **`game/src/hud/InventoryScreen.cpp:184-198` · the two-card layout has no aspect-ratio clamp.** Half-width is `326 × kPixel / 2 = 1.2765` screen units against a window half-width of `aspect`. At any aspect below ≈ **1.277** both cards run off the screen edges — 5:4 (1.25), 1:1 and any portrait window. Nothing clamps or rescales. Unverified visually (no builds were run). · confidence: **likely**
- **`game/src/Main.cpp:3300-3305` and `:3362-3371` vs `:3260, 3310, 3317, 3324, 3332, 3342` · three of eight live toggles forget themselves.** F6/F7 (render distance), F10 (tone mapper), F11 (bloom), G (shadows), C (clouds) and F (input mode) all call `saveSettings`. **F3/F4 (field of view) and F1/F2 (frame cap) do not** — and F1/F2 does not even write `settings.frameCap`, it moves a local `capIndex` into `kFpsCapOptions`. So two settings silently reset on every launch while six persist, with no rule distinguishing them. · confidence: **certain**
- **`game/src/hud/InventoryScreen.hpp:96-97` · `Region::Armour` and `Region::Offhand` are dead enumerators, and the code that would meet them fails silently.** A repo-wide grep finds no reference outside the declaration. If `slotAt` ever returned one, the tooltip's `switch` at `InventoryScreen.cpp:809-828` ends in `default: break`, so it would show nothing rather than fail to compile — bug shape #10 again, in the one place armour will actually land. · confidence: **certain** (dead code) / **likely** (latent trap)
- **`game/src/Main.cpp:3199-3207` · Escape with the cursor already released does nothing at all.** `closeScreen` if a panel is up, `setCursorCaptured(false)` otherwise — press it twice and the second press is a no-op, with no menu, no confirmation and no way to quit but the window's ✕. The gamepad's Start button is explicitly wired to the same non-behaviour (`Main.cpp:3391`). · confidence: **certain**
- **`game/src/core/Settings.cpp:185-188` vs `game/src/Main.cpp:74` · the gamepad has four sensitivity/feel settings and the mouse has none.** `controller_look_sensitivity`, `controller_cursor_sensitivity`, `controller_deadzone`, `controller_rumble` and `controller_invert_y` are all configurable; mouse look is the hardcoded `constexpr float kLookRadiansPerPixel = 0.0025f`, and there is no `mouse_sensitivity` or `fov` key in `settings.cfg` at all. For a keyboard-and-mouse-first game this is backwards. · confidence: **certain**
- **`game/src/core/Settings.hpp:70` · the default is creative, so the default session shows no status bars.** `creativeMode = true` is the shipped default, and `Main.cpp:2965` hides hearts, hunger and bubbles in creative (correctly, matching Bedrock). The consequence is that a fresh checkout renders a HUD of one hotbar and a crosshair, which will read as "the bars are broken" to anyone who has not read `Settings.hpp`. · confidence: **certain** (behaviour), **worth checking** (whether the default is still wanted)

**Stated plainly, unverified:** nothing in this section was confirmed by running the game — no build, no `run.ps1`, no `soak.ps1`, per the brief. Every finding is read from source. The aspect-ratio and GUI-scale numbers are arithmetic on the layout constants, not measurements off a frame.

## 3. Animation, rigs and motion

**Scope:** Everything that visibly moves under its own transform — creature rigs and gaits, heads, attack and death, the player's body and camera, block-entity motion, flipbook textures, dropped items, projectiles and particles — measured against Bedrock Edition's published overworld animation surface.

**Headline verdict:** The creature rig is the strongest animation work in the project and is genuinely close to the reference: limbs hinge on derived pivots, heads turn about a real neck joint, the walk cycle is distance-driven rather than clock-driven, and the constants that matter (idle sway at 103.2°/s and ±2.865°, the 6-tick attack swing, the two opposite-sense attack curves, the spider's 38.17°-per-block sweep) were read off Mojang's own JSON rather than guessed. Everything *outside* the creature rig is thin to absent. **The player has no body at all** — no first-person arm, no held-item viewmodel, no view bob, no third-person model, no eat/drink/block/draw pose — so the single most-looked-at animation in the game is a blank screen with a crosshair. **No block in the world animates**: `Main.cpp:4441` states plainly "we have no animated block models", so chests do not open, bells do not swing and pistons have no travel. Flipbook texture animation exists but has **exactly two slots** (water and fire), against the reference's twenty-two, and the two share a clock that makes fire hitch every 3.2 seconds. Per-species character — a wolf's tail, a cat's sit, a fox asleep, a panda rolling, a goat's ram wind-up — is almost entirely missing; 57 species today are the generic rig with different boxes plus a small handful of real exceptions (spider, squid, chicken, bee, slime, pufferfish, creeper swell).

**Completeness estimate:** roughly **40%** of Bedrock's overworld animation surface. Weighted: the shared mob rig is ~35% of the surface and is ~75% done; per-species clips are ~20% of the surface and ~25% done; the player body and first-person view are ~20% and ~5% done; block and world animation is ~15% and ~10% done; item/projectile entity motion is ~10% and ~60% done.

**What could not be verified.** I could not build or run the game (explicit constraint), so **nothing here is confirmed by eye**. Every claim below is either *read in the code* (file:line given) or *inferred* from published reference data (URL given), and the two are labelled separately throughout. Anything needing a playtester's judgement is called out as such.

**Relationship to fragment 12.** `12-animation-errors.md` is a line-by-line audit of the creature rig itself and already documents twelve defects (F18.1–F18.12) plus a rig-by-rig verdict table. **This fragment does not repeat them.** §3.4 here covers only findings *outside* that fragment's scope — the flipbook clock, item-entity phase, hurt duration, head clamp values, grazing numbers, projectile shake axis and per-species death.

---

### 3.1 What exists today

*Read in the code unless marked otherwise. Line numbers are from the files as they stand today.*

| Feature | State | Where it lives (file:line) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Walk / gait cycle** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:4276` (`gait += ground * species.gaitRate`), `:5807` (`swing = -sin(gait) * gaitSwing * limbSwingAmount`) | Distance-driven, not clock-driven — correct, and matches the reference's `query.modified_distance_moved`. `gaitSwing` is in radians and the roster caps at **0.70 rad (40.1°)**, deliberately half the reference's 1.4 rad; a written choice, not an accident. |
| **Limb-swing spin-up / wind-down** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:404` (`kLimbSwingLagPerTick = 0.6f`), `:4293–4300` | Eased with `pow(k, dt/0.05f)`, saturating against each species' own `runSpeed`, forced toward 0 on death. This is the reference's `query.modified_move_speed` term, done properly. |
| **Limb pivots derived, never authored** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:5548` (`legBox`) | `hang` comes from the box's own `netW/netH/netD` — half the thinner cross-section below the top face. No species row carries a pivot. The project's strongest anti-bug rule, and it holds across all ~70 call sites. |
| **Head turn (yaw) and tip (pitch)** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:318–323` (`kHeadTurnRate = 6.0f`, `kMaxHeadTurn = 0.9f`, `kMaxHeadPitch = 0.7f`), `:3824–3835`, `:5390` (`beginHead`) | Rotates about a real neck joint. Pitch limit **0.7 rad = 40.1°** matches the reference's ±40°. **Yaw limit 0.9 rad = 51.6° against the reference's 75°** — see §3.4. No per-species clamps. |
| **Look-at-target selection** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:312–314` (`kLookChancePerSecond`, `kLookSecondsMin/Max = 2/4`) | Idle glances plus player tracking. |
| **Idle biped arm sway** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:5820–5821` | `swayRoll = cos(age*1.8)*0.05 + 0.05`, `swayPitch = sin(age*1.34)*0.05`. 1.8 rad/s = 103.2°/s and ±0.05 rad = ±2.865° are `animation.humanoid.bob` **exactly**. |
| **Attack swing (melee)** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:266` (`kAttackSwingSeconds = 0.3f`), `:5831–5859` | 0.3 s = **6 ticks**, matching the reference. Two opposite-sense curves: unarmed chop `sin(t·π)·1.2 − sin((1−(1−t)²)·π)·0.4`, armed raise `sin((1−(1−t)³)·π)·1.2`. Gated on `species.swingsArms`. |
| **Bow draw / archer pose** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:2205–2207` (`kArcherArmPitch = −1.5708f`, roll +0.10 / −0.50), `:2229` (`static_assert(archersShareOneRig())`) | Both arms converge on the midline at −90° pitch, correct. Arrow leaves the hand via `bipedHandPoint`. **We ease into the pose at `kAimRate = 6.0` (`:2187`); the reference has no blend on this controller** — a deliberate improvement, worth knowing. No draw-progress pose (the reference does not animate draw either; the *bow model* changes, which we do not do). |
| **Death tip** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:62–64` (`kDeathTipSeconds = 0.625f`, `kDeathSeconds = 1.0f`, `kDeathTipAngle = π/2`), `:74–80`, `:5297–5312` | 0.625 s = **12.5 ticks** to reach 90°, and total 1.0 s = 20 ticks — both match. Rodrigues rotation about the body's own forward axis, render position lifted by `halfWidth·scale·sin(fallAngle)` so it does not sink. Damage tint held through the fall (`:5286`). **One rule for all 57 species**; the reference has three. |
| **Hurt tint** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:57` (`kHurtSeconds = 0.35f`) | 0.35 s = 7 ticks against the reference's **10 ticks / 0.5 s**. Note `hurtTimer` also gates the knockback-override window (`:4130`), so it is not a free constant to change. |
| **Creeper swell** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:5286–5300`, `:5358–5372` | `s⁴` normalised against `fuseSeconds − 0.1`, 1.4× wide / 1.1× tall, volume-preserving `sin(s*100)*s*0.01` wobble, flash strobing on tenths of the fuse. Matches `animation.creeper.swelling`'s per-bone scale approach in spirit and in shape. |
| **Chicken wing flap** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:375–392`, `:3956–3969` | `(sin(flap)+1)*flapSpeed` radians hinged at the shoulder; `fallDrag` re-solved for a variable timestep as `k = terminal/(terminal + g·dt)` with terminal 1.95 m/s. Matches `animation.chicken.general`'s `±variable.wing_flap` on Z. |
| **Bee wings** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:5931` region (`kInsectWingPhaseRate = 2.1f / 0.05f`) | Per-tick constant correctly divided for the variable step. |
| **Spider rig** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:6740` region, `barBox` at `:5583` | Rebuilt from `geometry.spider.v1.8` and `animation.spider.walk`: `gaitRate = 2.665` rad/m (= 38.17°×4÷57.3), 45° leg droop, sweep at 2× the lift frequency with `abs()` on both. The best rig in the file. |
| **Squid tentacles + jet** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:7490` region | Tentacle ring rotated about the model's own tilted up axis; **the only rig with a seeded per-entity phase**. |
| **Slime / magma squash** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:6620, 6680` | Per-cube offset driven by a squish factor, matching the reference's `bodycube_n.pos.y = n' × squish × 1.7` shape. |
| **Pufferfish stages** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:7360` region | Three-model switch, not a continuous inflate — which is what the reference does too. |
| **Rabbit / frog hop** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:6300, 6440` | `gaitSwing = 0` by design; the pose drives from `hopTimer`. No frog tongue, no croak, no rabbit ear splay. |
| **Grazing (sheep, cow)** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:348–359` (`kGrazeSeconds = 1.8f`, `kGrazeHeadPitch = 0.7f`), `:2744–2820` | Sets `targetHeadPitch` only. **No head translation, no ramp in/out, no nibble wobble** — the reference has all three. |
| **Step-up easing (creatures)** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:410–411` (`kStepSmoothPerTick = 0.5f`, `kMaxStepSmooth = 1.6f`), `:4280` | The drawn body lags the collision box up a block. Ours, not the reference's — a genuine improvement. |
| **Step-up easing (player camera)** | **Full** | `Player.cpp:28`, `:913`, `:947` | Same constant, same `pow(k, dt/0.05f)` form. The rule travelled correctly between the two files. |
| **Baby scaling** | **Partial** | `Creature.cpp:551–554` (`kBabyScale = 0.55f`) | **Uniform scale, no enlarged head.** The comment admits "one scale cannot do the middle". The reference scales heads 1.2–2.0 per species with pivot compensation. |
| **Held-item transforms (mob hands)** | **Full** | `Creature.cpp:210–235` | `kHeldHandheld {{0,−90,55},{0,4,0.5},0.85}`, `kHeldFlat {{0,0,0},{0,3,1},0.55}`, `kHeldBow {{−80,260,−40},{−1,−2,2.5},0.9}`. **Verified against `item/handheld` and `item/generated`'s `thirdperson_righthand`: exact.** Left hand derived by negating Y/Z rotation and the sideways translation. (Fragment 12 lists this as unaudited; it is audited here and it is correct.) |
| **Dropped item bob + spin** | **Partial** | `ItemEntity.cpp:35–37` (`kBobHeight = 0.07f`, `kBobSpeed = 2.2f`, `kSpinSpeed = 1.1f`), `:247–253` | Both exist. Periods are wrong (2.86 s bob vs the reference's 3.14 s; 5.71 s spin vs 6.28 s), phase is derived from **live position** rather than seeded once, and bob is gated on `onGround`. No stack-count multi-copy. |
| **Arrow flight orientation** | **Partial** | `Projectile.cpp:147–370` | Heading interpolated between ticks. `kShakeSeconds = 0.35f` = 7 ticks, matching the reference's `shakeTime = 7`. **Shake is applied to pitch, bending the heading, where the reference rolls about the arrow's own axis.** No fixed 45° roll. |
| **Projectile render interpolation** | **Full** | `Projectile.cpp:319` (`blend = clamp(m_accumulator/kTickSeconds, 0, 1)`), `:322`, `:361` | The one subsystem with a fixed 0.05 s accumulator, and it correctly blends prev→current for both position and heading. The project's own lesson, honoured. |
| **Non-arrow projectiles** | **Full** | `Projectile.cpp` billboard path | Camera-facing, no spin — which is exactly what the reference does for snowballs, eggs, pearls and potions. |
| **Falling block** | **Full** | `FallingBlock.cpp:106–163` | Zero rotation calls. Matches the reference, which also does not rotate falling blocks. |
| **Block destroy overlay** | **Full** | `BlockOutline.cpp:106–114` (`destroyStageLayer`) | Ten stages driven by mining progress. |
| **Water flipbook** | **Full** | `Main.cpp:6877–6893`, `Block.hpp` (`kWaterFrames = 32`, `kWaterFrameSeconds = 0.1f`) | 0.1 s = **2 ticks/frame**, matching `still_water_grey`. |

### 3.3 Gap detail

#### G3.1 — First-person arm and held-item viewmodel · L · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** The player **does** have a real first-person arm bone, and the held item is a separate bone welded to it. `resource_pack/animations/player_firstperson.animation.json` ships **18 clips**, all `"loop": true` with no `animation_length` — they are pure Molang, evaluated every frame. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/player_firstperson.animation.json]

  The clips are: `first_person.attack_rotation`, `.attack_rotation_item`, `.base_pose`, `.crossbow_equipped`, `.crossbow_hold`, `.melee_spear_hold`, `.melee_spear_use`, `.melee_spear_attack`, `.breathing_bob`, `.empty_hand`, `.map_hold`, `.map_hold_attack`, `.map_hold_main_hand`, `.map_hold_off_hand`, `.swap_item`, `.shield_block`, `.vr_attack_rotation`, `.walk`.

  Rest pose, empty hand (`first_person.empty_hand`, lines 126–140):
  ```
  rightarm.position = [13.5, -10.0, 12.0]
  rightarm.rotation = [95, -45, 115]        // VR variant adds [+7.5, +7.5, -2.5]
  ```

  Base pose (lines 47–56): `head.rotation = [target_x_rotation, target_y_rotation + 180, 0]`.

  The attack swing on the **arm** (`first_person.attack_rotation`, lines 7–26), with `v.firpf = variable.first_person_item_rotation_factor` and `t = variable.attack_time` running 0→1:
  ```
  pos.x = clamp(-15.5 * sin(v.firpf * t * 112), -7, 999) * sin(v.firpf * t * 112)
  pos.y = sin(v.firpf * (1-t)^2 * 200) * 7.5 - v.firpf * t * 15 + short_arm_offset_right
  pos.z = sin(v.firpf * t * 120) * 1.75
  rot   = sin(v.firpf * (1-t)^2 * 280) * [-60, 40, 20]
  ```
  The attack swing on the **item** (`first_person.attack_rotation_item`, lines 28–45, `"override_previous_animation": true`, bone `rightitem`):
  ```
  pos = [ -sin(sqrt(t) * pi * 100) * 10,  sin(sqrt(t) * pi * 2 * 60) * 10,  -sin(t * pi * 65) * 2 ]
  rot = [ -sin(sqrt(t) * pi * 20) * 25,  -sin(sqrt(t) * 75) * 15,  -sin(sqrt(t) * 25) * 15 ]
  ```
  Equip / swap (`first_person.swap_item`, lines 180–190): `rightarm.position.y = -10 * (1 - variable.player_arm_height)` — the arm drops 10 units and rises back as the new item is raised.

  Walk hand-bob (`first_person.walk`, lines 191–204):
  ```
  pos.x = sin(-walk_distance * 180) * hand_bob * 9.75
  pos.y = -abs(cos(-walk_distance * 180)) * hand_bob * 15 + short_arm_offset
  ```
  Idle breathing (`first_person.breathing_bob`, lines 117–124): `rightitem.position.y = bob_animation * sin(life_time * 45) * 0.5` — **45°/s ⇒ an 8.0 s period, ±0.5 units.**

  The `[JE]` `ItemInHandRenderer` publishes the timing that Bedrock does not: the raise is a clamped ramp of **±0.4 per tick**, so 0→1 takes **3 ticks = 0.15 s**, and the item model only latches to the new item once `mainHandHeight < 0.1`. Rest translation is `(±0.56, −0.52, −0.72)` with a `−0.6` equip dip. The swing envelope is `f2 = sin(sqrt(t) · π)` — **peaking at t = 0.25, strongly front-loaded** — applied as `ZP(i·f2·−20°)`, `XP(f2·−80°)`, `YP(i·−45°)`, with a separate `f1 = sin(t²·π)` driving `YP(i·(45 + f1·−20))`. The swing lasts **6 ticks = 0.3 s**. Hands lag the camera by **10%** of the smoothed pitch/yaw delta, which is what stops the viewmodel feeling welded to the screen. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Item#Item_in_hand]

  Item display transforms for the hand (`item/generated`): `firstperson_righthand` rotation `[0, −90, 25]`, translation `[1.13, 3.2, 1.13]`, scale `0.68`. `item/handheld` overrides the hands only. `block/block`: `firstperson_righthand` rotation `[0, 45, 0]`, scale `0.40`. **Bedrock has no `display` JSON** — `minecraft:render_offsets` is deprecated and the transforms are hardcoded, but they are visually equivalent to Java's, so Java's numbers are the usable source. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Model#Item_models]

- **What we have:** Nothing. `appendSpriteModel` has exactly six call sites (`SpriteModel.cpp`, `Creature.cpp` ×3, `ItemEntity.cpp` ×2, `Projectile.cpp`) and none of them is a hand. `Main.cpp:112` declares `kSwingSeconds = 0.45f` and `swingTimer` is advanced and tested at `:2559`, `:4489` and `:4567–4585`, but **it only rate-limits damage and reach** — no geometry is emitted. `Player.cpp` has no arm, no viewmodel, no bob. (Read in the code.)

- **What must be built:**
  1. A **viewmodel draw pass** that renders after the world with its own projection (the reference uses a narrower FOV for the hand so it does not distort at wide world FOV) and, critically, **clears depth first** so the arm never intersects a nearby block.
  2. An **arm model** — one box, the player skin's right-arm net — posed by the four transforms above.
  3. A **held-item bone** parented to the arm, driven by the existing `SpriteModel` path for flat items and the block-model path for blocks. **This is the fifth drawing site for a block**, and `CLAUDE.md`'s "a block is drawn in four places" warning applies directly: the mesher, the slot picture, the dropped entity, the thrown entity and now the hand. Give it the same owner as the drop path rather than a fifth copy.
  4. Wire `swingTimer` (already ticking) to the swing curve; **change `kSwingSeconds` from 0.45 to 0.30** to match the reference's 6 ticks, or keep 0.45 deliberately and write down why.
  5. The equip ramp, the walk bob and the breathing bob, in that order of value.
  6. Use poses last: eat/drink (`humanoid.use_item_progress`), shield block, bow draw, spyglass.

- **Numbers that matter:**
  - Swing: **6 ticks = 0.30 s**; envelope `sin(√t·π)` peaks at **t = 0.25** (1.5 ticks in).
  - Equip: **3 ticks = 0.15 s**, ramp rate 0.4/tick, latch threshold 0.1.
  - Rest arm: position `[13.5, −10.0, 12.0]`, rotation `[95°, −45°, 115°]`.
  - Rest item translation `(0.56, −0.52, −0.72)` blocks, equip dip `−0.6`.
  - Walk bob: `±9.75` units X, `−15` units Y (absolute-cosine, so **double vertical frequency**).
  - Breathing bob: **8.0 s period**, ±0.5 units.
  - Camera lag: **10%** of the smoothed look delta.
  - `firstperson_righthand` for a flat item: rot `[0, −90, 25]`, tr `[1.13, 3.2, 1.13]`, scale `0.68`. For a block: rot `[0, 45, 0]`, scale `0.40`.

- **Risks / dependencies:** The depth-clear is the trap — a viewmodel that writes depth into the world pass will z-fight and will also be occluded by the block you are mining, and the project has already paid for "a blended fragment still writes depth" three times. The item-in-hand path must reuse the drop's model resolution or it becomes a fifth divergent copy. Nothing else depends on this, and it depends on nothing — it can be built today.

#### G3.2 — Block-entity animation framework · L · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Bedrock publishes no block-entity curves (its `resource_pack/models/entity/` folder ships **only mob models plus arrow, experience_orb, fishing_hook, minecart, item_sprite, trident, fireworks_rocket, wind_charge, leash_knot, evocation_fang, llama_spit and shulker** — no chest, no bell, no piston), so the numbers below are `[JE]`, which uses the identical 1/16-block pivot convention and is visually indistinguishable. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/tree/main/resource_pack/models/entity]

  **Chest.** `ChestLidController.tickLid()` moves openness by **±0.1 per tick**, so a full open is **10 ticks = 0.5 s**. Per-frame it interpolates: `getOpenness(partial) = lerp(partial, oOpenness, openness)`. The renderer then eases it — `f = 1 − (1−x)³` — and applies `lid.xRot = −(f · π/2)`, so the **final angle is 90°** with a cubic ease-out. The lid pivot is `PartPose.offset(0, 9, 1)` ⇒ hinge at **y = 9/16 = 0.5625, z = 1/16 = 0.0625** in block space. A double chest shares one openness value through `ChestBlock.opennessCombiner`, so both halves move together. Ender chests use the same controller. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Chest]

  **Shulker box.** `OPENING_TICK_LENGTH = 10`, `MAX_LID_HEIGHT = 0.5F`, `MAX_LID_ROTATION = 270.0F`, progress ±0.1/tick — **linear, no easing**, unlike the chest. So: 10 ticks = 0.5 s, lid rises half a block while rotating 270°. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Shulker_Box]

  **Piston.** `TICKS_TO_EXTEND = 2` ⇒ **0.1 s**, `progress += 0.5` per tick, travel exactly 1.0 block, interpolated per frame by `getProgress(partial) = lerp(partial, progressO, progress)`. Sticky retraction is identical in reverse. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Piston]

  **Bell.** The published curve is `f4 = sin(f1/π) / (4 + f1/3)` radians, where `f1` is ticks since ringing. That is a sine of period **2π² ≈ 19.74 ticks ≈ 0.987 s** under **hyperbolic damping** — the first peak lands at t ≈ 4.93 ticks with amplitude ≈ **0.1772 rad = 10.15°**, and each subsequent peak is smaller by the `1/(4 + f1/3)` envelope. `DURATION = 50` ticks = **2.5 s**. Pivot `bell_body` at `offset(8, 12, 8)` ⇒ **(0.5, 0.75, 0.5)** in block space. The swing axis is perpendicular to the direction it was struck from. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Bell]

  **Doors, trapdoors, fence gates, levers, buttons, repeaters, cauldrons, composters:** no block entity and no renderer ⇒ **instant snap**. This is structural, not a quoted line — there is simply nothing to animate them. **Our behaviour already matches and this is not a gap.**

- **What we have:** Nothing, and the code says so. `Main.cpp:4441–4444`: *"The reference's swing is an animated model rather than a block state, and we have no animated block models, so the sound is the whole of it."* `Chest.hpp` carries inventory only — no openness, no open-count. `Block.hpp:4388`'s `lidTurns` is a **texture quarter-turn** consumed at `ChunkMesher.cpp:927` for asymmetric top textures such as beds; it has nothing to do with lids opening, and the name will mislead the next reader. (Read in the code.)

- **What must be built:**
  1. A **block-entity animation state** keyed by world position, living outside the chunk mesh (the mesh is static and rebuilt in bulk; a moving lid must not force a remesh). It needs to survive chunk unload/reload gracefully — the simplest correct answer is that it resets to closed, which is what the reference effectively does too.
  2. A **dynamic sub-mesh draw path**: a small per-frame vertex buffer for the handful of animated block entities in view, drawn with the world's own shader and texture atlas. Cap it — the reference caps chest rendering by distance.
  3. Chest first (highest value, and it is the one players open constantly), then piston, then shulker, then bell.
  4. The chest needs an **open-count**, not a boolean, so two players — irrelevant here, single-player — or a hopper interaction do not close it early. Simplify to a single flag plus a close timer.
  5. **Interpolate.** Every one of these is a fixed-tick value with an explicit `lerp(partial, prev, current)` in the reference. Our engine has no fixed tick loop outside `Projectile.cpp`, so the natural fit is to advance openness on `deltaSeconds` directly at 2.0/second (equivalent to 0.1/tick) and skip interpolation entirely — **that is correct here and is not a violation of the project's lesson**, because the lesson is about *fixed* steps needing a blend, and this would not be one.

- **Numbers that matter:**
  - Chest: **10 ticks = 0.5 s**, rate 0.1/tick = 2.0/s, final **90°**, ease `1 − (1−x)³`, pivot **(0, 0.5625, 0.0625)**.
  - Shulker: **10 ticks = 0.5 s**, **270°**, lid lift **0.5 block**, **linear**.
  - Piston: **2 ticks = 0.1 s**, 0.5/tick, travel **1.0 block**, linear + per-frame lerp.
  - Bell: `sin(t/π)/(4 + t/3)` rad, period **19.74 ticks ≈ 0.987 s**, first peak **10.15° at t ≈ 4.93 ticks**, total **50 ticks = 2.5 s**, pivot **(0.5, 0.75, 0.5)**.

- **Risks / dependencies:** The real cost is the dynamic draw path, not the curves — the curves are four lines each. Once that path exists, every subsequent animated block is cheap, which is why this is one gap and not four. It also unlocks G3.4's harder cases and any future block that needs to move. Watch the depth/transparency interaction: an open chest lid over a translucent water block will expose the "blended fragment writes depth" bug shape if the pass ordering is wrong.

---

#### G3.3 — Baby head scaling · XS–S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Baby scaling is **three independent layers**, and this is the part that is easy to get wrong.
  1. **Server-side `minecraft:scale`** inside the `baby` component group. Goat, sheep, ocelot and zoglin use **0.5**; panda and rabbit **0.4**; camel **0.45**; sniffer **0.45**.
  2. **A client-side counter-scale.** `resource_pack/entity/zombie.entity.json` and its siblings carry `"scale": "query.is_baby ? 2.0 : 1.0"`, which *undoes* the server's 0.5 so that a **dedicated baby geometry** — `"geometry": { "default": "geometry.zombie", "baby": "geometry.zombie.baby" }` — renders at its authored size. In other words, for humanoids the baby is a **different model**, not a scaled one.
  3. **Head enlargement.** `animation.humanoid.big_head` is literally `{"bones": {"head": {"scale": 1.4}}}` (`humanoid.animation.json:24–31`).

  Per-species head scale and the pivot offset that compensates for it:

  | Species | Head scale | Offset | Extra |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Humanoid (zombie, skeleton, husk, drowned, stray, player) | **1.4** | none | |
  | Villager / NPC / wandering trader | **1.5** | none | |
  | Cat | **1.5** | none | |
  | Wolf | **1.6** | `[0, 1, −2]` | |
  | Goat | **1.4** | `[0, 10, 4]` | |
  | Panda | **1.8** | `[0, −0.18, 0.15]` | body scale `[1.15, 1.15, 1.0]`, body offset `[0, 1.77, 0]` |
  | Pig / cow / sheep | **2.0** | `[0, 4, 4]` | |
  | Chicken | **2.0** | none | |
  | Sniffer | **1.2** | `[0, 1, 1]` | |
  | Llama | `[1.3, 1.2, 1.2]` | — | legs scale `[0.91, 0.56, 0.91]` |
  | Horse | `1.0 + 0.5 × (1 − model_scale × 16)` | — | continuous, tracks growth |

  [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/humanoid.animation.json] and the per-species `resource_pack/entity/*.entity.json` files.

- **What we have:** `Creature.cpp:551–554`, `kBabyScale = 0.55f`, applied uniformly to the whole model. The comment in place admits the limitation: *"we take the first and the last, since one scale cannot do the middle."* No head scale, no pivot offset, no baby geometry. (Read in the code.)

- **What must be built:**
  1. Add `babyHeadScale` (default 1.4) and `babyHeadOffset` (default zero) to `CreatureSpecies`, populate the eleven rows above, and leave every other species at the humanoid default.
  2. Apply the scale **inside `beginHead()`/`endHead()`** (`Creature.cpp:5390`) so it multiplies only the head frame — which is exactly what the reference does, and is why the neck-joint rig makes this cheap.
  3. Apply `babyHeadOffset` in the same frame, *after* the scale, in model units (÷16 for block space).
  4. Optionally raise `kBabyScale` from 0.55 toward the reference's 0.5, or leave it — 0.55 is close enough that the head is the visible difference, not the body.

- **Numbers that matter:** body **0.5** (0.4 panda/rabbit, 0.45 camel/sniffer); head **1.4** humanoid / **1.5** villager & cat / **1.6** wolf / **1.8** panda / **2.0** pig, cow, sheep, chicken / **1.2** sniffer. Offsets in the table, in 1/16-block model units. Panda additionally widens the body to `[1.15, 1.15, 1.0]`.

- **Risks / dependencies:** Fragment 12's **F18.6** notes that baby chickens draw hand-rolled quads that bypass `modelScale` entirely — **fix that first or the chicken will not respond to this change**. The head scale must not leak into the held-item transform for baby villagers/zombies (the item is on the arm, not the head, so it will not if it is applied inside `beginHead`). Low risk, high visible payoff — this is the best value-per-line item in the whole fragment.

#### G3.4 — Flipbook slots beyond two · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `resource_pack/textures/flipbook_textures.json` is a flat list of animated textures, each with an `atlas_tile`, a frame count and `ticks_per_frame`. Bedrock's `blend_frames` **defaults to true** (Java's `interpolate` defaults to false), which is why Bedrock can run lava at 16 ticks/frame and still look smooth — the frames cross-fade. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/textures/flipbook_textures.json]

  | Texture | Frames | Ticks/frame | Seconds/frame | Notes |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | `fire_0`, `fire_1` | 32 | **1** | 0.05 | Two layers; `fire_0`'s frame list is **rotated by 16** so the pair runs antiphase |
  | `still_water_grey` | 32 | **2** | 0.10 | ✅ we match this exactly |
  | `flowing_water_grey` | — | 1 | 0.05 | plus `"replicate": 2` |
  | `still_lava` | — | **16** | 0.80 | relies on frame blending |
  | `flowing_lava` | — | **10** | 0.50 | plus `"replicate": 2` |
  | `magma` | — | **10** | 0.50 | |
  | `sea_lantern` | — | **5** | 0.25 | |
  | `prismarine_rough` | — | **300** | 15.0 | very slow drift |
  | `campfire` | — | **2** | 0.10 | |
  | `campfire_log_lit` | — | **8** | 0.40 | |
  | `sculk_sensor_tendril_active` | — | **1** | 0.05 | |
  | `sculk_sensor_tendril_inactive` | — | **2** | 0.10 | |
  | `sculk`, `sculk_vein` | — | **20** | 1.00 | |
  | `stonecutter2_saw` | 3 | **1** | 0.05 | |
  | `kelp_*` | — | **4** | 0.20 | |
  | `seagrass` | — | **4** | 0.20 | |
  | `cauldron_water` | — | **2** | 0.10 | |
  | `lantern` | — | **8** | 0.40 | |

- **What we have:** Exactly two slots. `Main.cpp:6877–6893` calls `renderer.setAnimatedLayer` (water) and `renderer.setSecondAnimatedLayer` (fire) and nothing else. `Block.hpp` holds `kWaterFrames = 32` / `kWaterFrameSeconds = 0.1f` (correct) and `kFireFrames = 32` / `kFireFrameSeconds = 0.055f` (`:6541–6542, 7381–7383` — should be 0.05, and see §3.4 #1 for the clock bug). Lava, campfire, sea lantern, magma, kelp, seagrass, sculk and the rest are all still images. (Read in the code.)

- **What must be built:**
  1. Replace the two hard-wired setters with **a small array of animated layers** — a texture-layer index, a frame count, a seconds-per-frame and an independent phase accumulator each. Eight slots covers everything above that matters in the overworld.
  2. **Give each slot its own clock.** The present bug is entirely caused by two slots sharing one wrapped accumulator (§3.4 #1); an array of independent accumulators makes the bug structurally impossible rather than fixed-once.
  3. Wire the obvious ones in value order: **lava** (the most conspicuous still image in the game), campfire + campfire log, sea lantern, magma, kelp/seagrass, sculk sensor tendrils, lantern, cauldron water, stonecutter saw.
  4. Consider frame blending. Lava at 0.8 s/frame will strobe badly without it; if blending is not cheap in the current shader, run lava faster instead and record the divergence.

- **Numbers that matter:** all in the table. The two that most change the look are **lava 16 ticks/frame = 0.80 s with blending** and **fire 1 tick/frame = 0.05 s antiphase across two layers**.

- **Risks / dependencies:** The renderer's animated-layer plumbing is currently a pair of scalars; widening it touches the shader's uniform block. Frame blending doubles the texture fetch for the affected layers. Contained — no gameplay coupling at all.

#### G3.5 — Wolf tail, sit and shake-off-water · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** The wolf is the most animated ordinary overworld mob. `wolf.animation.json` ships **eight clips**: `angry`, `baby_scaling`, `head_rot_z`, `leg_default`, `setup`, `shaking`, `sitting`, `tail_default`. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/wolf.animation.json]
  - **Tail wag while moving:** `tail.rotation.y = cos(query.modified_distance_moved × 38.17) × query.modified_move_speed × 80.22` — i.e. the *same* 38.17°-per-block phase as the legs, so the tail is locked to the gait, at up to **80.22°** of yaw scaled by speed.
  - **Tail height as a health signal:** the tail's rest pitch tracks health. A hurt or hostile wolf drops its tail.
  - **Head tilt:** `head.rotation.z = variable.head_roll_angle × 57.3` — the inquisitive sideways tilt, which is what makes a wolf read as a dog.
  - **Sitting:** body **45°**, front legs **270°**, back legs **333°**.
  - **Shaking off water** (`shaking`): the published Java form is `sin(p·π) × sin(11·p·π) × 27°` applied to body roll over a **2-second** shake, with each body segment offset along `p` so the shake travels head-to-tail. That double-sine is the whole trick: the outer term is the envelope, the inner term is the 11-cycle shudder.
  - **There is no beg clip in Bedrock.** Begging is Java-only; do not build it.
- **What we have:** Nothing wolf-specific. The wolf runs the generic quadruped rig (`Creature.cpp`, verified correct by fragment 12's §18.2). `ANIMATION.md` §5.2 specifies the tail-as-mood-signal and the shake, and both are outstanding. (Read in the code and in `ANIMATION.md`.)
- **What must be built:**
  1. A **per-species clip hook** — one virtual-free `switch` on `species.kind` inside `buildMesh` after the generic pose is laid down, so a species can add rotations on top. This is the shared infrastructure for G3.8 as well, and building it here is most of this gap's cost.
  2. Tail bone on the wolf rig, yawed off the existing `gait` value — the phase is already there, it just needs `cos(gait) × limbSwingAmount × 1.40 rad`.
  3. Tail rest pitch driven by `health / maxHealth` and by whether the wolf is hostile.
  4. Head roll — reuse the existing head frame from `beginHead`.
  5. Sit pose (needs a `sitting` state, which taming will want anyway).
  6. Shake, triggered on leaving water.
- **Numbers that matter:** tail yaw amplitude **80.22° = 1.400 rad** at `cos(distance × 38.17°)`; head roll up to **57.3° = 1.0 rad**; sit body **45°**, front legs **270°**, rear legs **333°**; shake `sin(p·π)·sin(11·p·π)·27°` over **40 ticks = 2.0 s**, segments staggered along `p`.
- **Risks / dependencies:** The clip hook is the real work; the wolf itself is an afternoon once it exists. Sitting depends on a tamed/sitting state that may not exist yet — check the creature fragment (04). The 38.17°/block constant is already in the codebase as the spider's `2.665 rad/m`; derive it once rather than typing a second literal (this is precisely the "same value derived in two places" bug shape).

#### G3.6 — Player view bob · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `[JE]` `GameRenderer.bobView` is the published form and Bedrock is visually identical. With `d = −(walkDist + Δ·partialTick)` and `b = lerp(partialTick, oBob, bob)`:
  ```
  translate.x =  sin(pi * d) * b * 0.5
  translate.y = -abs(cos(pi * d) * b)          // the abs doubles the vertical frequency
  rotate.roll  = sin(pi * d) * b * 3.0 degrees
  rotate.pitch = abs(cos(pi * d - 0.2) * b) * 5.0 degrees
  ```
  `bob` is a smoothed horizontal speed that saturates around **0.11–0.13** at walking pace. The `abs` on the vertical term is the whole character of the effect — the head rises twice per stride, once per footfall. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Options#Video_Settings]
- **What we have:** Nothing. `Player.cpp` has no bob term anywhere; the camera translates and rotates with no gait coupling. The step-up easing at `Player.cpp:947` is a different thing (and is good). (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** A smoothed horizontal-speed scalar on `Player`, a distance accumulator (the player almost certainly already tracks distance for footstep particles — `Particles.cpp` has `spawnFootstep`, so check there first and reuse rather than adding a second accumulator), and four lines in the camera matrix. Gate it behind a settings toggle, because the reference does and because some players get motion sickness from it.
- **Numbers that matter:** X **±0.5·b** blocks, Y **−|cos|·b**, roll **±3.0°·b**, pitch **|cos(πd − 0.2)|·5.0°·b**, `b` saturating at **≈0.12**. The `−0.2` phase offset on pitch is deliberate — it makes the pitch lead the vertical drop.
- **Risks / dependencies:** None. No body needed, no new draw path — this is a camera matrix change and it can ship independently of G3.1. Highest ratio of felt improvement to lines changed in this fragment after G3.3.

#### G3.7 — Head-yaw clamp and per-species clamps · XS · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** The head clamp is **engine-internal and not published in the data files** — `animation.common.look_at_target` (`look_at_target.animation.json:4–16`) is simply `head.rotation = [target_x_rotation − this, target_y_rotation − this, 0]` with `"relative_to": {"rotation": "entity"}` and **no clamp at all**. The clamping happens before Molang sees the value. The only explicit Molang clamps in the entire vanilla pack are: **goat** `clamp(target_x, −40, 40)` and `clamp(target_y, −45, 25)`; **pillager with crossbow** `clamp(target_y, −45, 25)` / `clamp(target_x, −25, 45)`; **player with crossbow** `(−45, 5)` / `(−60, 45)`. **The spider is explicitly unclamped.** [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/look_at_target.animation.json]

  The engine values come from `[JE]`: `getMaxHeadYRot()` returns **75°** for most mobs, **60°** for villagers and **90°** for horses; head pitch is **±40°**. The goat's explicit `−40..40` corroborates the pitch figure independently.
- **What we have:** `Creature.cpp:319`, `kMaxHeadTurn = 0.9f` rad = **51.6°**, and `:323`, `kMaxHeadPitch = 0.7f` rad = **40.1°**. The pitch is right; the yaw is **23.4° short**. Both are applied in `think()` after a `std::remainder(..., kTwoPi)` so a head never spins the long way round — that part is correct and should not be touched. (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** Raise `kMaxHeadTurn` to **1.309 rad (75°)**. Add an optional per-species override for the three that differ: villager **60° = 1.047 rad**, horse **90° = 1.571 rad**, spider **unclamped**. Optionally add the goat's tighter pitch band.
- **Numbers that matter:** default yaw **75° = 1.30900 rad** (currently 0.9); villager **60° = 1.04720 rad**; horse **90° = 1.57080 rad**; pitch **40° = 0.69813 rad** (currently 0.7 — close enough, but derive it from 40° rather than leaving a magic 0.7).
- **Risks / dependencies:** `kHeadTurnRate = 6.0` rad/s means a wider clamp takes proportionally longer to traverse, which is fine. Watch for geometry: a 75° head turn on a wide-necked model (cow, iron golem) may expose the neck seam that 51.6° was hiding — **that is worth checking by eye and I could not**. If it does, the answer is a neck bone, not a smaller clamp.

#### G3.8 — Per-species clips for the remaining characterful mobs · L · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Grouped by species, with the numbers already extracted. All from `https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/tree/main/resource_pack/animations`.

  **Cat** (`cat.animation.json`): `lie_down`, `sit`, `sneak`, `sprint`, `walk`. Sit body **−45°**, tail1 **45°**. Sprint uses phase offsets of **17.19°** and **197.19°** between limb pairs — that ~180° split is what makes the sprint read as a bound rather than a trot.

  **Fox** (`fox.animation.json`): `sleep` body roll **−90°**, head `[0, −115°, cos(anim_time × 160) + 90]`, tail **−125°**; `sit` body **−60°**; `pounce` `body.rotation.x = vertical_speed × −7`; plus `crouch`, `wiggle`, `stuck`, and separate `baby_walk` / `baby_pounce`. Fox clips use **`"lerp_mode": "catmullrom"`** keyframes — smooth curves, not linear ramps.

  **Panda** (`panda.animation.json`): `rolling` is `body.rotation.x = (roll_counter / 32) × 360` ⇒ **32 ticks per revolution = 1.6 s**; `sneezing` is `counter < 15 ? −45 × (counter/14) : −45 + 9 × (counter − 15)` — a fast 15-tick wind-up then a 5-tick snap; `lying` = `lie_amount × −180`; `sitting` = `sit_amount × −90`.

  **Goat** (`goat.animation.json`): `ram_attack` drives the head 0 → **60° over 2.0 s**, with the delightful `"anim_time_update": "math.max(anim_time + (query.should_bow_head ? delta_time : -delta_time * 4), 0)"` — it **winds up at 1× and unwinds at 4×**, so the head snaps back four times faster than it lowers.

  **Bat** (`bat.animation.json`): `flying` `animation_length 0.5` ⇒ **2 Hz wingbeat**; wing Y keys +85° → −55° → +50° → +70° → +85°; the resting pose is body `[180, 0, 0]` — hanging upside-down is a whole-body flip, not a separate model.

  **Parrot** (`parrot.animation.json`): `dance`, `flying`, `sitting`, `standing`. Wings `∓(5 + variable.wing_flap × 57.3)` on Z; dance head Z = `dance.y × 23`; sitting legs **90°**.

  **Rabbit** (`rabbit.animation.json`): `move.v2` `animation_length 0.75`; back legs 0 → **125°** → 95 → 42 → 0; front legs 25.25 → −65 → −67.5 → 0; head **−34.58°**; ears splay **±15°** yaw.

  **Horse** (`horse.animation.json`): `eat`, `rear`, `tail`, `walk`. Rear is `body.rotation.x = −45 × variable.stand_anim`; the idle tail is `cos(life_time × 802) × 57.3` ⇒ a **0.449 s** flick — very fast, and it is what stops a standing horse looking dead.

  **Iron golem** (`iron_golem.animation.json`): `attack` arms = `−114 + ((1.5 × abs(mod(attack_animation_tick − frame_alpha, 10) − 5) − 2.5) / 5) × 57.3` — a **10-tick = 0.5 s** triangle wave, note the `− frame_alpha`, which is the reference doing sub-tick interpolation explicitly; `flower` = `−45.8 + ((0.25 × abs(mod(offer_flower_tick, 70) − 35) − 17.5) / 35)` ⇒ a **70-tick = 3.5 s** offer; the walk lurch is legs `modified_tcos0 × 6.0` with body and head rolling at `/1.5`.

  **Frog** (`frog.animation.json`): `croak` `animation_length 3.0` with a body scale punch `[1,1,1] → [1.3, 2.1, 1.6]` in **0.083 s**; `tongue` `animation_length 0.5`, head **−60°**, tongue scale `[0.5, 1, 5]` at **0.1667 s**; `jump` `"loop": "hold_on_last_frame"`, length **0.375 s**, body −20°, arms −56.14°, legs +45°.

  **Sniffer**: `walk` length **2.0 s**, legs ±35°, six legs staggered by **0.5833 s**.
  **Axolotl**: `idle_underwater` length **5.2 s**, catmullrom.
  **Turtle**: swim legs `clamp(cos(anim_time × 22.92) × speed × 28.65, −90, 90)`; `eggbelly.scale = is_pregnant ? 1 : 0`.
  **Dolphin**: `move` only, at **343.8°/s ⇒ a 1.047 s** cycle — the fastest ordinary gait in the game.
  **Allay**: `idle` length **2.0 s**, catmullrom, wings alternating between `[37.98, 6.50, 22.02]` and `[22.5, 67.5, 0]` every **0.5 s ⇒ 2 Hz**, arms Z ±31.21°.
  **Bee**: `flying` length **2.55 s**, wings **±35°** on Z with keys every **0.05 s ⇒ 10 Hz**; sting = `−175 × sin(attack_time × 180)`.
  **Phantom**: length 2.417 s, `"start_delay": "math.random(0, 2.417)"` — **randomised phase per entity**, wings `±16 × cos(148.969 × anim_time)`, with a `sound_effects` keyframe firing the flap sound at 1.4 s.
  **Silverfish**: 7 segments at `cos(life_time × 1031.4 + 27k)` with amplitudes 27/18/9/18/27/36/45° — a travelling wave down the body.
  **Ravager**: `biting` mouth `sin(min(anim_time / (bite_duration/2), 1) × 180) × 40°`; `roaring` 40°; `stunned` `[15, 0, 0]`; walk legs ±22.92°.
  **Pillager**: crossbow charge `lerp(−55.62, −90, crossbow_charge)`.
  **Cod / salmon**: `flop` tailfin `cos(animationamountblend × 45) × −25.75`, body ×2, head ×4; the swim clip uses 30.0.
  **Armadillo**: `walk` length **1.45833 s**, hind legs ±50°.
  **Camel**: `walk` length **1.5 s**, `"anim_time_update": "anim_time + max(1.215, pow(10, modified_move_speed) / 2.9) * delta_time"` — a floor on the gait rate so a stationary camel still shifts its weight.

  **Species with no clip at all — do not build one:** pig, cow, mooshroom (their JSON is `baby_transform` + `setup` only), enderman, llama (llama spit is a *separate entity*, not a clip), snow golem (only `piece1.rotation.y = target_y × 0.25`), witch (only a nose oscillator, `sin(life_time × 57.296) × 4.5`), skeleton/stray (attack only), drowned (attack only), zombie (attack + swimming). **And the villager has no work or trade clip in Bedrock** — that is a genuine BE↔JE divergence and Bedrock wins, so a villager standing at a lectern doing nothing is *correct*.

- **What we have:** The generic rig with different boxes for all of these. Fragment 12's §18.2 confirms the quadruped, biped, hopper, fish, swimmer and vermin rigs are all correct as generic rigs — the gap is character, not correctness. (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** The per-species clip hook from G3.5, then one species at a time. Order by how often the player sees them: **cat and horse** (tamed, always nearby), **fox and panda** (biome showpieces), **bat and parrot** (constantly in view when present), **goat**, **rabbit ears**, **iron golem flower**.
- **Numbers that matter:** all above. Note the repeating idioms: `catmullrom` for anything organic, `hold_on_last_frame` for one-shots, a randomised `start_delay` for anything that appears in groups (phantoms — and this is exactly the seeded-phase rule that fragment 12's F18.4 says did not travel to our herds).
- **Risks / dependencies:** Depends on G3.5's hook. Several clips need behaviour state that may not exist (sitting, sneezing, rolling, pouncing, ramming, croaking) — cross-check fragment 04 before committing to any given species. Each species is XS–S once the hook exists; the L rating is the aggregate.

#### G3.9 — Player third-person body and its poses · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `humanoid.animation.json` and `player.animation.json`. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/player.animation.json]
  - **Walk** (`humanoid.move`, lines 238–253): `leftarm = [v.tcos0, 0, 0]`, `rightarm = [−v.tcos0, 0, 0]`, `leftleg = [v.tcos0 × −1.4, −0.1, −0.1]`, `rightleg = [v.tcos0 × 1.4, 0.1, 0.1]`. With `v.tcos0 = cos(modified_distance_moved × 38.17) × modified_move_speed / gliding_speed_value × 57.3`, that is **arms ±57.3° and legs ±80.2°** — the **1 : 1.4 ratio** fragment 12's F18.5 flags as missing on our mobs. **38.17°/unit ⇒ a 9.43-block stride cycle.**
  - **Idle bob** (`humanoid.bob`, lines 31–42): `leftarm.z = −((cos(life_time × 103.2) × 2.865) + 2.865)`, right arm positive. **±2.865° about a +2.865° offset, at 103.2°/s ⇒ 3.488 s.** We already match this exactly on mobs.
  - **Attack** (`player.attack.rotations`, lines 11–23): `rightarm.x = −(sin((1 − (1−t)⁴) × 180) × 1.2 + sin(t × 180)) × 30.0`; the left arm term is ×10.0; peak ≈ −66° pitch and −60° yaw.
  - **Sneak** (`player.sneaking`, lines 279–303): `body.position = [0, −2, 0]`, `head.position = [0, −1, 0]`, arms `x = −5.7°`, legs `x = −28.0°`, `root.position = [0, 1.25, 9.0]`, `root.rotation.x = 28.0 − this` ⇒ a **28° forward lean**. The mob variant `humanoid.sneaking` uses **72°**, which is why a sneaking mob looks far more hunched than a sneaking player.
  - **Swim** (`player.swim`): `animation_length 1.3`, `"override_previous_animation": true`; left arm keys at `0: [0,180,180]`, `0.7: [0,180,287.2]`, `1.1: [90,180,180]`, `1.3: [0,180,180]`; `root.rotation = [swim_amount × (90 + target_x_rotation), 0, 0]`. `swim.legs` = `lerp(0, cos(life_time × 390) × 17.2, swim_amount)` ⇒ **±17.2° at a 0.923 s kick**.
  - **Crawl** (`player.crawl`): the same key set but `"anim_time_update": "query.modified_distance_moved / 15.0"` — distance-driven rather than clock-driven, length 1.3.
  - **Sleep** (`player.sleeping`): `head.rotation = [30 − this, −this, −this]`, `root.rotation = [−90, 270 − sleep_rotation − body_y_rotation, 0]`, with a 24-unit offset to put the body on the mattress.
  - **Use item** (`humanoid.use_item_progress`): `rightarm.rotation = [startup × −60 + interval × 11.25, startup × −22.5 + interval × 11.25, startup × −5.625 + interval × 11.25]`.
  - **Spyglass** (`humanoid.holding_spyglass`): `[clamp(target_x − 105 − (sneaking ? 15 : 0), −170, 180), clamp(target_y − 15, −60, 90), 5]`.
  - **Shield** (`player.shield_block_off_hand`): left arm `[−20, 20, 20]`.
  - **Bow** (`humanoid.bow_and_arrow`): `leftarm = [target_x − 90 − sin(life_time × 76.8) × 2.865 − this, target_y + 28.65, −cos(life_time × 103.2) × 2.865 − 2.865]` — note the **sway continues while aiming**, which fragment 12's F18.8 observes our archers drop.
  - **Elytra: out of scope** (not obtainable in the overworld).
- **What we have:** No player model, no third-person camera. `Player.cpp:573–619` lowers the eye height when sneaking and that is the entirety of the player's visible state. (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** A player model (the mob biped rig is already correct and can be reused wholesale — that is most of the saving), a third-person camera mode with collision, then the poses in the order walk → sneak → swim → sleep → crawl.
- **Numbers that matter:** arms **±57.3°**, legs **±80.2°** (ratio **1 : 1.4**), stride **38.17°/block**; sneak lean **28°** player / **72°** mob with body dropped 2 units; swim kick **±17.2°** at 0.923 s; sleep root `−90°` pitch.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Needs G3.1's model work to be worth anything, and needs a third-person camera that does not clip through terrain. If a third-person camera is not planned, **drop this to P3** — an invisible body is not worth animating. Note the sneak lean is a *root* rotation, which our rig expresses naturally through `place()`.

#### G3.10 — Zombie aggressive arm raise · XS · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** On acquiring a target, a zombie's arms rise from the neutral hang to roughly horizontal and stay there while it pursues. `ANIMATION.md` §5.5 records the intended numbers as **80° → 120°**, which corresponds to the reference's aggressive-pose blend on the humanoid rig; the arms interpolate in over the standard **0.2 s blend transition** rather than snapping. [https://github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples/blob/main/resource_pack/animations/humanoid.animation.json]
- **What we have:** Nothing. Our zombies walk with the neutral biped sway right up until the attack swing fires. `ANIMATION.md` §5.5 explicitly lists this as outstanding. (Read in the code and in `ANIMATION.md`.)
- **What must be built:** An `aggro` scalar on `Creature` easing 0→1 when a target is acquired (the targeting state already exists — `Creature.cpp` behaviour bodies write `swingTimer` at `:2024–2026`), and one added pitch term on the shoulder in `biped()`, gated on the species being an unarmed undead. Multiply the existing idle sway by `(1 − aggro)` so the two do not fight.
- **Numbers that matter:** rest → **80°–120° pitch** (1.396–2.094 rad); blend in over **4 ticks = 0.2 s**, which is Bedrock's de-facto default `blend_transition`.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Must not apply to armed bipeds (they already have the raise-and-swing curve) or to archers (`species.shootsArrows`, protected by the `archersShareOneRig()` static_assert at `Creature.cpp:2229`). Interacts with fragment 12's **F18.5** — if the arm amplitude is corrected to 1/1.4 of the legs at the same time, tune this on top of the corrected value, not the current one.

#### G3.11 — Breeding, taming and combat particles · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `minecraft:breedable` sets `inLove = 600` ticks = **30 s**. Entering love mode emits **exactly 7 HEART particles**, and so does a successful breeding. While in love, an ambient heart spawns **every 10 ticks**. Each particle gets a velocity of `gaussian × 0.02` per axis. Post-breed cooldown is **6000 ticks = 5 minutes**. Taming emits **7 HEART on success and 7 SMOKE on failure**, with the same spread. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Breeding] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Taming]
- **What we have:** `Particles.cpp` exposes seven spawners — `spawnBlockBreak`, `spawnSplash`, `spawnFootstep`, `spawnSmoke`, `spawnFlame`, `spawnEat`, `spawnExplosion` — plus `emitAmbient`. **No hearts, no crit, no sweep, no villager happy/angry, no taming smoke, no note, no totem.** `kMaxParticles = 3000`. Particles **shrink rather than alpha-fade** from `kFadeFrom` (`Particles.cpp:317–344`) because they run on the cutout path. (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** A `spawnHeart` (the smoke spawner already exists and can serve taming failure directly), wired to whatever breeding and taming code exists — check fragment 04, this may be blocked on the mechanics rather than the particles. Then crit particles on a falling attack and sweep particles on a wide swing, both of which need the player's attack path.
- **Numbers that matter:** **7** particles on the burst; **1 per 10 ticks = 0.5 s** while in love; love lasts **600 ticks = 30 s**; velocity `gaussian × 0.02` blocks/tick per axis; cooldown **6000 ticks = 300 s**.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Trivial once breeding exists. The shrink-not-fade rendering means a heart will pop out of existence rather than dissolve — acceptable, but if it reads badly the fix is an alpha-blended particle pass, which is a bigger change and carries the depth-write trap.

#### G3.12 — Hurt tint duration · XS · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** The damage red tint lasts **10 ticks = 0.5 s**. Notably, **there is no hurt *animation* anywhere in `bedrock-samples`** — the entity does not flinch or recoil; the tint is purely a render state applied by the engine, and the knockback is physics. The shader constants are unpublished; `[JE]` is approximately `lerp(albedo, red, 0.3)` with full-white specular suppressed. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Damage]
- **What we have:** `Creature.cpp:57`, `kHurtSeconds = 0.35f` = **7 ticks**. The tint is 30% short. We also correctly hold the tint through the death fall (`:5286`), which matches. (Read in the code.)
- **What must be built:** Change the constant to `0.5f`. **But read the dependency first.**
- **Numbers that matter:** **10 ticks = 0.50 s** (currently 7 ticks = 0.35 s).
- **Risks / dependencies:** **`hurtTimer` is not just a tint timer.** `Creature.cpp:4130` uses it as the knockback-override window — while `health > 0 && hurtTimer > 0`, the creature's `wish` vector is replaced by the shove velocity. Lengthening it from 0.35 s to 0.5 s makes every knockback **43% longer**, which changes combat feel and could change whether a mob can close distance between hits. **Split the two timers** — a `hurtTintTimer` at 0.5 s and a `knockbackTimer` left at 0.35 s — rather than changing one number and shipping a combat change by accident. This is exactly the bug shape in `CLAUDE.md`'s opening box: one value doing two jobs.
