### 5.3 Gap detail

**The y-mapping rule used throughout this section.** Our world is y 0–95 with sea level 24; Bedrock's is y −64–319 with sea level 63. Anchoring both at sea level and taking the ratios of the two halves gives:

```
below sea level:  ourY = 24 + 0.17 × (bedrockY − 63)
above sea level:  ourY = 24 + 0.28 × (bedrockY − 63)
```

These constants are not invented here — they are the ones the generator's own comments state (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:47`, `:165`, `Climate.cpp:155`) — and they are exactly calibrated: Bedrock y −64 maps to our y 2.4 (our bedrock band is 0–4) and Bedrock y 320 maps to our y 96.0 (our top). Every Bedrock y-value below is quoted raw **and** through this rule.

| Bedrock y | Ours | Bedrock y | Ours |
|---|---|---|---|
| −64 | 2.4 | 16 | 16.0 |
| −59 | 3.3 | 32 | 18.6 |
| −54 (lava level) | 4.1 | 39 | 19.9 |
| −51 (ancient city floor) | 4.6 | 50 | 21.8 |
| −40 | 6.5 | 56 | 22.8 |
| −32 | 7.9 | **63 (sea level)** | **24** |
| −24 | 9.2 | 72 | 26.5 |
| −16 | 10.6 | 80 | 28.8 |
| −8 | 11.9 | 96 | 33.2 |
| 0 | 13.3 | 128 | 42.2 |
| 8 | 14.6 | 192 | 60.1 |
| 15 | 15.8 | 320 | 96.0 |

Note the compression: **Bedrock's entire 127-block underground becomes 24 blocks here, and its 96-block "deepslate world" (y −64…0) becomes 11 blocks.** That single number explains most of what follows.

#### G5.1 — Loot tables and chest generation · M · P0 — ✅ **system built 2026-08-18; ~37 of ~40 tables still absent**

> ✅ **What was built, and where it diverged from the plan below.** `game/src/world/Loot.hpp`:
> `struct Entry { ItemId item; std::uint16_t weight; std::uint8_t countMin, countMax; }` (six bytes),
> `struct Pool { first, count, rollsMin, rollsMax, total; }` as a **slice of a flat `kEntries` array**
> rather than a `std::span`, and `struct Table { firstPool, poolCount; }` indexed by a `TableId` enum.
> Three flat arrays, under a kilobyte of `.rodata`, no heap and no allocation during a roll. Item 1 of
> the plan, in the shape the plan asked for.
>
> Five things the plan did not say, each of which turned out to matter:
>
> - **`ItemId::None` is the reference's own `empty` entry**, and it is how an item this game does not have
>   is kept out of a chest **without disturbing every other item's rate in the same pool**. The alternative
>   — deleting the row — silently re-weights everything beside it. The only village items we cannot make
>   are the snowball, the bundle and three horse armours, about 5% by weight and none of them in these
>   three tables.
> - **`Pool::total` is stored and `static_assert`ed against the sum of its own weights.** A mistyped weight
>   is then a build failure rather than a drop rate that is quietly wrong forever and biased toward the
>   last row. This is the `foodTablesAgree()` pattern the plan asked for, pointed at the one number that
>   cannot be checked by reading a single row.
> - **Nothing is modelled that no village table uses**: no conditions, no `quality`, no `bonus_rolls`, no
>   sub-table entries, and no function except `set_count` — which is folded onto the entry row as a count
>   range rather than modelled as a function. Modelling "functions" would be a plugin architecture for one
>   plugin. Item 4's deferral of enchanting turned out to be free rather than a compromise: **not one
>   Bedrock village loot table contains `enchant_randomly`, `enchant_with_levels` or an enchanted book.**
> - **The numbers are Mojang's shipped behaviour pack, not the wiki** — exactly as this gap warned. The
>   wiki blanks most weight cells and gets the butcher's meat and the plains house's poppy wrong. Where a
>   recent version changed a table, the pre-change baseline is used, because this game has no copper tier
>   and no spears.
> - **A `LootChest` block-id marker, which is item 2 and item 5 answered together.** Generation returns
>   blocks and only blocks, so it cannot hand out contents and stay pure in `(seed, chunkCoord)`. A village
>   therefore places one of **12 new ids** — 3 tables × 4 facings, `kBlockIdCount` 3,225 → 3,237 — carrying
>   nothing but which table it owes. The **first interaction rolls it** from `(worldSeed, block position)`
>   and `setBlock`s it into a plain chest. That write flags the chunk modified, so the chunk is loaded
>   rather than regenerated thereafter, **which closes a duplication exploit with no save-format bump**:
>   `saveChests` discards an empty chest rather than writing it, so *open → empty → save → reload* would
>   otherwise have found the marker still there and re-rolled it. The marker must be consumed **before**
>   any path writes Air over the cell, or a break spills an empty chest.
>
> **Item 3 (slot scatter) is built.** Item 4 (enchanting) is deferred and costs nothing. **`TableId`'s
> order is written into saved worlds** — an unrolled chest stores `(id − LootChestRunFirst) / 4` — so
> append, never insert.
>
> **What is still absent, which is most of it.** Roughly **37 of the ~40 overworld tables**: dungeon,
> mineshaft, stronghold corridor/crossing/library, desert pyramid, jungle temple, igloo, shipwreck ×3,
> buried treasure, ocean ruins ×4, pillager outpost, woodland mansion, ruined portal, ancient city ×2,
> trial chambers, trail ruins, **the three fishing tables**, and **the twelve remaining village tables**
> (armorer, butcher, cartographer, fisherman, fletcher, mason, shepherd, tannery, temple, and the four
> non-plains house biomes, which today all fall back to `VillageHouse`). And the harder half: **no
> structure other than a village exists to put a chest in**, so this gap's own "blocks 15 of the 25
> structures" line is unchanged in practice. **Never played** — no chest has been opened.

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Every generated chest is filled from a loot table — a JSON document of `pools`, each with a `rolls` count (fixed or a range) and a list of weighted `entries`, each carrying `functions` such as `set_count`, `enchant_randomly`, `enchant_with_levels`, `set_damage` and `looting_enchant`. The authoritative Bedrock source is the vanilla behaviour pack's `loot_tables/chests/*.json` (mirrored publicly at `github.com/Mojang/bedrock-samples`). The wiki's own tables live at `https://minecraft.wiki/w/Module:LootChest/chests`. Roughly 40 overworld chest tables exist (village house/armorer/weaponsmith/toolsmith/cartographer/mason/butcher/fletcher/fisherman/tannery/temple/shepherd ×5 biome variants, desert pyramid, jungle temple, jungle temple dispenser, simple dungeon, abandoned mineshaft, stronghold corridor/crossing/library, igloo chest, shipwreck map/supply/treasure, buried treasure, ocean ruin big/small warm/cold, pillager outpost, woodland mansion, ruined portal, ancient city, ancient city ice box, trial chambers ×several, trail ruins rare/common). [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Loot_table] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Chest]
- **What we had on 2026-08-17:** Nothing. `Chest.hpp:29-42` is `std::array<ItemStack, 27>` plus an `empty()` helper, and a grep of `game/src` for `loot` finds only `Creatures::Loot` (`Creature.hpp:1230`), which is the unrelated mob-drop table. **Read in the code, certain.**
- **What must be built:**
  1. A `game/src/world/LootTable.hpp` mirroring the reference's shape: `struct Entry { ItemId item; int weight; int minCount; int maxCount; std::uint8_t flags; }`, `struct Pool { int minRolls; int maxRolls; std::span<const Entry> entries; }`, `struct Table { std::span<const Pool> pools; }` — all `constexpr` tables, no allocation, so a `static_assert` can prove every weight is positive and every item id is real (this is the `foodTablesAgree()` pattern, and it is what stops the tables rotting).
  2. A `fill(Chest&, const Table&, noise::Stream& roll)` that is a **pure function of `(seed, structure origin, chest index)`** — it must not consult the world, or a chest re-rolls when re-generated.
  3. Slot scatter: the reference shuffles the chosen stacks into random empty slots rather than filling 0..n.
  4. Enchantment support can be deferred; start with `set_count` only and add `enchant_with_levels` when the enchanting system is asked about.
  5. Persist the filled chest exactly like a player chest — it already round-trips through `WorldStore`.
- **Numbers that matter:** 27 slots (`Chest.hpp`, matches Bedrock). Typical pool shapes: simple dungeon 1–3 rolls of a 17-entry pool; desert pyramid 2–4 rolls plus a bonus pool; buried treasure has a guaranteed heart-of-the-sea pool of exactly 1 roll. **I could not verify the current per-item weights from a citable wiki table within this task** — the wiki's `Module:LootChest` data is now versioned to a much later release and contains items that do not exist in 1.21.x. Treat the numbers as needing one fetch of `bedrock-samples/behavior_pack/loot_tables/chests/` at implementation time.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Blocks 15 of the 25 structures in §5.1's table. Nothing blocks *it*. This is the single highest-leverage item in this fragment.

#### G5.2 — Monster rooms (dungeons) and spawners · S · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** **14 attempts per chunk** — up to 10 in y 0–320 and up to 4 in y −58…−1. The room's interior is 7 or 9 blocks in each of width and length (so 7×7, 7×9, 9×7 or 9×9) and **6 tall**. A candidate position is rejected unless the walls have between 1 and 5 two-block-tall openings at floor level. The floor is **75% mossy cobblestone / 25% cobblestone**. Exactly one spawner sits at the centre: **zombie 50% / skeleton 25% / spider 25%**, and on Bedrock a zombie spawner has a **5% chance of being a zombie villager spawner**. **0–2 chests**, each given 3 placement attempts; a candidate must be an empty cell with exactly one solid side. **A Bedrock quirk worth copying deliberately or not at all: monster rooms can also generate above sea level.** [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Monster_Room]
  The spawner itself: activation radius 16 (spherical, measured from the block centre to the player's feet), 4 spawn attempts per cycle, delay 200–799 ticks, cap of 6 mobs within **16×10×16 on Bedrock** (centred on the lower-north-west corner) against 9×9×9 [JE], horizontal spawn area a taxicab diamond of 4, 15–43 XP when broken with a pickaxe. Bedrock spawners are waterloggable and fully transparent. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Monster_Spawner]
- **What we have:** `BlockId::MonsterSpawner` exists (`Block.hpp`, id 933) and nothing places it. `Cobblestone` and `MossyCobblestone` both exist. **Read in the code, certain.**
- **What must be built:** A `dungeonInCell`-style pure function alongside `Structures.cpp`'s tree grid — the tree cell machinery (`Structures.cpp:522`, candidate grid + `kReach` margin so a straddling structure is identical from both chunks) is exactly the right pattern and can be reused wholesale. Then a spawner block-entity with the tick logic, which is a gameplay item rather than a worldgen one.
- **Numbers that matter:** Our world has ~19 usable rock blocks between the bedrock band (top y 4) and typical surface. Bedrock's *lower* band (−58…−1) maps to **our y 3.4–11.9** and its upper band (0–320) maps to **our y 13.3–95**. With a 6-tall room that fits comfortably in both. Attempt counts must be restated per **32×32 column** to match `kOreVeins`' convention: Bedrock's 14 per 16×16 chunk = **56 per 32×32 column**, but scaled for our 4× shallower rock that becomes roughly **12–14 per column** to keep the same dungeons-per-cubic-metre. Room 7–9 across, 6 tall, floor 75/25 mossy.
- **Risks / dependencies:** The chests want G5.1. The spawner wants the mob-spawning system to accept an explicit spawn request — worth checking that it does before scheduling. This is the cheapest structure on the whole list and the one with the most gameplay per line.

#### G5.3 — Lava: the cave floor has landed, lakes and springs have not · S · P1

> ✅ **The lava floor landed on 2026-08-19 and this entry was a P0 until then.** `kLavaLevel = 6` in [game/src/world/TerrainGenerator.cpp](game/src/world/TerrainGenerator.cpp) fills carver-emptied cells at or below y 6, applied after the downward classification walk and before the ocean fill, with `static_assert`s pinning it above `kBedrockTop` and below `kSeaLevel`. **`BlockId::Obsidian` therefore has a natural source for the first time**, and every claim elsewhere in this file that it does not is stale — they are corrected, but check the date on any you find. **This closes the P0 half; lakes and springs remain and are P1.** *Not build-verified: no compilation has evaluated the tree as it stands (see the ✅ legend at the top of this file).*
>
> **Worth recording, because it is the rarest outcome in this document: the prediction below was right before the fact.** "Numbers that matter" reasoned from the y-mapping to **our y 5–7**, independently of anyone implementing it, and the constant landed on **6** — the middle of that range, reached by the implementer from the reference's aquifer rule by two routes that both round to 6. A mapped number agreeing with a separately-derived range is the only evidence available in a project with no reference build to diff against. **Source class: secondary, mapped not ported** — `bedrock-samples` publishes no worldgen data, so do not cite 6 as a reference constant.

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Below y −55 every air block produced by the noise router becomes lava, giving a flat lava sea whose surface is at **y −54**. Above that, aquifers can locally choose lava instead of water on a 64×40×64 cell grid (always water above y −10). Lava lakes generate as a `lakes` decoration step, **only above y 0 since 1.18**, in any biome except the deep dark, with a small air pocket above them. Lava springs generate underground throughout. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cave] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** **The floor, as of 2026-08-19.** Carver-emptied cells at or below `kLavaLevel = 6` are filled with lava. Lakes and springs are still absent — *this becomes false the moment `TerrainGenerator.cpp` or `Structures.cpp` gains a lava write outside the flood layer, which is the one grep that refutes it.* The pre-2026-08-19 text read "**Nothing.** … a grep … returns **zero hits**", which was correct when measured and is now wrong; it is kept here only to date the change.
- **What must be built:**
  1. ~~A lava floor: every cave cell below a `kLavaLevel` becomes lava rather than air.~~ ✅ **Landed 2026-08-19.**
  2. Surface lava lakes: a per-column rarity roll producing a small basin, in the same style as the existing decoration hashes.
  3. Lava springs: a single source block in a rock face, which is the cheapest of the three.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's lava surface y −54 maps to **our y 4.1** — which is *inside our bedrock band* (`kBedrockSolid = 0`, `kBedrockTop = 4`). So the mapped value is unusable as-is; the honest choice is **our y 5–7** for a lava floor, i.e. a 1–3-block-thick sea directly on the bedrock roof. That is thin but it is what a 96-block world affords, and it is the clearest single illustration of the height constraint. **This range was written before the implementation and the code landed on 6.** Lava lakes above Bedrock y 0 → **our y ≥ 13**.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Fluid simulation and player damage already exist (lava is placeable), so this is worldgen-only. **The cross-system consequence is now resolved: obsidian has a natural source as of 2026-08-19**, so nothing downstream of it is blocked by generation any more.

#### G5.4 — Mineshafts · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Placement is `spacing 1 / separation 0` with a **0.4% probability per chunk** — i.e. not a grid at all, a per-chunk roll — so mineshafts are dense and overlapping. Corridors are 3 tall with oak (or dark oak, in the badlands variant) fences and planks, cobwebs, rails, chest minecarts, and **cave spider spawners inside cobweb clusters** (the only place other than a monster room where a spawner generates naturally, and unlike the monster room there can be any number of them). The badlands variant generates much closer to the surface. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Mineshaft] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** Nothing. All four rail families exist as block ids (`RailRunFirst`…`ActivatorRailRunLast`), as do `Cobweb`, `Torch`, all fence and plank types, and `Chest`. **Read in the code, certain.**
- **What must be built:** The first *jointed* structure in the codebase — a corridor generator that walks a graph from a start point. Two design constraints from this repo's own rules make this harder than it looks: generation must be a **pure function of `(seed, chunkCoord)` with no neighbour reads** (CLAUDE.md, non-negotiable), so a mineshaft cannot be "grown" chunk by chunk. The village system already solves exactly this problem — `Village.cpp` plans the whole village deterministically from the cell seed and then each chunk renders only the part that falls inside it (`village::Nearby` holds ≤4 plans). **Reuse that shape; do not invent a second one.**
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's y range for a standard mineshaft is roughly −64…10 → **our y 2.4–15.4**, which is a 13-block band and enough for a 3-tall corridor with a floor. Per-chunk probability 0.4% restated per 32×32 column ≈ **1.6%**. Chest minecarts: 3 per mineshaft on average.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.1 for the chest minecarts. Minecart entities must exist for chest minecarts specifically — otherwise place plain chests and note the divergence.

#### G5.5 — Cave biomes: dripstone, lush and deep dark · L · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Three underground biomes selected by the **`depth` parameter**, which increases by 1/128 per block below the surface, rather than by any surface climate. **Dripstone Caves**: surface rule is plain stone; `dripstone_cluster` features (height 3–6, radius 2–8, density 0.3–0.7, layer thickness 2–4, search range 12) and `large_dripstone` columns (radius 3–19, search range 30, height scale 0.4–2.0, capped at a 0.33 radius-to-cave-height ratio); pointed dripstone `chance_of_taller` 0.2, directional spread 0.7. It also carries a **large copper ore variant, size 20, 16 tries, y −16…112, dripstone caves only**. **Lush Caves**: generate under any biome whose humidity ≥ 0.7; located from the surface by azalea trees growing over rooted dirt and hanging roots; `vegetation_patch` places moss, cave vines with glow berries, dripleaf and spore blossoms; **clay blob size 33 with 46 tries per chunk, lush caves only**; axolotls and tropical fish. Note Bedrock's lush caves are drier than Java's. **Deep Dark**: generates under low-erosion (mountainous) regions and never below oceans; sculk patches, veins, catalysts and shriekers (sensors only inside ancient cities); **no regular mob spawning at all**; the warden arrives after 4 shrieker triggers; it is the only biome where lava lakes cannot generate. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cave] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Deep_Dark] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Lush_Caves] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Dripstone_Caves]
- **What we have:** Nothing, and the reason is structural: `Climate` (`Climate.hpp`) has five fields and `biomeAt` (`Biome.cpp:333`) takes a column, not a position. **Every block these three biomes need already exists** — Moss Block/Carpet, Dripstone Block, Pointed Dripstone, Sculk + Catalyst + Vein + Sensor + Shrieker, Azalea + Flowering Azalea + both leaf types, Glow Lichen, Big/Small Dripleaf, Cave Vines, Glow Berries, Spore Blossom, Rooted Dirt, Hanging Roots, Calcite, Tuff, Smooth Basalt, Reinforced Deepslate. **`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md`'s "Named divergences" claim that none of them exist is stale — see §5.4 #4.**
- **What must be built:**
  1. Add `depth` to `Climate` and a `biomeAtDepth(seed, x, y, z)`. The cheapest honest version: keep the existing 2D surface biome for surface rules and decoration, and add a **separate** 3-entry cave-biome lookup consulted only by the cave-decoration pass. That avoids touching the 30-row box search and avoids the risk of a cave biome bleeding into a surface rule.
  2. A cave-decoration pass that runs after carving, walks each carved cell, and asks whether it is a floor, a ceiling or a wall — the mesher already has to answer that question, so the predicate exists somewhere.
  3. Three feature sets. Dripstone is the easiest (two features, both purely local). Lush is next. Deep dark should be deferred until an ancient city is on the schedule, because sculk without the city is scenery.
- **Numbers that matter:** `depth` increases 1/128 per block down in Bedrock's 384-block world; over our 96 that is **1/32 per block** if the *fraction* is preserved, or **1/128** if the absolute rate is. Preserve the fraction — the biome bands are stated as fractions. Our caves live between y 5 and the noodle ceiling at y 34 (`kNoodleCeiling`), so the whole cave-biome band is ~29 blocks tall. Large dripstone columns of radius 3–19 will not fit; cap at radius 3–6. Deep dark's "erosion < −0.22 and depth > 0.9" test maps directly, since erosion is dimensionless.
- **Risks / dependencies:** The `depth` parameter is a real change to the climate contract and touches `Climate.hpp`, which everything reads. Doing it as a separate lookup (step 1 above) contains the blast radius. Deep dark depends on G5.21 (ancient city) to be worth anything.

#### G5.6 — Stone-variant and soil blobs · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Nine `ore`-type features that place stone and soil rather than metal, all in the `underground_ores` decoration step:

  | Blob | Size | Tries/chunk | y range | Notes |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Dirt | 33 | 7 | 0…160 | uniform |
  | Gravel | 33 | 14 | −64…320 | uniform |
  | Granite / Diorite / Andesite (lower) | 64 | 2 each | 0…60 | uniform |
  | Granite / Diorite / Andesite (upper) | 64 | 1-in-6 each | 64…128 | uniform |
  | Tuff | 64 | 2 | −64…0 | uniform |
  | Clay | 33 | 46 | −64…256 | **lush caves only** |

  Size 33 yields up to ~160 blocks and size 64 up to ~864 — these are *large*. Bedrock generates tuff **after** the metal ores, unlike Java. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ore_(feature)]
- **What we have:** Nothing. `kOreVeins` (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:197`) has 9 rows and all 9 are metals or gems. Gravel, clay and andesite appear only as biome `patch` blocks on the *surface*. **Consequence read in the code, certain: `BlockId::Granite` and `BlockId::Diorite` (`Block.hpp:125-126`) are never written by any generation path, so they cannot be obtained in a survival world.**
- **What must be built:** Three extra rows on `kOreVeins` plus a `replaces` predicate (a blob must replace stone *and* deepslate, and dirt/gravel must not eat air). `placeVein` already handles sizes this large — the spindle formula is size-agnostic — but the `kVeinReach = 6` neighbourhood radius will need raising for size-64 blobs, and that is a **border-consistency change**: get it wrong and a granite blob is cut in half at a chunk edge.
- **Numbers that matter:** Mapped to our world — dirt 0…160 → **y 13.3–51.2**; gravel −64…320 → **the whole world**; granite/diorite/andesite lower 0…60 → **y 13.3–23.5**, upper 64…128 → **y 24.3–42.2**; tuff −64…0 → **y 2.4–13.3**. Tries per chunk restated per 32×32 column is ×4, then scaled down for our shallower rock: dirt ≈ 7, gravel ≈ 14, each stone type ≈ 3, tuff ≈ 3 per column. Sizes should be scaled down too — a size-64 blob (864 blocks, ~12 across) in an 11-block-deep deepslate layer would be a wall; **use size 24–33 for the stone types here.**
- **Risks / dependencies:** None. This is the highest visual return per line of code on the whole list — it is what makes an underground read as rock rather than as a texture.

#### G5.7 — Surface structure batch A: desert pyramid, jungle temple, igloo, swamp hut, pillager outpost · L · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** All five are single fixed (or near-fixed) buildings on a spacing grid.

  | Structure | Spacing / separation (chunks, JE `structure_set`) | Biome | Contents |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Desert Pyramid | 32 / 8 | Desert | 4 chests around a hidden chamber over a **TNT-and-pressure-plate trap**; an archaeology room with suspicious sand |
  | Jungle Temple | 32 / 8 (BE id `temple`) | Jungle, Bamboo Jungle | 2 chests, a **lever puzzle**, an arrow-dispenser trap on tripwire |
  | Igloo | 32 / 8 | Snowy Plains, Snowy Taiga, Snowy Slopes | Surface hut; **~50% have a basement** (ladder under the carpet) with a chest, a brewing stand, and a zombie villager + villager in cells. BE differs from JE in window and villager details |
  | Swamp Hut | 32 / 8 | Swamp, Mangrove Swamp | No chest. Spawns a **witch and a black cat**; the cauldron/potion details differ between BE and JE |
  | Pillager Outpost | 32 / 8, **20% probability**, never within 10 chunks of a village | Most non-ocean surface biomes | A watchtower plus tents/cages; 1 chest; pillagers spawn from designated columns; a caged allay; a chance of an iron golem in a cage |

  All five sit on a `heightmap` anchor and use terrain adaptation to avoid floating. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Desert_Pyramid] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Jungle_Pyramid] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Igloo] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Swamp_Hut] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Pillager_Outpost] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** Nothing. The *machinery* however is all present and proven: `Village.cpp` already does grid cell → deterministic plan → per-chunk render, a site-roughness test (25 probes, reject if the range exceeds `kSiteRoughness = 11`), a biome gate, a water gate, a cave-carved gate, and a platform under the building. **A single-building structure is strictly simpler than a village and should reuse `village::Nearby`'s shape rather than a new one.**
- **What must be built:** One `Structure` concept covering "a fixed blueprint placed on a spacing grid in a biome", with the five (and later ten) blueprints as data. The blueprints are the work, not the placement. Traps need pressure plates, TNT, tripwire and dispensers — check each exists before scheduling; `Cobweb`, `Chest`, `Iron Bars` and `Sandstone` all do.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's 32/8 chunk grid is 512 blocks spacing / 128 separation in *its* 16-block chunks. Ours are 32 blocks, so **state these in blocks like `Village.cpp` deliberately does**: 512 spacing / 128 separation. That is comfortably denser than our village grid (448/160), which is right — a village should be the common find. Pillager outpost 20% probability and the 10-chunk (160-block) village exclusion both map directly. Structure heights: pyramid ~20 above ground, outpost tower ~14, igloo ~5 plus a ~9-deep basement. **All five fit in our 96-block world with room to spare** — height is not the blocker here, blueprints and G5.1 are.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.1 for four of the five. Witch, pillager, allay and zombie-villager mob types must exist; with 57 species in the game most probably do, but that is **inferred, not verified** in this pass.

#### G5.8 — Ocean content · L · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:**
  - **Ocean Ruins** 20/8: cold and warm variants; the cold variant splits **30% "big" / 70% "small"**; pieces are buried using structure voids so they emerge partially from the seabed; 1–2 chests; the warm variant carries suspicious sand for archaeology.
  - **Shipwreck** 24/4: several orientations (upright, sideways, capsized, beached), wood-type pairs, and up to **3 chests** — map, supply and treasure — with the map chest holding the buried-treasure locator. Bedrock uses stripped logs and acacia where Java does not.
  - **Buried Treasure** spacing 1 / separation 0 with a **1% probability per chunk**, placed at **chunk-relative x=8, z=8 on Bedrock** (9,9 on Java). One chest, always containing a heart of the sea.
  - **Ocean Monument** 32/5, **58×58 blocks**, roof at **y 56** on Bedrock, base around y 39; requires deep-ocean-tagged biomes in a 29-block radius; contains 8 gold blocks in the central chamber behind elder guardians; no chests.
  - **Coral reefs**: warm ocean only. Bedrock uses four distinct generators — `coral_feature` (4 shapes), `coral_crust_feature`, `sea_anemone_feature` (y ≥ 48) and `coral_hang_feature` (y ≥ 50) — and **Bedrock coral reefs contain no sea pickles**, unlike Java.
  - **Icebergs**: **1/8 chance per chunk on Bedrock**, frozen/deep-frozen ocean only, 30% snow-capped, blue ice at 1/100, elliptic shape 20% of the time (Bedrock-only); circular radius 0–11, height 3–13 (90%) or 10–34 (10%), depth 3–18. Hardcoded to sea level.
  - **Kelp**: 1/18 chance per chunk, absent from frozen, deep frozen and warm oceans; grows as a **column to near the surface**. Seagrass tall-chance 0.6. Sea pickles 1/6 per chunk in groups of 1–4, warm ocean only.
  [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ocean_Ruins] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Shipwreck] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Buried_Treasure] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ocean_Monument] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Coral_Reef] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Iceberg]
- **What we have:** `TerrainGenerator.cpp:633-660` places single blocks on the seabed — one of 5 coral blocks at 5%, a sea pickle at 1.8%, seagrass or kelp at 14% — and nothing else. **Kelp is one block tall, never a column** (read in the code, certain). No structure of any kind exists in water.
- **What must be built:** Ruins, shipwrecks and buried treasure are all G5.7's blueprint system with a submerged anchor instead of a surface one, and are the cheapest ocean content. Coral reefs, kelp columns and sea-pickle clusters are decoration changes inside the existing seabed pass and are cheaper still. **The ocean monument is the one item genuinely blocked by world height** — see below.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's monument spans y 39 → 56, i.e. **17 blocks of structure with its roof 7 below sea level**. Mapped: base y 19.9, roof y 22.8 — **a 3-block-tall monument**, which is absurd. Our deep ocean floor sits around y 11 and sea level is 24, so the deepest water column available is **13 blocks**; a monument needs ~24. **An ocean monument cannot be built at the current world height without either shrinking it beyond recognition or deepening the ocean, and deepening the ocean costs surface height elsewhere because the continentalness spline is one curve.** Everything else maps fine: shipwreck 24/4 → 384/64 blocks; ocean ruins 20/8 → 320/128 blocks; buried treasure 1% per 16×16 chunk → **4% per 32×32 column**, at column-relative 16,16. Icebergs 1/8 per chunk → 1/2 per column, height 3–13 → **1–4 in our scale** (which is barely an iceberg; consider keeping Bedrock's absolute heights here rather than scaling, since icebergs sit above water where we have 66 blocks of headroom).
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.1; G5.15 for the monument specifically; elder guardian and drowned mob types.

- **Bedrock behaviour:** 30 overworld ore placements. The metal and gem rows, with `size` / `tries per chunk` / `y range` / `distribution` / `air-exposure discard`:

  | Ore placement | Size | Tries | Bedrock y | Ours (mapped) | Dist | Discard |

  | Redstone uniform | 8 | 4 | −64…15 | 2.4…15.8 | uniform | — |
  | Redstone lower | 8 | 8 | −64…−32 | 2.4…7.9 | triangle | — |

  | **Emerald (10 mountain biomes only)** | 3 | 100 | −16…480 | 10.6…96 | triangle | — |

  Size is not a block count: 3→4, 4→5, 7→10, 8→10, 9→13, 10→16, 12→23, 17→37, 20→52. Empirically, the layer where each ore is most abundant is: coal 45, copper 43, iron 14, lapis −2, gold −18, redstone −59, diamond −59, emerald 85. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ore_(feature)]
  Separately, **ore veins** are a distinct noise-driven system that is part of cave generation, not decoration: copper veins y 0…50 (thickest 20–30) surrounded by granite, iron veins y −60…−8 (thickest −40…−28) surrounded by tuff; 70% of the vein volume is left unchanged, of the rest 10–30% is ore, of which 98% is normal ore and 2% is a raw-metal block; a single vein can exceed 2,000 ore blocks. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ore_vein]
- **What we have:** 9 rows in `kOreVeins` (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:197`), attempts stated **per 32×32 column**:

  | Ore | size | attempts/column | min / peak / max | airDiscard |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | AncientDebris | 3 | 3 | 3 / 8 / 16 | 1.0 |
  | Emerald | 3 | 36 | 10 / 46 / 62 | 1.0 |
  | Diamond | 5 | 2 | 3 / 6 / 17 | 0.7 |
  | Lapis | 6 | 3 | 3 / 13 / 25 | — |
  | Gold | 7 | 3 | 3 / 9 / 20 | 0.5 |
  | Redstone | 7 | 10 | 3 / 5 / 17 | — |
  | Iron | 7 | 35 | 3 / 14 / 27 | — |
  | Copper | 8 | 26 | 10 / 26 / 39 | — |
  | Coal | 12 | 70 | 8 / 26 / 70 | 0.5 |

  Copper, gold, lapis, redstone and coal map remarkably closely to Bedrock. The gaps, all **read in the code, certain**:
  1. **`OreVein` has no biome field.** Emerald generates in every biome including plains and ocean floors; Bedrock restricts it to 10 mountain biomes. Infested stone and the badlands gold bonus are likewise impossible to express.
  2. **No upper iron band.** Bedrock's single largest ore placement is iron at 90 tries per chunk above y 80 — the reason mountains are worth mining. Our iron stops at y 27 (mapped Bedrock y 56).
  3. **No upper coal band** — ours ends at y 70, Bedrock's runs to the build limit at 30 tries.
  4. **No second variants** — no buried lapis, no large/buried/lower diamond, no copper large.
  5. **AncientDebris is in the table.** This is a *Nether* ore in Bedrock. Here it feeds `Smelting.cpp:23` → `EmberiteScrap`, our netherite-tier equivalent, and since the Nether is permanently cut this is almost certainly **deliberate** — it is the only way the tier is reachable. Flagging it so nobody "fixes" it. See §5.4 #8.
  6. `veinHeight` does not produce the triangle its comment promises — **this is a real bug, see §5.4 #1**, and it matters most here because five of the nine rows are triangle rows.
- **What must be built:** A `BiomeTag` mask column on `OreVein` (the tag bitmask at `Biome.hpp:80-101` already answers "is this a peak/highland biome" and "is this badlands"), three or four extra rows, and the `veinHeight` fix. All of it is table work in one file.
- **Numbers that matter:** All in the table above. One caution: our attempts are per 32×32 column over a ~24-block-deep rock volume; Bedrock's are per 16×16 chunk over a ~127-block one. **The volume ratio is (32×32×24)/(16×16×127) ≈ 0.76**, so Bedrock's per-chunk figure is very nearly the right per-column figure for us *if the y-range is mapped too* — a happy accident of the two scalings, and worth writing down before someone multiplies by 4.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Biome-gating an ore means `placeVein` must sample the biome at the vein origin, which is one extra `biomeAt` call per attempt — cheap, but it must be sampled at the **origin**, not per block, or a vein straddling a biome edge comes out different from each side and violates the border-consistency rule.

#### G5.10 — The 24 missing biomes · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** See the full table in §5.1. The climate bands the boxes are cut from are the reference's own and we already use them: temperature −1/−0.45/−0.15/0.2/0.55/1; humidity −1/−0.35/−0.1/0.1/0.3/1; continentalness mushroom −1.2…−1.05, deep ocean …−0.455, ocean …−0.19, coast …−0.11, near-inland …0.03, mid-inland …0.3, far-inland …1.0; erosion 7 bands at −1/−0.78/−0.375/−0.2225/0.05/0.45/0.55/1; peaks-and-valleys valley −1…−0.85, low …−0.2, mid …0.2, high …0.7, peaks …1.0. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Biome] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** 30 rows in `Biome.cpp:47-330`, using exactly those band constants (verified: T −0.45/−0.15/0.20/0.55, H −0.35/−0.10/0.10/0.30, C −0.455/−0.19/−0.11, E −0.375 and 0.45–0.55, PV −0.85/0.20/0.70). The **jungle weirdness split is at −0.05, not 0** — a deliberate divergence already in the code.
- **What must be built:** Split into three tiers.
  - **Tier 1, pure table rows (11):** Lukewarm / Deep Lukewarm / Cold / Deep Cold / Deep Frozen Ocean (temperature slices of the ocean row — trivial, since bed material is depth-gated not biome-gated so nothing else changes), Savanna Plateau, Wooded Badlands, Windswept Savanna, Windswept Forest, Sunflower Plains, Birch Forest. Each needs at most one new surface-noise rule or one tree-list entry. **Effort: XS each.**
  - **Tier 2, one new feature each (10):** Ice Spikes (spike feature), Mushroom Fields (huge mushrooms + a `C −1.2…−1.05` island band), Flower Forest (tall flowers — blocked on missing block ids), Old Growth Pine/Spruce Taiga (mega conifer + podzol/coarse-dirt surface noise + boulders), Old Growth Birch Forest (super birch), Eroded Badlands (hoodoos), Cherry Grove (cherry tree + pink petals), Mangrove Swamp (mangrove tree + roots + a y 61–63 water rule + mud floor), Dark Forest done properly (dark oak + a dense low canopy), Pale Garden.
  - **Tier 3, blocked (3):** the cave biomes — G5.5.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's mangrove swamp puts water at y 61–63 with a Mud floor → **our y 23.5–24**, i.e. a one-block water table, which is *exactly* the same problem the sugar-cane rule has (§5.4 #7): our vertical resolution near the waterline is one block where Bedrock has three. Mangrove swamp will need its own rule rather than a mapped constant. Mushroom fields' continentalness band −1.2…−1.05 is **outside our continentalness spline's defined range** — the spline extrapolates linearly beyond −1.10 (`Climate.cpp:160`), so the band is reachable but the height it produces is unverified.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Adding rows changes the enum, and **the enum order is the selection priority** (`Biome.cpp:333`) — inserting in the wrong place silently changes which biome wins an overlap. The `BiomeId` value is also written into save data indirectly via generated chunks; a reorder means a `kChunkFormatVersion` bump. **Append, do not insert**, unless a priority change is intended.

#### G5.11 — Trees, huge mushrooms and the missing woods · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Per-biome weighted tree lists. Numeric attempts-per-chunk are **not published on the wiki**; the figures below come from `RESEARCH.md` §15.7, which is a **Java datapack dump `[JE]`** and should be treated as indicative: plains 0.05/chunk, forest 10.1, dark forest 16, taiga 10.1, savanna 1.1, jungle 50.1, sparse jungle 2.1, bamboo jungle 30.1, swamp 2.1 (water depth 2), mangrove swamp 25 (water depth 5), meadow 1/100. Species mixes: savanna acacia 0.8 else oak; taiga pine 0.333 else spruce; plains fancy oak 0.333 else oak, both with a 0.05 bee-nest chance; jungle fancy 0.1 / bush 0.5 / mega 0.333 / else jungle. **Every list carries `fallen_*_tree` at 0.0125.** Heights run from 1 log (jungle bush) to 30–31 (mega jungle, mega spruce, mega pine); dark oak 6–8; the canopy sits 1 above the highest log (3 for fancy oak); leaf clusters are 5–7 across; branched trees carry 1–6 branches of 1–6 logs, and **regular oak, regular jungle, all birch and all spruce have no branches at all**. Fallen trees: oak 4–7 logs, birch 5–8, super birch 5–15, spruce 6–10, jungle 4–11, with a 75% chance of vines on the stump. **Huge mushrooms** generate in Mushroom Fields, Dark Forest and — on Bedrock only — Swamp; height 5–7 with a 1-in-12 chance of 9, 11 or 13; brown is a 7×7 flat canopy with the corners missing, red is a dome of five 3×3 slabs. **Boulders** (`forest_rock`, mossy cobblestone) generate in Old Growth Pine and Old Growth Spruce Taiga **only** — not, as is often assumed, in windswept gravelly hills. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tree] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Huge_mushroom]
- **What we have:** 7 variants in `Structures.cpp` — Oak, Branching (fancy), Spruce, Pine, JungleSmall, JungleMega, JungleBush — selected by a 3-value `TreeShape` on the biome row (`Tall` / `Round` / `Jungle`). Four woods reach the world (`Structures.cpp:279-291`): oak, birch (a **1-in-4 roll on any `Oak` variant, in every biome**), spruce, jungle. `DarkOakLog` and `AcaciaLog` exist in `Block.hpp` and are **never written by any generation path — read in the code, certain, and it means neither wood is obtainable in survival**. Densities live on the biome rows: Jungle 0.88, DenseForest 0.80, BambooJungle 0.62, Taiga 0.50, Forest 0.45, SnowyTaiga 0.42, Grove 0.38, Swamp 0.14, Plains 0.10, SparseJungle 0.09, Meadow 0.04, Savanna 0.04, WindsweptHills 0.03, GravellyHills 0.02, SnowyPlains 0.01, SnowySlopes 0.01. Jungle dressing (cocoa at 20% of small trees on the lowest 3 logs, vines on 75% of trunks) is present and good.
- **What must be built:** (a) an `Acacia` variant with the diagonal trunk and flat canopy, wired to Savanna; (b) a `DarkOak` variant with the 2×2 trunk, wired to DenseForest; (c) `fallen` variants at ~1.25%; (d) mega spruce/pine for the old-growth taigas; (e) huge mushrooms; (f) boulders. Each is a new `TreeVariant` enum value plus a builder function — the file is well-shaped for this and the additions are independent of each other.
- **Numbers that matter:** All heights above are **absolute block counts and must NOT be mapped** — a tree is a tree regardless of world height, and our surface band (y 4–90) has 66 blocks above sea level, so even a 31-block mega spruce fits. Our current heights: Pine 6–8, Spruce 5–7, Branching 6–10, Oak 4–6, JungleBush 1, JungleMega 11–18, JungleSmall 5–10 — **all shorter than Bedrock's**, which is a legitimate choice given the height budget but worth a decision rather than an accident. Bedrock dark oak 6–8 and acacia 5–8 fit as-is.
- **Risks / dependencies:** None. This is self-contained in one file and is the most visible-per-effort item after G5.6.

#### G5.12 — Amethyst geodes · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** A `local_modifications` step feature — it runs **before** ores and **overrides caves, aquifers and canyons**, which is why a geode is never sliced open by a cave. **1 chance in 24 per chunk**, y **−58…30**. Concentric shells by distance field: smooth basalt at 4.2, calcite at 3.2, amethyst block at 2.2 of which **8.3% become budding amethyst**, and hollow air at 1.7. `outer_wall_distance` 4–6, `distribution_points` 3–4, `point_offset` 1–2, min/max generation offset ±16. **Crack chance 95%** with a base crack size of 2.0 — so nearly every geode has an opening. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Geode] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Amethyst_Geode]
- **What we have:** Nothing. **Every block exists**: `AmethystBlock`, `BuddingAmethyst`, `AmethystCluster` and all three bud sizes, `Calcite`, `SmoothBasalt`.
- **What must be built:** A single self-contained pure function: pick a centre from the cell hash, evaluate the distance field with the 3–4 offset distribution points, write the shells. It is ~80 lines and touches nothing else. **The one subtlety is ordering** — it must run *before* `isCave` is consulted, or a cave will eat the geode. Our generator carves first and decorates after (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:467-870`), so the geode pass must either write into the pre-carve pass or be allowed to overwrite air.
- **Numbers that matter:** y −58…30 → **our y 3.4…18.4**, a 15-block band that comfortably holds a geode of outer radius ~6. Chance 1/24 per 16×16 chunk → **1/6 per 32×32 column**. Shell radii (4.2 / 3.2 / 2.2 / 1.7) are absolute and should not be scaled — the geode is small enough already. Budding fraction 8.3%, crack chance 95%.
- **Risks / dependencies:** None. Best candidate for a first "real feature" after the blob work, because it proves the pre-carve ordering problem in a contained way.

#### G5.13 — Villages: what is missing inside them · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Spacing 34 / separation 8 chunks. The **bell is the meeting point** and the biome sampled at the meeting point decides the whole village's style — which is exactly the rule we already implement. Building foundation platforms are **circular on Bedrock and square on Java**; ours is circular, which is correct. **2% of villages generate as zombie villages** (cobwebs, no doors, zombie villagers). Cats spawn at 1 per 4 beds up to 5. **Bedrock iron golems spawn periodically once the village has ≥10 villagers and ≥20 beds**, unlike Java's "a villager who slept and has a workstation summons one". One camel per desert village meeting point; two armour stands per taiga village. **Zombie sieges are Java-only.** 13 job-site blocks map 1:1 to 13 professions: armorer/blast furnace, butcher/smoker, cartographer/cartography table, cleric/brewing stand, farmer/composter, fisherman/barrel, fletcher/fletching table, leatherworker/cauldron, librarian/lectern, mason/stonecutter, shepherd/loom, toolsmith/smithing table, weaponsmith/grindstone. Bedrock's village bounding box is 65×25×65. Every building type has its own chest loot table. A known Bedrock bug, **MCPE-100217**, is that Bedrock villages do not reliably generate the expected per-type structure sets. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Village] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Villager]
- **What we have:** A genuinely complete village generator (`Village.cpp`, 1342 lines): 448-block grid, 160 separation, `kReach = 56`, measured at 81 villages per 841 cells ≈ one per 1,450 blocks. 25-probe site test with a `Reject` enum (None/Biome/Water/Carved/Rough) and `kSiteRoughness = 11`. 11 designs (TownCentre, SmallHouseA/B/C, MediumHouse, LargeHouse, Workshop, Library, Temple, Farm, AnimalPen) over 5 palettes, a 12% empty-plot chance mirroring the reference's `empty_pool_element`, a 9-across town centre with a stone well, bell, 4 torches and 4 market stalls each carrying a job block, 4 streets 3 wide and 16–25 long with plots at a 6-block pitch alternating sides, `kJobSiteCount = 13`, one iron golem, and residents at 5% babies with adults 90% unemployed / 10% nitwit.
- **What must be built, in order of value:**
  1. ✅ **Chests in houses with per-building loot tables** — G5.1. This is the difference between a village being a place and being scenery. **Landed 2026-08-18.** Three tables — weaponsmith, toolsmith and plain house — placed in `Village.cpp:1038` at the interior corner furthest from the job block, with hand-stepped exceptions for `LargeHouse` (the ladder owns that corner) and `Workshop` (the counter does), both backed against the +X wall. A chest is placed as a `LootChest` marker id and rolled on first interaction; see G5.1. **The ten remaining building-type tables are not written** — every other design's house falls back to the plains-house table, and the smiths are the only two job buildings with their own.
  2. **Villagers with starting professions.** Right now nobody has one (`Village.cpp` resident roll), so a fresh village offers no trades at all until the profession-assignment system runs — worth verifying whether it does.
  3. Crops in the Farm design's plots (farmland and 4 crop types exist).
  4. Zombie villages at 2%.
  5. Cats at 1 per 4 beds, camels in desert villages, armour stands in taiga villages.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock 34/8 chunks = **544 / 128 blocks**; ours is 448 / 160. Ours is therefore *denser in spacing but more separated*, giving a similar density — no change needed. Village bounding box 65×25×65 (Bedrock) vs our `kReach = 56` half-extent = 112 across, so ours is a larger footprint; that is a deliberate visual choice. Cats 1 per 4 beds max 5; golem threshold ≥10 villagers and ≥20 beds; zombie village 2%.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.1 for item 1. Items 2–5 are gameplay-side rather than worldgen-side and may belong to another fragment.

#### G5.14 — Carvers: cave carvers and ravines · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Noise caves (which we have) are *not* how caves reach the surface — **carvers are**, and they still run in 1.18+ alongside the noise caves. A cave carver starts at y −56…180; 1 in 4 has a main room 1–14 blocks tall and 5–15 in diameter with 1–4 trunks leading off it; a trunk-to-branch length is 85–112 blocks; trunk thickness varies horizontally ~2–38 and vertically ~1–36, branches ~2–7 and ~1–7. Carvers cannot carve red sand or snow blocks. **Canyons (ravines)** are 85–127 long, under 15 wide, up to 62 deep, starting at y 10…72; on Bedrock they can reach bedrock with lava at the bottom; they are filled with stone under rivers and swamps and water-filled in oceans. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cave] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Canyon]
- **What we have:** Three noise systems and a 2D "cave mouth" hack (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:290-330`): an entrance field at wavelength 230 / threshold 0.26 / width 0.14 that relaxes `kCaveSurfaceMargin` **for the spaghetti carver only** and opens fully in about 12% of columns; submerged columns never open. No ravines at all. **Read in the code, certain.**
- **What must be built:** A carver is a *path*, and paths break the purity rule the same way mineshafts do. Same answer: plan the whole carver deterministically from a cell seed (the village pattern), then let each chunk carve only the part inside it. A ravine is the cheaper of the two and gives most of the visual payoff.
- **Numbers that matter:** Ravine start y 10…72 → **our y 15.0…26.5**. Depth up to 62 → **our ≤11 blocks below its start**, so a ravine here is a 11-deep, ≤15-wide, 85–127-long gash — still dramatic at our scale, and it would reach from near the surface to near bedrock, which is arguably *better* than Bedrock's proportions for a shallow world. Carver start y −56…180 → **our y 2.8…56.8**. Main room 1–14 tall → keep 1–8. Branch length 85–112 → keep absolute; a 100-block cave is 3 chunks long and that is fine.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Ravines interact with G5.3 (lava at the bottom) and G5.17 (water fill in oceans). They must respect the same `surfaceCarvedAt` predicate the village site test and the tree gate already use (`TerrainGenerator.hpp`), or villages will start appearing over ravines.

#### G5.15 — World height 96 → 192 · XL · P2

**This is the question the brief asks directly, so here is the direct answer: no, 96 blocks is not the single biggest constraint. G5.1 (loot) is.** Height blocks four specific things and squeezes several more, but **19 of the 22 gaps in §5.2 can be built at 96 today.** That said, it is the constraint that gets worse the longer it is left, because every constant added in the meantime is tuned to 96.

- **Bedrock behaviour:** y −64…319, **384 blocks**, sea level 63, lava level −54, clouds at y 191–195, non-Amplified terrain capped around y 256. Caves and Cliffs Part II shipped as Bedrock 1.18.0 on 30 November 2021 and the height change was its headline. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Altitude] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** `kWorldHeightChunks = 3` (`TerrainGenerator.hpp:18`) × `Chunk::kSize = 32` = 96, sea level 24 (`Biome.hpp:69`), surface clamped 4…90 (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:26-27`). Measured surface min/mean/max 8 / 31.2 / 87, 23.3% of columns below sea level.
- **What it actually prevents — quantified:**

  | Thing | Needs | We have | Verdict |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Ocean Monument | ~24 blocks of water column (base y 39, roof y 56 = 17 tall, 7 under the surface) | 13 blocks max (deep ocean floor ≈ y 11, sea level 24) | **Impossible** |
  | Ancient City | floor at Bedrock y −51 → our y 4.6, plus ~25 blocks of interior | y 4.6 is on top of the bedrock roof; 25 blocks up is y 30, above sea level | **Impossible** |
  | Trial Chambers | Bedrock y −40…−20 → our y 6.5…9.9, a 3-block band, for a multi-room complex | 3 blocks | **Impossible** |
  | Full Stronghold | multi-level, 20+ blocks of vertical extent under the surface | ~19 usable blocks between bedrock roof and mean surface | **Very tight; a one-level stronghold only** |
  | Mountain biomes | Bedrock peaks reach y 256 → our y 78; jagged peaks are ~120 blocks above sea level there | our max surface is 90, i.e. 66 above sea level | **Works, but peaks are ~half scale.** This is already visible: the erosion gain was lowered from 2.35 to 1.75 after a "too many peaks" playtest |
  | Cave layering (3 distinct depth bands) | Bedrock has 127 blocks below sea level | we have 24, of which 5 are bedrock band and 6 are the surface margin — **13 usable** | **Works but flat.** This is why cave biomes will feel thin even once G5.5 lands |
  | Ore band separation | 9 Bedrock bands spread over 384 | 9 of ours over 96, several overlapping | **Works** — the mapped table in G5.9 shows the bands survive |
  | Lava sea | Bedrock y −54 → our y 4.1 | inside the bedrock band | **Forces a fudge** (G5.3) |
  | Mineshafts, dungeons, geodes, fossils, all surface structures | ≤ 20 blocks each | fine | **No problem** |

- **What raising it would cost — honest estimate:**
  - **Memory and streaming, linearly.** A `Chunk` is 64 KB of block ids (2 bytes × 32,768) + 32 KB of light + 4 KB of waterlogged bits = **100 KB**, and `Chunk.hpp` stores them as dense `std::array`s with no sparse/empty-chunk representation. At the default `renderDistance = 12` (`Settings.hpp`) the load span is 25×25 columns = 625 columns × 3 chunks = 1,875 chunks ≈ **188 MB resident**. Going to 6 chunks (192 tall) doubles that to ~375 MB; going to 12 (384 tall) quadruples it to ~750 MB. **The mitigation is obvious and should land first: an all-air chunk needs no storage**, and above y 90 every chunk is air by construction.
  - **Generation and meshing time, linearly** in the same ratio, minus whatever the empty-chunk fast path saves. Meshing is already threaded (M12), so this is a throughput cost rather than a stutter one — but chunk *upload* is main-thread.
  - **Save format.** `kChunkFormatVersion = 4` (`WorldStore.cpp:81`) exists precisely for this; bump it and old chunks regenerate. **This is the cheap part.** Note the standing lesson: water flow calls `setBlock`, which marks a chunk modified, so merely standing near an ocean writes chunks to disk — old saves in `saves/` **will** be stale and must be deleted or migrated, and "the fix didn't work" will otherwise be the first symptom.
  - **Retuning, and this is the real cost.** Every constant in the generator is calibrated to 96: `kSeaLevel = 24`, `kMinSurface`/`kMaxSurface` 4/90, `kReliefBlocks = 22`, the 7 continentalness spline points (11…35), the 8 erosion relief points, the 6 peak profile points, `factor` 4.6–6.2, `kBedrockTop = 4`, `kDeepslateAlways`/`kNever` 9/15, the `freezesAt` lapse rate 0.0173/block above y 29, `kNoodleCeiling = 34`, `kCaveSurfaceMargin`/`kCaveFadeDepth`/`kCavernSurfaceMargin` 6/10/12, all 9 ore bands, `kShallowBedDepth = 6`, `kSandstoneDepth = 3`, and the tree height ranges. **None of these can be scaled mechanically** — the spline points are heights, the margins are absolute, the lapse rate is a gradient. Budget a full re-tuning pass and a playtest round, not an arithmetic pass.
- **Recommendation:** **`kWorldHeightChunks = 3 → 6` (192 blocks, sea level 48).** It doubles memory rather than quadrupling it, it unblocks ocean monuments (26 blocks of water column), strongholds and a reduced ancient city, it roughly doubles cave layering to 26 usable blocks, and it lets mountains reach ~2× their current relief. 384 buys little more that a player would notice at the cost of 4× everything. **Schedule it after G5.1 and G5.6 but before G5.16/G5.21**, because those structures are the ones that need it and everything else is cheaper to build once and not retune.

#### G5.16 — Strongholds · L · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Strongholds do not use the spacing/separation grid; they are placed in **concentric rings** around the origin, with Bedrock's ring counts and radii differing from Java's. A stronghold is a jigsaw of corridors, spiral staircases, five-way crossings, libraries (one- or two-storey, with bookshelf loot chests), storerooms, prison cells, fountain rooms, and one **End portal room** with a silverfish spawner — the only naturally generated silverfish spawner in the game. Two loot table types: corridor chest and library chest. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Stronghold]
- **What we have:** Nothing. All the blocks exist — `StoneBricks` with Chiseled/Mossy/Cracked, `IronBars`, `Chest`, `Bookshelf`, `SeaLantern`, `MonsterSpawner`, `Cobblestone`.
- **What must be built:** The most complex jigsaw structure on the list. It should be **last** among the underground structures, after mineshafts have proven the deterministic-path pattern.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock strongholds sit largely below sea level with a vertical extent of ~20 blocks. Our usable rock between the bedrock roof (y 5) and mean surface (y 31) is **26 blocks**, so a single-level stronghold fits *now* and a proper multi-level one needs G5.15. Ring radii are absolute distances from the origin and should not be scaled.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.1, G5.15. **End dependency, noted in one line as the brief asks: the End portal room's frame is an End feature — build the stronghold and the portal room, place the frame blocks as decoration with no destination, and revisit if the End is ever added.**

#### G5.17 — Aquifers, lakes and springs · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Aquifers are a 1.18 replacement for water lakes, which were **removed** in Bedrock beta 1.18.0.21. Each aquifer cell is Empty, Flooded, or has a local fluid level. Above the preliminary surface an aquifer is always Flooded; where erosion < −0.22 **and** depth > 0.9 it is always Empty (in practice only the deep dark qualifies); otherwise aquifer noise below 0.4 gives Empty and above 0.8 gives Flooded. The local water-level cell is **16×40×16** and the water-vs-lava cell is **64×40×64**; above y −10 the fluid is always water. Water springs generate below y 192; the Java config is `rock_count 4, hole_count 1`. Lava lakes generate above y 0 only. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Cave] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** An elegant substitute rather than an implementation. Water fills whatever the **uncarved** terrain left empty (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:625`), so a cave under the sea stays dry and the ocean never drains into it. **This gets aquifer-like behaviour for free and is the right call for a small world** — but it means there is no water underground at all: no underground lakes, no springs, no waterfalls, and no wet caves.
- **What must be built:** The cheap version, and the one worth doing first, is **springs**: a single water source in a rock wall at a low rarity, letting the existing fluid simulation do the rest. Full aquifers are only worth it alongside G5.5 (lush caves want water) and G5.14 (ravines want water in oceans).
- **Numbers that matter:** Water springs below Bedrock y 192 → **our y ≤ 60**, effectively everywhere underground. Aquifer cells 16×40×16 → at our scale **16×8×16**. Lava-vs-water cell 64×40×64 → **64×8×64**. "Always water above y −10" → **above our y 11.9**, i.e. almost everything.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G5.3 for the lava half. Flowing water underground is a performance question the fluid system must be asked about before this is scheduled.

#### G5.18 — Badlands banding, red sand and the two variants · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** The badlands surface rule is the most elaborate in the game. Above y 256 → orange terracotta. Above y 74 → if the surface noise falls in (−0.909…−0.5454), (−0.1818…0.1818) or (0.5454…0.909), plain terracotta, else the **hoodoo banding**. Otherwise red sand over red sandstone. An erosion hole gives orange terracotta; water 6 deep or less gives white terracotta. The banding itself is **192 layers of randomly coloured stained terracotta generated per seed** (red, orange, yellow, brown, white and light gray) above y 63, each layer shifted by up to 7 blocks by noise. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Badlands]
- **What we have:** `BiomeId::Badlands` with plain terracotta as `top`/`filler` and a clay `patch` — no banding, no red sand. **`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` says this is because we lack the terracotta colours; that is stale — all 16 dyed terracotta and all 16 glazed variants exist in `Block.hpp`.** See §5.4 #4. The one genuinely missing block is `RedSand` (and by extension red sand's use in the ocean-floor rule), which would need one new id and one texture row.
- **What must be built:** A 192-entry (or, scaled, 48-entry) `constexpr` colour band table seeded per world, a noise offset per column, and three extra branches in the top-block sequence at `TerrainGenerator.cpp:520-560`. It is a surface rule, not a feature — no new machinery.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's banding starts above y 63 (sea level) → **our y 24**, i.e. all badlands terrain above the waterline. 192 layers over Bedrock's 257-block above-sea range → scaled to our 66-block range that is **~48 layers**, or keep 192 and let each layer be a fraction of a block, which reads better. Layer shift ≤7 blocks → **≤2 blocks** at our scale. The three surface-noise windows are dimensionless and map unchanged. Eroded badlands hoodoos are a separate feature (a pillar generator) and are the expensive half.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Needs one new block id (`RedSand`), which is an art request rather than a code one. Everything else is available today.

#### G5.19 — The decoration architecture: no feature/placement vocabulary · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Decoration runs in **11 ordered steps**: 1 raw_generation, 2 lakes (lava only, since water lakes were removed), 3 local_modifications (geodes, icebergs), 4 underground_structures (trial chambers, buried treasure, mineshafts, trail ruins, monster rooms, fossils), 5 surface_structures (everything else, plus desert wells and blue ice), 6 strongholds (unused in practice), 7 underground_ores (ore blobs plus the sand/gravel/clay disks), 8 underground_decoration (infested blobs), 9 fluid_springs, 10 vegetal_decoration (trees, bamboo, cacti, kelp), 11 top_layer_modification (freeze the top layer). Each feature is a `configured_feature` (what to place) wrapped in a `placed_feature` (where and how often), with modifiers such as `count`, `rarity_filter`, `in_square`, `heightmap`, `biome` and `block_predicate_filter`. A chunk's feature list is assembled from **that chunk plus its 8 neighbours**, and features may write into the whole 3×3 area, which is why the step order is not strictly honoured in practice (MC-55596). [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** Nothing resembling this. Every decoration is a per-column hash inline in `generateChunk` (`TerrainGenerator.cpp:633-820`) — a roll, a threshold, a write. That is fast, perfectly pure, and immune to MC-55596 by construction, which is a genuine advantage. **But it cannot express "N attempts per chunk", "1 in 24 chunks", or "place this in a 7×3×7 patch around a point"**, which is the vocabulary every remaining item on this list is specified in. Trees and villages each rolled their own placement machinery (`Structures.cpp`'s 8-block cell grid; `Village.cpp`'s 448-block cell grid), and a third and fourth will be written for dungeons and geodes unless this is addressed.
- **What must be built:** Not a framework — the standing rule here is no abstraction without a second implementation in sight, and there are now *four*. The minimum useful thing is a small set of free functions: `cellCandidate(seed, salt, cellSize, reach)` (already implemented twice — extract it), `attemptsInColumn(seed, salt, n)` yielding n positions, and `heightAtSurface`. That converts "14 attempts per chunk" from prose into a call.
- **Numbers that matter:** The step order above matters in exactly two places for us: **geodes must run before caves** (G5.12) and **ores must run after caves** (already true, `TerrainGenerator.cpp:820`).
- **Risks / dependencies:** This is the item that makes G5.2, G5.4, G5.7, G5.8, G5.12 and G5.20 cheaper. Doing it *first* is tempting and probably wrong — do it after the second of those, when the shared shape is actually visible.

#### G5.20 — Fossils, desert wells, boulders and disks · XS · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:**
  - **Fossils**: Desert, Swamp and Mangrove Swamp; **2 attempts per chunk, each 1 in 64**; y 0…320 or −63…−8 depending on the variant; 4 skull and 4 spine variants; bone-block integrity 0.9 with a 0.1 ore overlay (coal above y 0, diamond below y −8); block counts 32–86 for a skull and 37–121 for a spine.
  - **Desert wells**: **1 in 500 per chunk on Bedrock** (1 in 1000 on Java); needs sand on solid ground across a 5×5; sandstone with slabs, one water source, and two suspicious sand blocks below.
  - **Boulders** (`forest_rock`): mossy cobblestone, **Old Growth Pine Taiga and Old Growth Spruce Taiga only**.
  - **Disks**: placed in the `underground_ores` step at the waterline — sand radius 2–6, gravel 2–5, clay 2–3, and grass/dirt 2–6 in mangrove swamp only.
  [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Fossil] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Desert_Well] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_generation]
- **What we have:** None of the four. `BoneBlock`, `SuspiciousSand`, `SuspiciousGravel`, `MossyCobblestone`, `Sandstone`, `Clay` and `Gravel` all exist.
- **What must be built:** Four small pure functions, each under 60 lines. Disks are the cheapest and would immediately improve every river and lake shore, which currently transition from grass straight to the depth-gated bed material.
- **Numbers that matter:** Fossil bands −63…−8 → **our y 2.6…11.9**; 0…320 → **our y 13.3…96**. 2 attempts × 1/64 per 16×16 chunk → **8 attempts × 1/64 per 32×32 column**. Desert well 1/500 per chunk → **1/125 per column**. Disk radii 2–6 are absolute and map unchanged.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Desert wells and fossils want the archaeology system for suspicious sand to be worth anything; place them anyway, since both are visual landmarks first.

#### G5.21 — Woodland mansion, trail ruins, trial chambers, ancient city, ruined portals · XL · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Woodland mansion 80/20 — the largest structure in the game, three floors on a cobblestone foundation, dark oak throughout, many loot chests and several secret rooms including a rare spider spawner room; dark forest only. Trail ruins 34/8 — a buried archaeology structure whose only "loot" is suspicious gravel, gated on a `has_structure_trail_ruins` biome tag on Bedrock. Trial chambers 34/12, **y −40…−20**, generated in new chunks only, containing trial spawners and vaults. Ancient city 24/8 at **100% probability**, floor **always y −51**, footprint about 220×220, deep dark only, with redstone-trapped basements and its own loot tables including the ice box. Ruined portals 40/15, with a mossiness table by biome and a Bedrock-specific 20% crying obsidian chance. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Woodland_Mansion] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Trail_Ruins] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Trial_Chambers] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ancient_City] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ruined_Portal]
- **What we have:** Nothing.
- **What must be built:** These are the late-game set and should be scheduled as a block, after G5.1, G5.5, G5.7 and G5.15. `TrialSpawner`, `Vault` and `DecoratedPot` are **absent from `Block.hpp`** and would be new ids.
- **Numbers that matter:** Ancient city floor y −51 → **our y 4.6, which is on top of the bedrock roof at y 4** — blocked until G5.15. Trial chambers y −40…−20 → **our y 6.5…9.9, a 3-block band** — blocked until G5.15. Woodland mansion and ruined portals are **surface** structures and fit at the current height; mansion 80/20 chunks → **1280 / 320 blocks**, ruined portal 40/15 → **640 / 240 blocks**.
- **Risks / dependencies:** **Nether dependency, in one line as the brief asks: a ruined portal's frame leads nowhere without the Nether. The structure is entirely an overworld generation feature and is worth building for its loot chest and its silhouette; treat the frame as decoration and note it.** Trail ruins and trial chambers depend on archaeology and the trial system respectively, both outside worldgen.

#### G5.22 — World types, structure location and the world border · S · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Bedrock offers **Infinite, Flat, Void (Creator/Editor only), Single Biome (settable in `level.dat` only) and Old (a fixed 256×256 world, removable since beta 1.18.0.22)**. **Bedrock flat worlds generate no structures and no features at all** — the Classic Flat preset is grass ×1, dirt ×2, bedrock ×1 with the surface at y −60 and the biome set to Plains. **The world border is a Java-exclusive feature**; Bedrock has only the hard 30,000,000-block boundary, so this is very nearly a non-gap. Seeds: a text seed is hashed with Java's `String.hashCode()` to a 32-bit value; Java and Bedrock share terrain and biomes for a given seed but **structure placement differs between the editions**; the overworld PRNG is xoroshiro128++; Bedrock's default seed is 3257840388504953787. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_type] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_border] [https://minecraft.wiki/w/World_seed]
- **What we have:** One world type. Seeds are a `std::uint32_t` threaded through every generation function as a pure input, which is architecturally *stronger* than the reference — our generation has no chunk-order dependence whatsoever, so a given `(seed, coord)` always produces the same chunk regardless of visit order. World spawn is a ring search (`Main.cpp:1921-1955`) requiring dry, uncarved ground within 512 blocks, which is simpler than Bedrock's 66-coordinate climate-fitness scan but strictly better behaved — **Bedrock can and does spawn a player underwater and drowning.**
- **What must be built:** A `WorldType` enum consulted at the top of `generateChunk`, with Flat as a fixed layer stack and Single Biome as a forced `biomeAt` return. Both are a handful of lines and are worth having primarily as **testing tools** — a flat world makes structure and mechanics testing enormously faster and is the kind of thing that pays for itself in one debugging session.
- **Numbers that matter:** Classic Flat surface at Bedrock y −60 → **our y 3.5**, but for a flat world the honest choice is our sea level, y 24, with the 4-block stack on top. Bedrock's hard boundary 30,000,000 blocks is far beyond any float precision we have; **worth checking what our coordinates do at ~10,000,000** as a separate matter.
- **Risks / dependencies:** A `WorldType` field must be persisted in `WorldStore` (`kFormatVersion = 3`, `WorldStore.cpp:26`) or a flat world reloads as an infinite one.

#### Answers to the specific questions asked, in one place

- **Is 96 blocks the single biggest constraint on everything else?** **No — G5.1 was, and as of 2026-08-18 it has moved rather than gone.** The loot *system* is built, so the constraint is no longer "there is nowhere to put the concept" but "~37 tables are unwritten and no structure other than a village is placed". Height still blocks exactly four things outright (ocean monument, ancient city, trial chambers, a multi-level stronghold) and halves mountain relief; the other 18 gaps in §5.2 can all be built today. Full quantification and cost estimate in **G5.15**.
- **Is there a loot/chest-generation system at all?** ✅ **There is now — as of 2026-08-18.** *Was:* "**No.** `Chest.hpp:29-42` is 27 empty `ItemStack`s and nothing else." `world/Loot.hpp` holds `Entry`/`Pool`/`Table` in three flat `constexpr` arrays and rolls without touching the heap. **But only 3 of ~40 tables are written and all three are village tables**, and no structure other than a village is placed, so the "blocks 15 of the 25 structures" claim is unchanged in practice — the *system* is no longer the blocker, the tables and the structures are. **G5.1.**
- **Are there dungeons and spawners?** **No.** `BlockId::MonsterSpawner` exists (id 933) and nothing places it; there is no monster room generator. **G5.2.**
- **Which structures are placed but empty or decorative?** Only one qualifies: **villages** — fully built, fully furnished, and ✅ **as of 2026-08-18 no longer containing zero chests**; weaponsmiths, toolsmiths and plain houses each get one, though **zero employed villagers** stands. Trees are complete. Everything else is not placed at all, so there is nothing decorative-but-empty to find. **G5.13.**
