### 8.3 The riding foundation — a design sketch

Everything in §8.2 from G8.2 to G8.11 is the same four problems wearing different art. Solve them once.

#### 8.3.1 The data model — one link, stored on the rider

Bedrock puts a `LinksTag { entityID, LinkID }` on the entity and the wiki itself marks the semantics "Unknown" ([Bedrock entity format](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Bedrock_Edition_level_format/Entity_format)); Java puts a `Passengers` list on the vehicle. **Neither is worth copying literally.** This project already has a settled answer to "two things that must agree": store the fact once and re-derive the other side — that is why chests pair by derivation and why a villager stores `bedCell` and nothing else (`Creature.hpp:1180-1186`).

So:

```
// On the rider. 0 = on foot. Player and Creature both carry it.
std::uint32_t vehicleId = 0;
std::uint8_t  seatIndex = 0;
```

and **occupancy is derived by scan**, not stored. The vehicle population is capped in the tens (`Creature.cpp:40` caps creatures at 14 per spawn cycle; a vehicle vector will be comparable), and `Creatures::creatureById` already establishes that a linear scan across a population this size is the accepted answer here (`Creature.hpp:1421-1424`).

The vehicle id space must be shared with the creature id space, because **a mount is a creature and a boat is not**. Two id counters would make `vehicleId` ambiguous. Either (a) hand `Vehicles` its own counter and tag the id with a one-byte `RideKind { Creature, Vehicle }`, or (b) — cheaper and recommended — move `m_nextId` (`Creature.hpp:1435`) into a tiny shared `EntityIds` counter that both systems draw from, so an id is globally unique and `vehicleId` alone is enough. Option (b) is about 15 lines and removes a whole class of "the boat and the horse both think they are #7" bug.

#### 8.3.2 The vehicle itself — a fourth entity system, in the established shape

`ItemEntities`, `Projectiles` and `FallingBlocks` agree on a house style precise enough to follow without a decision:

- a `std::vector<PlainStruct>` owned by one class, retired by swap-down;
- `spawn(...)` / `update(world, dt)` / `buildMesh(world, ..., DrawRange) const`;
- **the mesh is rebuilt every frame, not transformed**, because world meshes are drawn with an identity model matrix (`ItemEntity.hpp:48-52`, `FallingBlock.hpp:38-40`);
- the system **reads the world and never writes it**; anything it wants done to the world is handed back (`FallingBlocks::Crushed`, `Creatures::takeLoot`, `takeGrazed`).

A vehicle follows all four. Add one more rule it must not break: **`Vehicles` must not know `Player` exists.** It moves a hull; the loop that owns the player puts the player in the seat. That is the same hand-off as `Creatures::takeLoot` and it is what keeps the passenger relationship out of the physics.

```
struct VehicleSpecies {          // one row per kind, like ProjectileSpecies
    ItemId item;                 // what it drops and what places it
    float  halfWidth, height;    // Bedrock boat: 0.70 half-width, 0.455 height
    int    seatCount;            // boat 2, chest boat 1, minecart 1
    glm::vec3 seats[2];          // Bedrock's rideable.seats[].position
    float  lookClampRadians;     // boat 90° each side; 0 = free
    int    health;
    bool   floats;               // boat yes, minecart no
    bool   ridesRails;           // minecart yes
};
```

**Run it on the fixed tick, and interpolate.** Copy `Projectile.cpp:164-183` verbatim: `kTickSeconds = 0.05f`, an accumulator, a `kMaxTicksPerFrame` guard, and `blend = m_accumulator / kTickSeconds` for rendering. This is not optional for a boat — Bedrock's boat drag is a per-tick multiply (`v *= c` where c is 0.9 on water, 0.98 on ice, 0.989 on blue ice), and applying it once per frame at 120 fps is six times the intended drag. `Projectile.hpp:40-46` already records this exact lesson, and `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #7 records it again.

#### 8.3.3 Control transfer

The current chain is `PlayerInput` → `updatePlayer(player, input, world, dt)` → `camera.position = player.renderEyePosition()` (`Main.cpp:4137`). The camera is already *derived* from the player every frame, and that is the whole trick: **put the player in the seat and the camera follows for free.**

What must change:

1. **Split `updatePlayer`.** `updateSurvival` is already a separate function inside `Player.cpp` (`:153`); the locomotion is the body of `updatePlayer` from `:539`. Expose them as `updatePlayerMotion` and `updatePlayerSurvival`. A passenger skips the first and *keeps* the second — that is what makes a sunk boat drown you, a burning minecart burn you, and hunger still tick while riding.
2. **Route input by state.** If `player.vehicleId != 0`, build a `VehicleInput { throttle, turn, jump, dismount }` instead of a `PlayerInput` and hand it to `Vehicles::update` / `Creatures::updateMount`. Bedrock's keyboard boat model since beta 1.5.0.0 is **W forward, S reverse, A/D turn, and mouse-look does not steer** ([Boat](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Boat)) — so `moveDirection`'s camera-relative flattening (`Main.cpp:4093-4097`) must be bypassed entirely, not reused.
3. **Write the seat back.** After the vehicle ticks: `player.position = vehicle.position + rotateY(species.seats[seat], vehicle.yaw)`; `player.velocity = vehicle.velocity`; `player.onGround = vehicle.onGround`; `player.fallDistance = vehicle.fallDistance`. Use the *interpolated* vehicle transform, or the camera judders at 20 Hz.
4. **Clamp the look.** Bedrock limits a boat rider to a 180° forward arc (`lock_rider_rotation: 90`); Java allows 210°. `engine::Camera::addLook` is the one place to clamp, gated on the ride state.
5. **Suppress conflicting inputs.** Sneak is dismount, not crouch. Jump is dismount on a boat and *jump-charge* on a horse. Block placement and breaking stay live (the reference allows both while riding).

#### 8.3.4 Seat transforms — the numbers, read from Bedrock's own behaviour pack

| Vehicle | Seats | Offset(s) `[x, y, z]` | Look clamp |
|---|---|---|---|
| Boat | 2 | driver `[0, −0.2, 0]`, passenger `[0.2, −0.2, 0]` and `[−0.6, −0.2, 0]` | 90° each side |
| Bamboo raft | 2 | same X/Z, `y = +0.1` | 90° |
| Chest boat | 1 | `[0.2, −0.2, 0]` | 90° |
| Minecart | 1 | `[0, −0.2, 0]` | free |

Source: `Mojang/bedrock-samples` `behavior_pack/entities/{boat,chest_boat,minecart}.json`, `minecraft:rideable`. `passenger_max_width` on the boat is **1.375** — that is the exact numeric form of the wiki's "a mob can ride a boat if it is narrower than a boat" ([Riding](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Riding)).

A horse's seat offset is not published; measure it off our own model when the rig exists. The reference's clearance figures constrain it: **horse + rider fit through a 2.75-block gap; below that the rider suffocates. The horse alone fits 1.625 blocks and suffocates below 1.75. Neither fits a 1-block-wide gap** ([Horse](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Horse)).

#### 8.3.5 Dismount

Bedrock's search is fully specified and worth copying exactly, because a dismount that drops you in a wall is the kind of bug that only shows up in play:

> Check the eight horizontally adjacent blocks in this order, relative to the direction of travel: **right, left, rear-right, rear-left, front-right, front-left, rear, front.** A valid destination has a solid top surface below and enough headroom and width. If none, check one level up, then one level down, then crawl-height spaces (players only). If still none, use the vehicle's own position. Eject one block in the air and let the body settle. ([Minecart](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart))

The boat overrides the first step: the player is placed **in the direction they are facing** (in front of the boat if looking straight up or down), preferring land ([Boat](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Boat)).

We already have the primitives: `playerOverlapsBlock` (`Player.hpp`), `worldCollisionBoxes` (`Collision.hpp:29`) and `World::highestSolid`. The search is ~40 lines and should live in **one** function that every vehicle calls — this is precisely the shape of `CLAUDE.md` bug #14 ("a rule that did not travel"), and a boat with its own copy and a minecart with another is how it gets paid for a second time.

Dismount triggers to wire from day one: the dismount control; the vehicle being destroyed; the boat going underwater (Bedrock **expels all passengers**); the player dying; and later, the activator rail.

#### 8.3.6 Save and load

Three records change; **`kChunkFormatVersion` does not need to move.** Rails are already block ids in the chunk format and a vehicle is an entity, not a block, so the terrain format is untouched.

| File | Now | After | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `VXPL` player | `kFormatVersion = 3` (`WorldStore.cpp:26`) | **4** | `SavedPlayer` gains `std::uint32_t vehicleId` + `std::uint8_t seatIndex`. Note `SavedPlayer` has a `static_assert` on `is_trivially_copyable_v` — both new fields are fine |
| `VXCR` creatures | `kCreatureVersion = 3` (`:97`) | **4** | `SavedCreature` gains `id` (it has none today — see §8.6), plus `persistent`, `tamed`, `temper`, `saddled`, and the three equine stats |
| `VXVH` vehicles | — | **new, version 1** | New magic + record, written and read exactly like `saveCreatures` / `loadCreatures` (`WorldStore.cpp:602-650`) |

The load order matters and is the one genuinely fiddly part: **resolve links after every entity exists.** Load creatures, load vehicles, load the player, *then* walk the three sets and re-point `vehicleId`. Because ids are re-issued by a counter today, `restore` must be changed to *accept* an id rather than mint one, and the counter seeded past the highest loaded id.

Bedrock's own persistence rule is worth adopting: *"When a player leaves a world, all entities riding or being ridden by that player disappear from the world, and reappear with the player when they rejoin"* ([Riding](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Riding)). That neatly sidesteps "the boat saved 300 m from where the player saved".

#### 8.3.7 What it costs

| Piece | New/changed lines (est.) | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Shared id counter | ~15 | `Creature.hpp/.cpp` + one new tiny header |
| `updatePlayer` split | ~30 changed, 0 new behaviour | `Player.hpp/.cpp` |
| Lift `moveAxis` / `blockingPlaneAlong` out of `Player.cpp`'s anonymous namespace | ~90 moved | `Player.cpp:404-505` → `Collision.hpp` |
| `Vehicle.hpp` / `Vehicle.cpp` (species table, tick loop, physics, mesh) | ~500 | new |
| Seat transform + control routing + camera clamp | ~120 | `Main.cpp`, `engine/render/Camera.hpp` |
| Dismount search (one owner) | ~60 | `Vehicle.cpp` |
| Save records + 2 version bumps + link resolution | ~180 | `WorldStore.hpp/.cpp`, `Main.cpp` |
| **Foundation total** | **~1,000** | **L — 2 to 4 sessions** |

Every vehicle after that is **S to M**: a boat is one row in the species table plus a hull mesh and one drag rule; a minecart is one row plus the rail-follower.

---

### 8.4 Gap detail

#### G8.1 — The riding foundation · L · P0

Fully specified in §8.3. The one thing to add here is the **sequencing argument**: do not build this speculatively as a "general entity system". `CLAUDE.md` is explicit that abstraction waits for a second real case. Build it *with* the boat, in the same session, and let the boat be the first concrete user — then the horse is the second case that proves the seams are in the right place. Building the foundation alone and calling a milestone done would produce exactly the speculative structure the architecture rules forbid.

---

#### G8.2 — Boats · L · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** A boat is crafted from 5 matching overworld planks; the Bedrock-only wooden-shovel ingredient was removed in 1.20.10. It holds **2 entities** (`seat_count: 2`), is entered with *use*, and exited by sneaking, jumping, clicking the right stick, or the touch "Leave Boat" button. Its collision box in Bedrock is **1.4 wide × 0.455 high** (Java: 1.375 × 0.5625). Mobs are pulled in on contact (`pull_in_entities: true`) and cannot get out on their own. Riding a boat over a lily pad **drops the lily pad** and stutters the boat. Boats **nullify fall damage** for themselves and their passengers. Underwater, all passengers are expelled. Bedrock boats **do not sink** in downward-flowing water (Java's do) and **have no air resistance** — a boat launched off a cliff keeps its horizontal speed all the way down. Boats always drop themselves as an item. [Boat](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Boat), [Transportation](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation)
- **What we have:** Nothing. No item id, no entity, no recipe, no texture. `slipperiness()` (`Block.hpp:6320`) already returns exactly the coefficients the physics needs, and `Fluid.hpp` already models water level and flow — so two of the three hard parts are done.
- **What must be built:**
  1. `ItemId::Boat` (+ one per wood family, or one generic boat with a wood field in `damage` — the stowbox at `WorldStore.hpp` already establishes that trick). Append at the end of the enum; `Item.hpp:101-108` warns that inserting shifts every saved id.
  2. Recipe rows in `Recipe.cpp` (5 planks, U shape).
  3. Placement: consume the item, spawn a hull at the aimed water surface. Reuse the "aim at a fluid" ray already used by the bucket (`Main.cpp:4983` passes `filling = true` to `raycast` so it stops on water).
  4. The hull mesh. This is real work — a boat is not a cube, and `CLAUDE.md` bug #12 says to read `models/entity/boat` rather than guess. Two paddles that swing with throttle.
  5. The physics (below).
  6. Damage/destroy → drop the boat item. `Explosion.cpp` and the melee path already exist.
- **Numbers that matter (all Bedrock unless marked):**

  | Surface | drag `c` per tick | μ = 20(1−c) s⁻¹ | Top speed | Max yaw |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Water | 0.90 | 2.0 | **0.40 b/tick = 8.00 b/s** | 10°/tick = 200°/s |
  | Ice / packed / frosted | 0.98 | 0.4 | **2.00 b/tick = 40.0 b/s** | 50°/tick = 1000°/s |
  | Blue ice | 0.989 | 0.22 | **3.636 b/tick = 72.73 b/s** | 90.9°/tick = 1818°/s |
  | Land (default 0.6) | 0.60 | 8.0 | **0.10 b/tick = 2.00 b/s** | 2.5°/tick = 50°/s |
  | Slime block (0.8, eff. 0.32) | — | 4.0 | 0.0588 b/tick = 1.176 b/s | 5°/tick |
  | Honey block | — | 8.0 | 0.0526 b/tick = 1.053 b/s | 2.5°/tick |

  Reverse thrust is **one-eighth** of forward: water reverse **1.01 b/s (0.0505 b/tick)**, land reverse **0.24 b/s (0.012 b/tick)**. Acceleration to top speed takes **9.4 s** (4.7 s from a running start). Forward thrust 0.04 m/tick² = 16 m/s², reverse 0.005 m/tick² = 2 m/s², torque 1°/tick² = 400°/s² — **these three are documented for Java only [JE]; the Bedrock row on that table is literally `{{Info needed}}`**, but the wiki states the constants are "proportionally scaled to produce the same top speed / max yaw rate between the two editions", so the top speeds above are correct for Bedrock and the accelerations should be tuned to hit the 9.4 s figure. ¼-slope rapids reach **7.0 b/s** (7.3 with sprint FOV). Global Bedrock speed cap: **16 b/tick = 320 m/s**. Bedrock health is **40** today, dropping to **4 with 0.1 HP/tick regen** in preview 26.40 to match Java. Lava does **4 damage/tick = 80/s**. Buoyancy: `base_buoyancy 1.0`, `movement_type "waves"`, `big_wave_probability 0.03`, `big_wave_speed 10.0`. Boat fuel value: **1200 ticks = 60 s**, smelting 6 items. [Boat](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Boat), [Transportation](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation), `bedrock-samples/behavior_pack/entities/boat.json`

  **The single most important consequence:** the drag table is *already* `slipperiness()`. Water and air are 0.9 (a fourth value we do not have — add it), and every other row is the block's own slipperiness. Write the boat's drag as `c = onWater ? 0.9 : slipperiness(blockBelow)` and the 40 b/s ice boat falls out for free, with no ice-specific code and no second table to drift.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1. The paddle animation needs `ANIMATION.md`'s procedure. `Fluid.hpp` gives flow direction, so downstream/upstream behaviour is reachable — but Bedrock's "boats float up rather than sinking in a downward flow" is a *divergence from Java* that should be written down when implemented, because it is counter-intuitive and will look like a bug. The boat is a **solid collision entity** in the reference (players and falling blocks are stopped by it) and we have no entity-versus-entity collision at all today; shipping without it is an acceptable first cut but must be a named divergence.

---

#### G8.3 — Minecarts on plain rail · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Crafted from 5 iron in a U. Boarded with *use*; **"once inside, an external impulse may be needed"**. Top speed is **exactly 8 blocks/second per axis of travel** — confirmed independently by the Bedrock component default `minecraft:rail_movement { max_speed: 0.4 }` (blocks/tick). Diagonally that is √128 = **11.314 b/s**; on 3-D track with slopes, √192 = **13.85 b/s**. A player holding forward *does* add momentum in Bedrock (the wiki: *"a riding player can still move it uphill at the lowest speed in Bedrock Edition"*). Off the rails, a cart **decelerates within one or two blocks** and snaps back when pushed onto track. A cart hitting an opaque block bounces back; a transparent one stops it. **Ice has no effect on minecarts at all.** A player in a cart takes no fall damage if the cart lands on rail. Riders do not collide with or suffocate in transparent blocks but *do* suffocate in opaque ones. A cart is destroyed by one hit from a pickaxe/sword/axe (>4 HP), and by cactus, lava and fire, and always drops itself. **The furnace minecart does not exist in Bedrock** — the page is tagged Java/Legacy-Console exclusive and Bedrock's ids are listed "unused"; converted Legacy worlds turn them into plain minecarts. [Minecart](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart), [Rail](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Rail), [rail_movement component](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/minecraft/creator/reference/content/entityreference/examples/entitycomponents/minecraftcomponent_rail_movement)
- **What we have:** The rails, completely, as blocks. Nothing else.
- **What must be built:** `ItemId::Minecart` + recipe; the entity (one `VehicleSpecies` row, `ridesRails = true`); and the rail follower — a small state machine that reads `railShape(blockAt(cell))`, projects velocity onto the shape's axis, handles the four slope shapes with a ±0.5-block Y ramp, and hands off cell-to-cell. The junction rules are worth copying literally: the **south-east rule** (a cart entering a T-junction from behind the curve goes straight; from either other leg it follows the curve), and the **downhill rule** (*"at non-curve rail junctions, minecarts always travel downhill if they can, ignoring the south-east rule"*).
- **Numbers that matter:** cap **0.4 b/tick / 8.0 b/s per axis**; diagonal 0.5657 b/tick / 11.314 b/s; 3-D 0.6926 b/tick / 13.85 b/s; ¼-slope track 7.1 b/s. Gap-jumping over unconnected curves reaches **0.5 b/tick / 10 b/s**. Bedrock cart collision box **0.98 wide × 0.7 high**. Utility carts have **6 HP**; a plain cart uses the boat damage model (10 damage per HP, −1/tick, destroyed above 40). Coasting from full speed: a player-occupied cart runs **309 m** (full speed for the first 176 m); an empty chest/hopper cart 165 m; a fully loaded one 40 m. An empty cart at full speed climbs **10 blocks** on unpowered rail; **with a rider, 24 blocks.** Push model: `legacy_minecart`, `strength_multiplier 0.1`, `push_scale_self 0.5`, `push_scale_other 0.25`. Minecart *merging* into trains is **[JE] only**. [Minecart](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart), [Tutorial:Minecarts](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tutorial:Minecarts)
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1 and G8.4. The follower is the first code in the project that walks a graph *through* block ids rather than reading one cell, so it needs a hard guard against pathological loops. **Do not tie the follower to the fixed 20 Hz tick and then also interpolate the rail snap** — the cart's position must be exact on the rail line and only the *along-track* parameter interpolates.

---

#### G8.4 — Rail auto-connection, curves and slopes · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Bedrock's rule differs from Java's and is simpler. **With no adjacent rails, a new plain rail lays north-south** (Java aligns it to the player's facing [JE]). At the end of a line it continues the axis. With two adjacent rails on its level or one level up/down, it configures itself straight or curved to connect them. At a **T-junction (three adjacent) it becomes a curve** joining two sides. Placed among four, "the centre rail always curves south-to-east". Existing rails **re-orient**: a north-south rail flips to east-west when one is placed east or west of it, and a rail next to a rail one level up becomes a ramp — **slope preference order west, east, south, north**. Powered/detector/activator use a shorter rule: two adjacent on non-opposite sides, or three or more → east-west; none → north-south, but re-orienting to east-west if one later appears east or west. **Only the plain rail may curve.** A rail sits on any block whose top face has a rim — a full block, a hopper, a top slab, upside-down stairs, a top trapdoor — and **breaks and drops when unsupported**. Rails cannot attach to a side or bottom. In Bedrock, **flowing water breaks rails** (beta 1.7.0.2). [Rail](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Rail), [Powered Rail](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Powered_Rail)
- **What we have:** `railAt(family, shape, powered)`, `railShape`, `railSlopes`, `railSlopeToward` — the complete shape vocabulary, already `constexpr` (`Block.hpp:2038-2101`). Placement is one line that always picks shape 0 or 1 (`Main.cpp:5618-5624`).
- **What must be built:** One function, `railShapeFor(world, cell, family, playerFacing)`, that reads the four horizontal neighbours at y, y+1 and y−1 and returns a shape. Then two call sites: placement, and a **neighbour-update pass** that re-derives the four neighbours' shapes whenever a rail is placed or broken. The second is the part that is easy to forget and is what makes track feel alive.
- **Numbers that matter:** the ten shapes are already numbered identically to Bedrock's `rail_direction` metadata — 0 north-south, 1 east-west, 2-5 ascending east/west/north/south, 6-9 curves south-east/south-west/north-west/north-east. Our `railShape` returns exactly this ordering and `railSlopeToward(shape)` maps 2-5 onto `FaceDirection` — **verify that mapping against Bedrock's order before trusting it**, because `FaceDirection` order and Bedrock's east/west/north/south order are not obviously the same and this is exactly `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #5. Sloped rail hitbox height is half a block; a flat rail's outline is 2/16 tall and it floats 1/16 above the ground (already correct at `Block.hpp:4237`).
- **Risks / dependencies:** None — this is self-contained `Block.hpp` + `Main.cpp` work and can ship *before* minecarts exist, which makes it a good standalone slice. The neighbour-update pass touches the block-change path and must not run inside the mesher.

---

#### G8.5 — Horses, donkeys and mules: taming, saddling, riding · L · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** A wild horse is tamed by repeatedly mounting it. **Temper starts at 0 out of 100.** On the first mount a random threshold 0–99 is drawn; the horse is tamed if temper *exceeds* it, otherwise the player is bucked and **temper += 5**. Food also raises temper: sugar +3, wheat +3, apple +3, carrot +3, golden carrot +5, golden apple / enchanted golden apple +10, hay bale none. Golden carrots and golden apples also trigger love mode in *tamed* horses. Tamed horses have **two equipment slots** — saddle and horse armour — opened by sneak+use, or by the inventory control while mounted; **shears remove them, armour first then saddle.** A ridden saddled horse **automatically runs up any one-block slope.** Jump is a **charge bar**: hold jump to fill it, release for a jump proportional to the fill. Donkeys and mules take a **chest (15 slots)** instead of armour; a mule is horse × donkey and is sterile. Horses can be leashed and towed behind a boat. [Horse](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Horse), [Riding](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Riding)
- **What we have:** Species rows for Horse, Mule, Donkey with correct-looking boxes and `stepHeight = 1.0` (`Creature.cpp:692-707`). The milk-a-cow path (`Main.cpp:4998`) is a working "use item on the creature the ray hits". `Creatures::aimedAt`/`findAimed` gives the pick. `Saddle` exists as an item with no recipe. Nothing else — no ownership, no per-individual stats, no container UI for a creature.
- **What must be built:** per-individual state on `Creature` (`tamed`, `owner` is unnecessary in single-player, `temper`, `saddled`, `armourTier`, and the three equine stats); a saddle recipe; a horse-inventory screen (two slots — `InventoryScreen.cpp` already hosts chest and furnace panels, so this is a third panel, not a new screen); a jump-charge HUD bar (`hud/StatusBars.cpp` is 142 lines and already draws segmented bars); breeding and love mode; and the ridden control model, which is a *steered mount* rather than a *driven vehicle* — the player supplies direction and the mount supplies speed and the jump.
- **Numbers that matter (Bedrock, [Horse](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Horse) and [Transportation](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation)):**
  - **Health:** 15–30 HP, mean 22.5. An odd value hides its last half-heart in the bar.
  - **Speed:** internal attribute **0.1125–0.3375**, mean 0.225; conversion factor ≈ **43.17** blocks/s per unit. → **min 4.86 b/s (0.243 b/tick), average 9.71 b/s (0.486 b/tick) [the Transportation table says 9.49 — the two wiki pages disagree], max 14.57 b/s (0.7285 b/tick).** For comparison, the player walks 4.317 and sprints 5.612. **About 82% of horses beat a minecart's 8 b/s.**
  - **Jump strength:** attribute **0.4–1.0**, mean 0.7. Non-linear: 0.4 → **1.153 blocks**, 0.7 → **3.124 blocks**, 1.0 → **5.9197 blocks**. The wiki has no closed form and links an external gist; build a 7-point lookup and interpolate.
  - **Breeding (current algorithm, JE 1.19.4 / BE 1.19.70 onward):**
    `base = (|x−y| + (MAX−MIN)×0.3) × ((rand+rand+rand)/3 − 0.5) + (x+y)/2`, then reflect off the bounds (`if base > MAX: base = 2·MAX − base`). Run independently per stat. Note the *older* "average of the parents plus a random third" description is obsolete.
  - **Coat/markings:** 44.44% parent A's colour, 44.44% parent B's, 11.11% random; markings 40/40/20.
  - **Clearance:** horse + rider need **2.75 blocks**; the horse alone fits **1.625** but suffocates below 1.75; neither fits a 1-block-wide gap.
  - **Donkey / mule speed: 7.38 b/s (0.369 b/tick).** Skeleton/zombie horse **8.43 b/s**. Donkey chest **15 slots**.
  - **Horse armour is 6 tiers now, not 5** — copper (4 points) was added between leather and iron.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1 and **G8.6 is a hard blocker** — a horse tamed and left at home is deleted by `Creature.cpp:4837` the moment the player walks 90 m away, and shipping taming without persistence would be a worse bug than not shipping taming. Second risk, and it is a design one: **our horse's `runSpeed` is 4.5 m/s, below a sprinting player's 5.612.** A ridden horse must not reuse `runSpeed` — that number was tuned for how a wandering herd *looks*. Either add a `riddenSpeed` field or derive the ridden speed from the equine attribute and leave `runSpeed` alone; do not "fix" `runSpeed` upward, because that changes how every unridden horse behaves.

#### G8.6 — Creature persistence for owned animals · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Tamed and named mobs never despawn. Bedrock's `Persistent` byte is on the base entity tag.
- **What we have:** `Creature.cpp:4833-4841` retires any creature past `m_activeRadius` unconditionally. `SavedCreature` (`WorldStore.hpp`) has `kind, x, y, z, yaw, health, scale, charged, playerBuilt, profession` — **and no id.**
- **What must be built:** a `persistent` flag on `Creature` and `SavedCreature`, checked in the retire loop; an `id` field in `SavedCreature`; and `Creatures::restore` changed to accept an id and seed `m_nextId` past the maximum loaded. `kCreatureVersion` 3 → 4.
- **Numbers that matter:** `kBaseRadius = 90.0f` (`Creature.cpp:33`) is the floor; the active radius otherwise follows render distance (`Main.cpp:2433`). `kMaxCreatures = 14` per spawn cycle.
- **Risks / dependencies:** Cheap and self-contained, but it interacts with the population cap — persistent animals must not count against the cap that governs *ambient* spawning, or a stable of six horses makes the world feel empty.

#### G8.7 — Leads and leash knots · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** **5 string → 2 leads** (changed from 4 string + 1 slimeball in JE 25w18a / BE Preview 1.21.90.21 — our recipe is already the new one). *Use* a lead on a mob to tie it; *use* on a fence to create a **leash knot** entity (0.5 tall × 0.375 wide) and tie the mob there; a tied mob **stays within about 5 blocks of the post**. Multiple leads on one post. Sneak+use on another leashable mob chains them. **A lead stretches a maximum of 12 blocks** (16 for a happy ghast) — if the mob can move toward the holder it does, otherwise the lead breaks. It also breaks on projectile hits, on shears, on breaking the knot, and on removing the fence. **It always drops as an item at the mob's position** when broken or removed. A lead does *not* break when the animal dies. **Boats are unaffected by leads while a player is a direct passenger**, but a boat carrying a mob can be towed. When the holder is more than 7 blocks above the ground the mob dangles. Hostile mobs are *not* broadly excluded in Bedrock — hoglins, zoglins, striders and skeleton horses are all leashable. [Lead](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Lead)
- **What we have:** the item and its recipe (`Item.hpp:332`, `Recipe.cpp:416`), a `lead.png` sprite, and nothing else.
- **What must be built:** an entity-to-entity (or entity-to-cell) link — the *same* plumbing as §8.3.1, which is why this is P2 rather than P3: once the passenger link exists, the leash link is a second user of it and costs much less. Then a knot entity, a spring/pull force on the leashed creature's movement controller, and a catenary rope mesh. The rope is the only genuinely new rendering: a 16-segment sagging line, rebuilt each frame like everything else.
- **Numbers that matter:** snap distance **12 blocks**; fence tether radius **~5 blocks**; knot box 0.5 × 0.375; dangle threshold 7 blocks above ground. Bedrock's boat leash component: `soft_distance 2.0`, `hard_distance 4.0`, `rotation_adjustment 90`. Pull force is **not published** — the wiki gives only the qualitative rule. **Bedrock bug worth knowing:** MCPE-157182 — if a chunk unloads containing a leashed mob, the lead sometimes breaks and drops.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1's link. Leads are the cheapest way to make the existing herd animals feel owned, and they are a prerequisite for llama caravans (G8.11).

---

#### G8.8 — Saddled pig and carrot on a stick · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Saddle a pig, hold a carrot on a stick, and the pig walks where you point. Pressing *use* triggers a boost. [Pig](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Pig), [Carrot on a Stick](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Carrot_on_a_Stick)
- **What we have:** the pig (`Creature.cpp:645`), the carrot (`Item.hpp:168`), the fishing rod. No combination item, no saddle use.
- **What must be built:** `ItemId::CarrotOnAStick` + recipe (fishing rod + carrot), the boost timer, and reuse of G8.5's saddle slot.
- **Numbers that matter:** ridden pig **2.42 b/s (0.121 b/tick)**; boost peak **5.20 b/s (0.260 b/tick)** = **2.15×**; average over a full boost cycle **4.19 b/s (0.2095 b/tick)**. Boost duration is random, **140–980 ticks (7–49 s)**. Carrot on a stick durability **25**, **7 per boost** → about 3 full boosts, and it reverts to a plain fishing rod when it breaks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1, G8.5's saddle. Genuinely small once those exist, and it is the cheapest possible *proof* that the riding foundation generalises past boats.

---

#### G8.9 — Camel · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Two passengers. Tall enough that most ground mobs cannot reach the rider. Sits and stands with an animation delay. Dashes on command. Spawns at desert villages, which puts it firmly in scope. [Camel](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Camel), [Transportation](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation)
- **What we have:** the species, with `height = 2.375` and `stepHeight = 1.5` — **both already the reference's own values** (`Creature.cpp:688-691`). This is the closest any species is to being rideable.
- **Numbers that matter:** walk **3.885 b/s** ([Camel](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Camel)) or **3.794 b/s** ([Transportation](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation)) — the two pages disagree; sprint **8.203** or **8.0 b/s (0.41 / 0.40 b/tick)**. **Dash cooldown 2.75 s**; max dash **12 blocks forward and 1 up**. Dash *speed*, charge time and duration are **not published** — tune to hit the 12-block figure. Health 32 in the reference against our 16 (`Creature.cpp:689`) — worth checking separately.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1 (and it is the second two-seat vehicle after the boat, which is the right way to prove the seat array is not boat-specific).

---

#### G8.10 — Containers on vehicles · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Chest boat (shapeless chest + boat) exists in Bedrock since 1.18.30, holds **27 slots**, and carries **only one rider** because the chest occupies the second seat. Chest minecart and hopper minecart exist (hopper cart = **5 slots**, throughput **1 item per 2 ticks = 10 items/s in Bedrock**, against Java's 20/s [JE]). Since Bedrock 1.19.0, breaking a chest/hopper minecart drops **the combined item** plus its contents. Donkey/mule chest is **15 slots**; a llama's is **strength × 3**. [Boat with Chest](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Boat_with_Chest), [Minecart with Chest](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart_with_Chest), [Minecart with Hopper](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart_with_Hopper)
- **What we have:** `Chest` (`world/Chest.hpp`), `PlacedChest`, `StowedBox` — and critically, **the stowbox trick**: contents keyed by a handle stored in the item stack's `damage` field, so contents travel with an item with no format bump (`WorldStore.hpp`). That is exactly the mechanism a chest boat needs when it is picked up.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1–G8.3. Low novelty, decent payoff, and `InventoryScreen` already does the hard UI part.

---

#### G8.11 — Llamas: strength, caravans, spitting · M · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Llamas are tamed like horses but **cannot be steered when ridden** — this is the one mount where the player is a passenger, not a driver. Strength is 1–5 and gives **strength × 3** chest slots. Leashing one llama to another forms a **caravan** (up to 10). They spit for ranged damage. [Llama](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Llama)
- **Numbers that matter:** llama speed attribute 0.175 → **≈7.56 b/s (0.378 b/tick)** (inferred from the infobox, same attribute as a donkey). Caravan cap **10**. **Spit range, cooldown, caravan follow distance and join radius are all unpublished** — the wiki says only "up to nine nearby llamas".
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.1, G8.7. Low priority because the caravan is the most bespoke behaviour in the whole section and the payoff is narrow.

---

#### G8.12 — Powered, detector and activator rail behaviour · M · P3

See §8.5 — this gap is entirely about the redstone question and is costed there.

---

#### G8.13 — TNT minecart · S · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Shapeless TNT + minecart. Base explosion power **4** on the wiki, plus a random bonus up to 1.5 × velocity capped at 7.5, so at speed ≥ 5 the power is random in [4, 11.5]; **Bedrock's own `tnt_minecart.json` says `power: 3`, `fuse_length: 4`** — flag the conflict and prefer the behaviour pack. Activator-rail fuse **4 s (80 ticks)**; other triggers 0–1.95 s. **In Bedrock a TNT minecart only explodes when it lands on the ground**, not when merely touched or spun; it also detonates instantly after a fall of more than 3 blocks unless it lands on rail. Bedrock additionally allows priming with flint and steel, a fire charge, or a Fire Aspect item. Drops itself if it never explodes. [Minecart with TNT](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart_with_TNT)
- **What we have:** `Explosion.cpp` (497 lines) is complete and already handles block destruction, creature damage and the drop hand-off; `Creatures::applyExplosion` and `Main.cpp:6376` wire it up. So this is a trigger and a fuse, not a blast system.
- **Risks / dependencies:** G8.3. Without an activator rail (blocked by §8.5), the only reachable triggers are the fall-landing rule and a hand-lit fuse — which is enough to be useful and needs no divergence.

---

#### G8.14 — Scaffolding climbing · XS · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Scaffolding is climbed by walking into it (not by pushing into a wall, as a ladder is); **sneak descends it fast** — unlike a ladder, where sneak *holds position*. It is also the model for how leather boots let a player climb powder snow.
- **What we have:** `BlockId::Scaffolding` (`Block.hpp:843`) and `isClimbable(id) = isLadder(id) || isVine(id)` (`:3337`).
- **What must be built:** add scaffolding to `isClimbable`, then a branch in `Player.cpp:798-812` — because scaffolding's rules are *inverted* from a ladder's on both the push test (any direction, not into a face) and sneak (descend, not hold). Do not widen `isClimbable` alone: `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #2 is exactly this — widening a family predicate and killing every early-out behind it. Grep every caller of `isClimbable` first; `Player.cpp:192` uses it to reset fall distance, and that behaviour *is* correct for scaffolding.

| Gap | Bedrock number | Our state |
|---|---|---|
| Cobweb horizontal | **≈1.08 b/s (0.054 b/tick)** = ~25% of walking; fall **0.0039 b/tick ≈ 13 s per block**; all fall damage negated | Block exists, no effect |
| Powder snow | "similar to cobwebs" — **exact multiplier unpublished**; freeze at +1 tick to a cap of 140, then 1 HP per 40 ticks; leather boots let you climb it | Block exists, no effect (also listed in §7 as a survival gap) |
| Bubble column up (soul sand) | **14.0 b/s (0.70 b/tick)** | Soul sand exists as a block; **its only overworld source in the reference is ancient cities**, so an upward column is effectively Nether-gated for us — say so and move on |

### 8.5 The redstone question for rails

The user's decision — *"there is no signal engine. Nothing powers anything."* (`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md:2196`) — is settled, and this section is about what it costs the rail system specifically, not about reopening it.

**What is reachable with no signal engine at all:**

- **Plain rail, all ten shapes.** No power, no logic. Curves, slopes, T-junctions, the south-east rule and the downhill rule are all pure geometry.
- **The plain minecart**, ridden or empty, and every chest/hopper/TNT variant's *inventory* behaviour.
- **Gravity-driven track.** A cart released from a drop travels a real distance: from H=1 it runs 2.77 m, H=2 → 4.59 m, H=3 → 5.81 m, H=5 → 7.87 m, H=10 → 11.65 m, and asymptotically ~15.9 m from any great height ([Minecart](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart)). A downhill mine track is genuinely useful with nothing else.
- **Player-pushed carts**, and a rider holding forward — Bedrock explicitly allows a rider to keep a cart moving, even uphill at the lowest speed.
- **All four rail types as craftable, placeable, mineable blocks** — which is what already ships.

**What is not reachable, and why:**

- **Powered rail** needs a boolean "am I powered". Its whole behaviour is that binary: powered → **+0.06 blocks/tick of speed added per tick along the direction of travel** (= +1.2 b/s per tick, ≈24 b/s² sustained), capped at 8 b/s per axis; unpowered → a brake that stops a loaded cart **within about one block, even on a downslope**. Power also propagates **up to 8 rails each way from the source, so one source lights up to 17 rails** ([Powered Rail](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Powered_Rail)).
- **Detector rail** is a signal *producer*. With nothing to consume a signal it is inert by definition. Its only non-redstone behaviour is the comparator read, which is also redstone.
- **Activator rail** ejects riders, disables hopper carts and primes TNT carts — it needs a signal *input*, so it is inert too.

**The honest subset, and the recommended divergence.**

Three options, in increasing cost:

1. **Plain rail only (zero extra cost).** Ship G8.3 + G8.4, leave the other three families as decorative blocks and say so in the divergence list. A downhill mine track works, a flat one does not. This is defensible and is what "the smallest honest subset" literally means.
2. **The "adjacent to a live block" divergence (recommended, ~XS on top of G8.3).** Define one rule: *a powered rail is on when any of its six neighbours is a **`BlockId::RedstoneBlock`***. Nothing else — no propagation, no wire, no levers, no repeaters, and therefore no signal engine. The redstone block already exists (`Block.hpp:221`, and `isRedstoneComponent` at `:2116` already counts it), it is craftable, it is *always* on in the reference too, and a player placing one under a powered rail is doing exactly what the reference would have them do with a lever. This buys the entire boosted-rail experience — flat track at 8 b/s, uphill climbs, standing starts — for one predicate. **Do not extend the 8-rail propagation**; require one redstone block per powered rail and call that the divergence. It is expensive in gold and redstone, which is thematically right.
   - The tuning numbers that make this useful: on level track, **1 powered rail every 34 blocks holds a rider-occupied cart at the full 8 b/s; every 38 blocks gives 7.97 b/s** (a 0.4% loss) and is the recommended optimum. Degradation past that: 39 → 7.75, 40 → 7.72, 45 → 7.12, 50 → 6.49, 59 → 5.80 b/s. An empty utility cart needs **1 every 27**; a full one **1 every 6**. From a standstill, **3 powered rails in a row** reach top speed (the [Rail](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Rail) page says 7; the [tutorial](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tutorial:Minecarts) page says 3 — pick 3 and note the conflict). Climbing at speed in Bedrock 1.21.8 needs **2 powered per 3 plain**. ([Tutorial:Minecarts](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Tutorial:Minecarts))
3. **A furnace minecart instead (do not do this).** It is the obvious "self-propelled cart with no redstone" answer and it is **wrong for a Bedrock-referenced game: the furnace minecart does not exist in Bedrock.** The wiki tags it Java/Legacy-Console exclusive, Bedrock's ids are listed "unused", and converting a Legacy world turns furnace carts into plain ones ([Minecart with Furnace](https://minecraft.wiki/w/Minecart_with_Furnace)). Adding it would be inventing a divergence, which `CLAUDE.md` forbids in as many words. Its numbers, for the record only: 4.0 b/s constant, 720 m per coal, 3600 ticks per fuel, pulls up to 4 carts — all [JE].

**Detector and activator rails have no honest subset.** Leave them decorative and say so. The single exception worth considering later: an activator rail could eject riders on contact with no power at all, as a hard-coded "this rail always ejects" — but that changes what the block *is*, and a decorative rail is a smaller lie than a rail that behaves differently from the reference.

### 8.6 Errors and inconsistencies noticed while reading

- **`world/Block.hpp:6315-6325`** · `slipperiness()`'s doc comment states the reference's values — *"Ice and packed ice are 0.98 there, blue ice 0.989, **slime 0.8**"* — and the function body has no branch for `SlimeBlock`, so slime returns the 0.6 default. The comment and the code disagree, and the comment is right about the reference. Read in the code. **High confidence.** Consequence today is small (slime bounces via a separate constant at `Player.hpp:46`), but a boat's drag table is *the same function*, so this becomes a wrong boat speed the moment G8.2 ships — the reference's boat-on-slime figure is 1.176 b/s and ours would come out at 2.0 b/s, the land value.
- **`game/src/Main.cpp:5618-5624`** · Rail placement calls `railAt(family, alongX ? 1 : 0, false)` for every family, so **only shapes 0 and 1 are reachable in play**. The four slope shapes and four curve shapes exist as ids, are drawn, are named by `blockName`, and can never be placed. Read in the code, and already recorded as a named divergence in `SYSTEM_MEMORY.md:2196`. **Certain.** Listed here because a divergence that makes 8 of 40 ids unreachable is a *dead-code* risk of exactly the kind `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #2 describes — nothing exercises `railSlopes`, `railSlopeToward` or shapes 6-9, so a mistake in them is invisible.
- **`item/Item.hpp:993`** · `Saddle` has an id, a display name, `stack = 1` and a sprite, and **no recipe and no consumer**. `grep ItemId::Saddle` across `game/src` returns zero hits outside the item table. It cannot be obtained and would do nothing if it were. **Certain.**
- **`item/Recipe.cpp:416`** · `Lead` *is* craftable (5 string → 2), and nothing consumes it either. So the player can craft an item whose only effect is to occupy a slot. **Certain.** Worth noting the recipe is the *current* Bedrock one (changed from 4 string + 1 slimeball in BE Preview 1.21.90.21) — this looks wrong against older references and is right.
- **`world/Creature.cpp:4833-4841`** · A creature past `m_activeRadius` is retired with no persistence flag of any kind. Combined with **`world/WorldStore.hpp` `SavedCreature` having no `id` field**, this means (a) any animal you tame and leave behind is deleted, and (b) creature ids do not survive a save/load, so any link stored against an id would dangle. Read in the code. **Certain.** This is the hard blocker under G8.5 and the reason it is L rather than M.
- **`world/Creature.cpp:692-695`** · Horse `walkSpeed = 2.0`, `runSpeed = 4.5`. The reference's *slowest* horse is 4.86 b/s and its average is 9.49–9.71. Our fastest horse is slower than a sprinting player (5.612). **Certain** as a fact; **inferred** as a problem — these were plainly tuned for how a wandering herd reads on screen, and are fine for that. Flagged because the obvious implementation of "ride a horse" is to reuse `runSpeed`, and that would produce a mount slower than walking away from it. Same shape at Camel `runSpeed = 2.8` against Bedrock's 8.0 sprint and Donkey `3.8` against 7.38.
- **`world/Creature.cpp:689`** · Camel `health = 16`; the reference's camel is **32**. Read in the code against the wiki infobox. **Medium confidence** — the roster may be deliberately scaled, but the neighbouring rows (pig 10, horse 16 against the reference's 15-30 range) suggest this one is just low.
- **`world/Player.cpp:799-806`** · `kClimbSpeed = 2.4` against the reference's 2.35 (good), but `kSlideSpeed = 1.4` against the reference's **3.0 descending**. Descending a ladder takes more than twice as long as it should. **Medium confidence** — 1.4 may be modelling "let go and slide" rather than "hold down and climb down", but the code does not distinguish the two and the reference does.
- **`world/Block.hpp:3337`** · `isClimbable` is `isLadder || isVine`. `Scaffolding` (`:843`) is a real block that is not climbable, so a placed scaffold is decorative and blocks the space it occupies. **Certain.**
- **`world/Player.cpp:404-537`** · `moveAxis`, `blockingPlaneAlong`, `surfaceMotion` and `climbableAt` are all inside an anonymous namespace closed at `:537`, i.e. private to `Player.cpp`. Any vehicle needs the identical swept-AABB resolution against `worldCollisionBoxes`. **Certain**, and called out as a design instruction rather than a bug: a boat with its own copy of `moveAxis` is `CLAUDE.md` bug shape #14 ("a rule that did not travel") waiting to happen. Lift them into `Collision.hpp` *before* writing the first vehicle, not after.
- **Wiki-side conflicts worth recording so they are not "fixed" twice:** horse average speed is 9.714 b/s on the Horse page and 9.49 on Transportation; camel walk 3.885 vs 3.794 and sprint 8.203 vs 8.0; donkey 7.56 vs 7.38; standstill-to-full-speed is "seven powered rails" on the Rail page and "three in a row" on Tutorial:Minecarts; the TNT minecart is power 4 on the wiki and `power: 3` in Bedrock's own `tnt_minecart.json`. Prefer the entity page over Transportation for mounts, and prefer `bedrock-samples` over the wiki for anything the behaviour pack states directly — that is the precedent already set by the creeper swell distances (`Creature.cpp:654-659`).

## 9. Audio coverage and remaining visual work

**Scope:** Overworld only — the audio surface (`engine/src/audio/AudioEngine.cpp`, `game/src/core/Sounds.*`, `tools/make-reference-sounds.ps1`, every `sounds.play*` call site) and the rasterised visual surface (`engine/src/render/Renderer.cpp`, `engine/shaders/*`, `ChunkMesher.cpp`, `Particles.cpp`, `Weather.cpp`) measured against Bedrock; nothing requiring ray tracing or GI.

**Headline verdict:** Both halves are further along than a first look suggests and both fail in the same shape — *the machinery is built and the trigger is missing.* On audio, the mixer, the bank loader, the 57-event table, the 34 voice families and 497 recordings are all real and working, **there is background music (eight tracks) and there is cave ambience** — but **16 of the 57 events are staged, loaded, and never played by any call site**, there are **no UI sounds whatsoever**, and the settings expose **2 volume categories against Bedrock's 11**. On visuals the renderer is genuinely strong (deferred PBR, four-cascade shadows, real single-scattering sky, marched water reflections, raymarched clouds, weather, wet surfaces), and what is missing is almost entirely *content-facing* rather than renderer capability: **grass, leaves and water are not biome-tinted at all**, so twenty-seven biomes render one shade of green; there are **no stars**; there is **no enchantment glint, no name tags and no screen overlays** (fire, underwater, pumpkin, vignette, damage); and the particle catalogue is **7 emitter kinds against Bedrock's ~90 identifiers**. The block outline *does* exist, but as a single scaled box rather than the interaction shape. Nothing in this fragment is an optimisation — see `audit.md` §5, §6 and §11.3, which are not repeated here.

**Completeness estimate:** audio: 60% → **~70%** · visual: 72%

**Events staged, loaded, and never triggered from any call site (16 of 57):** `DigCoral`, `StepCoral`, `StepLadder`, `Breath`, `BowHit`, `Click`, `ItemBreak`, `Fizz`, `SplashBig`, `Swim`, `Drink`, `LevelUp`, `Fire`, `Lava`, `LavaPop`, `Water`. Verified by grepping every `SoundEvent::` use in `game/src/` and both resolver switches. Three of those are *unreachable by construction*, not merely unwired — see §9.6.

> ✅ **Closed on 2026-08-18, and the count is now 1 of 60.** Fifteen of the sixteen have call sites, and
> the three *unreachable by construction* cases went with them: `SoundMaterial::Coral` is returned and
> `Ladder` is an enumerator, so both resolve. **`LevelUp` is the only survivor and it is deliberate** —
> there is no XP moment to mark, `Sounds.cpp` files it as `SilentOnPurpose`, and the recording stays
> staged for the day one lands.
>
> **The real product of that round is not the twelve sounds; it is `Sounds::sweep()`.** A hand-kept
> `eventUse` table now classifies every event as played, deliberately silent, not-yet-wired or
> unclassified, and the sweep names every disagreement in the log at startup — orphaned recordings,
> events with nothing staged, mute creature voices, and any new `SoundEvent` whose author forgot to add
> a row. MSVC's C4062 is off even at `/W4` and this build does not enable it, so a runtime sweep is the
> only net available without a build change. **A future orphan announces itself; this one took twenty
> milestones to notice.**
>
> It also paid for itself on the way in: wiring `ItemBreak` exposed a **fourth** hand-rolled tool-wear
> path — the bow, reading its own durability constant and zeroing its own slot — which `wearTool` should
> always have owned. A missing *sound* was the symptom of a missing call to the owner.
