### 9.5 Gap detail

#### G9.1 — Sixteen staged sound events never fire · S · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** every one of these has a live event. Level-up is `random.levelup` [BE] / `entity.player.levelup` [JE] at **volume 0.75 for levels above 30, `(level/30)×0.75` below**, pitch 1.0, and **plays only at level multiples of 5 with a 5-second minimum between plays**. Item pickup is `random.pop` [BE] at **volume 0.25, pitch 0.6–2.2** (JE: 0.2 / 1.6–3.4). Item burnt in lava is `random.fizz` [BE] at **0.5 / 1.8–2.4**. Underwater ambience is `ambient.underwater.loop` at **volume 0.65, pitch 1.0, distance 16**, with `.additions` at 90%, `.rare` at 9% and `.ultra_rare` at 1%. Swim is `random.swim` [BE], **pitch 0.6–1.4**, volume scaled by momentum. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Player#Sounds, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Item_(entity), https://minecraft.wiki/w/Experience, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ambience]
- **What we have:** all sixteen are in `kStems` (`Sounds.cpp:12-40`), all sixteen have recordings named in `tools/make-reference-sounds.ps1:44-137`, all sixteen are decoded at startup by `Sounds::load` (`Sounds.cpp:284-317`), and none is referenced by a single `sounds.play*` call. The header's own comment at `Sounds.hpp:20-24` predicts exactly this failure mode — "a mismatch fails silently as an event that never sounds" — and `has()` (`:227-230`) exists to detect it, but nothing calls `has()` outside the loader.
- **What must be built:**
  1. `LevelUp` → the XP threshold crossing near `Main.cpp:5303` (which already plays `Orb`).
  2. `ItemBreak` → tool durability reaching zero (`Tool.cpp`).
  3. `Drink` → the potion branch beside the `Eat`/`Burp` pair at `Main.cpp:4909-4914`; a potion is a drink, not a meal.
  4. `Fizz` → an `ItemEntity` or a fluid meeting lava (`ItemEntity.cpp`, `Fluid.hpp`); also water poured on lava.
  5. `Breath` → the drowning tick in `Survival.hpp`.
  6. `BowHit` → the arrow-strikes-entity path in `Projectile.cpp` (the arrow-strikes-*ground* case already plays `HitLand` at `Main.cpp:6059`).
  7. `SplashBig` → the same edge as `Splash` (`Main.cpp:4252`) when the entry speed exceeds Bedrock's 0.25 momentum threshold.
  8. `Swim` → a distance accumulator while `player.inWater`, mirroring the footstep accumulator at `Main.cpp:4152-4170`.
  9. `Fire`, `Lava`, `LavaPop`, `Water` → ambient loops; see G9.6.
  10. `Click` → see G9.2.
  11. `DigCoral`/`StepCoral`/`StepLadder` → see §9.6, these are unreachable rather than merely unwired.
- **Numbers that matter:** 16/57 = **28% of the event table is dead**. Level-up every 5 levels with a 5 s floor. Pickup pitch 0.6–2.2. Underwater loop volume 0.65.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none — every recording is already staged and loaded. This is the highest ratio of player-audible change to effort anywhere in this fragment. **Add a startup probe that logs `has(event)` for all 57 and asserts every event has both recordings and at least one call site**, or this will re-rot; the project's own bug-shape #10 is exactly this.

#### G9.2 — No UI sounds at all · S · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `random.click` [BE] / `ui.button.click` [JE] is one of the ten original sound events. Screen-specific results have their own: `ui.loom.take_result` (**volume 1.0 [BE] / 0.5 [JE]**, pitch 1.0, distance 16, caption "Loom used"), `ui.cartography_table.take_result` (caption "Map drawn"), `ui.stonecutter.take_result`, `hud.bubble.pop` [BE] / `ui.hud.bubble_pop` [JE]. The whole family sits in the `ui` category [JE] / `sound` category [BE]. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Sounds.json, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Closed_captions]
- **What we have:** `SoundEvent::Click` with `random/click.ogg` staged (`make-reference-sounds.ps1:86`) and zero call sites. `WoodClick` *is* wired but only for world blocks — buttons and levers at `Main.cpp:5176`, `:5184`.
- **What must be built:** one `sounds.playGlobal(audio, SoundEvent::Click, 0.25f)` at each of: hotbar slot change (`Hotbar.cpp`), screen open/close (`InventoryScreen.cpp`), tab switch, slot pick-up and slot put-down (`SlotOps.cpp:*`), recipe select (`InventoryScreen.cpp`), and craft-result take. Eight screens ship today (`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` "Game Architecture"), and every one of them is silent.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock plays UI sounds **non-positionally** and at full `sound`-category volume; a 0.2–0.3 multiplier is what stops a click-heavy inventory session becoming fatiguing.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none. Note the correct Bedrock ID spelling is `ui.loom.take_result` with dots, not underscores — worth recording if a settings screen ever enumerates categories.

#### G9.3 — Two volume categories, applied once at startup · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the Audio settings tab exposes **11 sliders** — Global (default **50%**), Music (default **30%**), Sound, Environmental audio, Blocks, Hostile mobs, Friendly mobs, Other players, Musical blocks, Weather, Text to speech (all others default 100%). The engine categories are `main`, `music`, `record`, `weather`, `block`, `hostile`, `neutral`, `player`, `ambient`, `texttospeech`, `sound`. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings#Audio, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Sound#Categories]
- **What we have:** `Settings::soundVolume` and `Settings::musicVolume` (`Settings.hpp:68-69`), pushed into the engine exactly once at `Main.cpp:1003-1004`. `AudioEngine` has one `masterVolume` and one `musicVolume` in `Impl` (`AudioEngine.cpp:74-75`) and applies them per-sample in the mix loop (`:126-127`).
- **What must be built:** a `SoundCategory` enum on `SoundPlay` (a `uint8_t`, defaulting to a `Sound` catch-all); a `std::array<float, N>` of bus gains in `Impl`; `voice.bus` set at `play()` time; and the mixer's `const float bus = voice.music ? musicVolume : 1.0f` (`AudioEngine.cpp:110`) replaced by an array index. Then map the 57 events and 34 voice families onto categories — voices split by whether the species is hostile, which `Creature.hpp`'s species table already knows.
- **Numbers that matter:** 11 categories; Bedrock's non-100% defaults are Global **50%** and Music **30%** (ours is 1.0 and **0.55**, which is closer than it looks).
- **Risks / dependencies:** the settings *screen* is M34; this change is worth making now anyway, because `settings.cfg` can carry the rows and the screen is then a view over data that already exists. Making the volumes live rather than startup-only is two lines in the settings reload path.

#### G9.4 — Music cadence and selection · XS (cadence) / M (selection) · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** gameplay music replays **10–20 minutes after the previous track ends** = **12000–24000 ticks**; the wiki carries a `{{Verify}}` noting this "seems to be much shorter in BE", so treat the BE number as unconfirmed. [JE] offers a Music Frequency option: Default 10–20 min, Frequent 10 min, Constant 5 s. The track is **selected by the current biome** — Bedrock added `music.overworld.grove`, `.snowy_slopes`, `.jagged_peaks`, `.stony_peaks`, `.dripstone_caves`, `.lush_caves`, `.deep_dark` in Preview 1.21.0.24 and `.forest` in 1.21.90.25. Creative uses a separate set. Menu music starts **1–30 s** after the title screen appears. Bedrock **fades music out on world quit** and **pauses it in the game menu**. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Music, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Bedrock_Edition_history_of_sound_events]
- **What we have:** `kMusicGapSeconds = 210.0f` (`Sounds.cpp:71`) — **3.5 minutes**, against Bedrock's 10–20. `tickMusic` (`:391-405`) picks uniformly at random **with replacement**, so the same track can play twice in a row. There is no menu music (no menu), no creative set, no biome selection, and no fade — `playMusic` hard-cuts the previous voice (`AudioEngine.cpp:252-286`).
- **What must be built:** (a) raise the gap to a random **600–1200 s** — one line plus the existing `nextRandom`; (b) remember the last handle and re-roll once if it repeats — three lines; (c) an optional biome→track table keyed off the same `Biome` lookup the mesher uses, which is the only part that is M-effort.
- **Numbers that matter:** 210 s → 600–1200 s. 8 tracks staged (`make-reference-sounds.ps1:118-122`) against Bedrock's ~30 overworld tracks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none. Note this is the one place where our number is *not conservative* — music is currently 3–6× more frequent than the reference, which is the sort of thing that reads as "constantly playing" after an hour.

#### G9.5 — Cave ambience is a timer, not a mood · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour (Java's documented algorithm; BE's is flagged `{{Info needed}}` on the wiki):** a **0–100% mood value** updated every client tick. Each tick one random block inside a **17×17×17 cube centred on the player's eye** is sampled: any sky light → **−1/1000 per level**; block light > 1 → **−(blockLight−1)/6000**; block light == 0 → **+1/6000**. At 100% the sound plays and mood resets to 0. In complete darkness that is **one cave sound every 6000 ticks = 5 minutes**. **23 cave recordings**, all volume 1.0, pitch 1.0, distance 16. The legacy algorithm (which the wiki suggests Bedrock may still use) picks from the 27 points at offsets ±4 on each axis, requiring the block be air with **sky light 0 and block light ≤ random(0,8)** — which is where the "at least 4 blocks away, and it comes from somewhere" quality originates. Bedrock still varies cave-sound pitch **0.8×–1.0×**; Java fixed it at 1.0 in 20w10a. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ambience#Mood_algorithm]
- **What we have:** `Main.cpp:4260-4271` — a **22-second** countdown, and on expiry a single `world.skyLightAt` at the player's head. Fires when `sky <= 2 && player.position.y < 40.0f`, via `playGlobal` (unpositioned). Eight recordings staged, not 23.
- **What must be built:**
  1. **Delete the `y < 40` clause.** It is the bug: a sealed room, a covered ravine or a mineshaft at y=70 has sky light 0 and will never make a noise. The reference's test is darkness, not depth, and darkness is already the other half of the condition.
  2. Replace the fixed timer with the mood accumulator — a single `float m_mood` ticked once per frame against one randomly sampled block in a 17³ cube. That is roughly fifteen lines and it needs `blockLightAt` alongside the existing `skyLightAt`.
  3. **Play it positionally**, at the sampled block, with rolloff 16, instead of `playGlobal`. This is most of what the effect is for.
  4. Stage the remaining 15 cave recordings — one row in `make-reference-sounds.ps1:113-115`.
- **Numbers that matter:** 17³ sample cube; +1/6000 per tick in full darkness → **5 minutes**; our current 22 s poll is ~13× more frequent when the gate passes, and infinitely less frequent above y=40.
- **Risks / dependencies:** needs a per-block light query that already exists for sky light; confirm `World` exposes `blockLightAt` and, if not, that is the only new API.

#### G9.6 — Underwater, fire and lava ambience · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `ambient.underwater.loop` at **volume 0.65**, plus `.additions` (90% chance, 8 recordings), `.rare` (9%, 8 recordings, volumes 0.45–1.0) and `.ultra_rare` (1%, 5 recordings) — **22 recordings total**, playing whenever the player's *head* is underwater. Note that Bedrock only gained underwater ambience in **1.21.120**. Entry/exit are `ambient.underwater.enter`/`.exit`. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ambience]
- **What we have:** `Water`, `Fire`, `Lava`, `LavaPop` staged and never played. `player.inWater` is already tracked and its edge already fires a splash (`Main.cpp:4252-4256`).
- **What must be built:** a small "ambient loop" helper that retriggers a handle on a timer while a predicate holds — the rain loop at `Main.cpp:6771-6779` is already exactly this shape (3.4 s retrigger, because the mixer has no loop point) and should be generalised rather than copied a fourth time. Underwater: retrigger `Water` while `player.inWater`, with a 9%/1% roll for a rare variant. Fire/lava: the emitter cache in `Particles.cpp:193-260` already finds torches, fire, lit furnaces and lava within range each half-second and is the natural place to hang a positional `Fire`/`Lava` retrigger, with `LavaPop` as an occasional one-shot.
- **Numbers that matter:** 0.65 loop volume; 90/9/1 rarity split; the mixer's lack of a loop point is why everything here must be a retrigger (`Sounds.cpp` comment at the rain rows).
- **Risks / dependencies:** **this is the project's own bug shape #14 — a rule that exists in one place and did not travel.** The rain retrigger is correct and commented; the same pattern is owed to three other loops. Write it once.

#### G9.7 — Creature footsteps · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** every mob has `mob.<name>.step` and pays the same distance-driven cadence as the player (Java: ≈**1.667 blocks travelled per step**; not wiki-documented, flagged as decompiled knowledge). Horses use the volume and pitch of the block they stand on. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Block_sound_type]
- **What we have:** `playVoice` handles Idle/Hurt/Death only (`Sounds.hpp:213`, `Sounds.cpp:371-389`); `CreatureSound` has three enumerators (`Creature.hpp:831`). The golem's *idle* recording is literally `mob/irongolem/walk` (`make-reference-sounds.ps1:174`) because it has no ambient of its own — a footstep standing in for a voice, which is a hint that the footstep path is what is actually missing.
- **What must be built:** a `stepDistance` float per creature, accumulated in `Creature::step`, emitting a `CreatureSound::Step` into `m_voices` past the threshold; `Main.cpp:5929-5932` then resolves it through `stepSoundFor(soundMaterialFor(blockUnder))` rather than through the voice bank. That reuses the whole material table for free.
- **Numbers that matter:** ~1.667 blocks per step; our player uses 2.1 (`Main.cpp:2369`). Volume should be well under the player's 0.32 to avoid a herd drowning the world.
- **Risks / dependencies:** at mob-cap population this is the one audio change that could plausibly exhaust 48 voices; cap it by distance before enqueueing.

#### G9.8 — Closed captions · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** off by default; **1.5 s dwell, configurable 1–4 s in 0.5 s steps**; position selectable (top right default / chat height / bottom right); background opacity follows the chat background (70%); separate toggles to hide the player's own sounds and to hide weather/ambient captions. Generic block captions are `subtitles.block.generic.break` "Block broken", `.footsteps` "Footsteps", `.hit` "Block breaking", `.place` "Block placed". [JE] shows a `<` or `>` arrow toward off-screen sources and fades the text as the sound fades. [https://minecraft.wiki/w/Closed_captions, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Settings#Accessibility]
- **What we have:** nothing; no `subtitle` field on any event.
- **What must be built:** a `const char*` column beside `kStems` in `Sounds.cpp:12-40` and beside `kVoiceStems`, a small ring of (text, age, direction) in `Sounds`, and a HUD draw using the existing text primitives (`HudPrimitives.cpp`). The direction arrow falls out of the same dot-against-right the panner already computes (`AudioEngine.cpp:257-261`).
- **Numbers that matter:** 1.5 s default dwell, 1–4 s range; 91 rows of caption text (57 events + 34 families).
- **Risks / dependencies:** this doubles as the **cheapest possible diagnostic for G9.1** — an event that never appears as a caption during a play session is an event that never fires.

#### G9.9 — No biome tinting of grass, foliage or water · M · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** `grass.png`, `foliage.png` and `dry_foliage.png` are **256×256** colormaps indexed with the **bottom-right corner as (0,0)**, temperature increasing along +X and downfall along +Y, clamping to the nearest edge outside the used lower-left triangle. Grass-tinted: grass blocks, short/tall grass, ferns, sugar cane, bushes. Foliage-tinted: vines and oak/jungle/acacia/dark-oak/mangrove leaves. **Spruce `#619961` and birch `#80A755` are fixed**, biome-independent (Bedrock ships these as `evergreen.png`/`birch.png`). Hardcoded overrides: swamp grass is XZ-noise-driven — `< −0.1` → **`#4C763C`**, else **`#6A7039`**; badlands grass **`#90814D`**, foliage **`#9E814D`** [JE] / **`#AEA42A`** [BE]; dark forest is `(c & 0xFEFEFE)` averaged with **`#28340A`** → **`#507A32`**; cherry grove **`#B6DB61`**; pale garden `#778272`/`#878D76`. Sample climate rows: plains 0.8/0.4 → grass `#91BD59`, foliage `#77AB2F`; forest 0.7/0.8 → `#79C05A`/`#59AE30`; jungle 0.95/0.9 → `#59C93C`/`#30BB0B`; taiga 0.25/0.8 → `#86B783`/`#68A464`; snowy plains 0.0/0.5 → `#80B497`/`#60A17B`; birch forest 0.6/0.6 → `#88BB67`/`#6BA941`. Water surface default **`#3F76E4`**, swamp **`#617B64`**, warm ocean **`#43D5EE`** [JE] / **`#02B0E5`** [BE], frozen ocean `#2570B5` [BE], mangrove swamp `#3A7A6A`, lush caves `#44AFF5` [BE], river `#0084FF` [BE]. **Bedrock does blend across borders** — the average of plant/water colours over a square centred on the block — but exposes no radius slider; [JE] offers 3×3 (Fast) and 5×5 (default). Sky and fog colour use a **Gaussian blur over a 5×5×5 block region** in both editions. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Biome&action=raw&section=21, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Biome&action=raw&section=33, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Water&action=raw&section=27]
- **What we have:** nothing. `Biome` (`Biome.hpp:176-222`) carries `warmth`, `top`, `filler`, `patch`, `steep`, `treeDensity`, `grassDensity`, `flowerShare` — **no colour of any kind**. Grepping `ChunkMesher.cpp` and every shader for `tint`/`grassColo`/`foliageColo`/`waterColo` returns only unrelated comments. Every grass block, every leaf and every ocean in 27 biomes uses the raw texture.
- **What must be built:**
  1. Add `grassTint`, `foliageTint` and `waterTint` (packed `uint32` RGB) to the biome row, sourced from the climate table above — this is a data edit, not an algorithm, and it is the whole reason to do it this way rather than shipping a colormap image: `warmth` already exists as the temperature axis.
  2. In the mesher, look up the tint for the column's biome and **multiply it into the vertex colour** — but note the trap recorded at `TIMELINE.md` M23: for world geometry those three vertex channels are **sky light, block light and face shade**, not a tint. There is no spare channel. The honest options are a **fourth vertex byte** (the vertex is 32 bytes; `Vertex.hpp` would need a look) or a **per-layer tint index** in the material storage buffer the G-buffer already reads (`Renderer.hpp:326`), with the *biome* supplied per-chunk via push constant. **The second is much cheaper and does not touch the vertex format.** Its limitation is that a chunk spanning two biomes gets one answer — which argues for the per-vertex route if border blending is wanted.
  3. Apply the tint in `gbuffer.frag` only where the layer is marked tintable — that is one bit in the existing material word, and it must be keyed by **texture layer**, not by block, so 640 shaped variants inherit it for free (the project's own `shapedParent` precedent).
  4. Border blending: average the tint over a 3×3 or 5×5 column neighbourhood at mesh time. Cheap where the tint is per-vertex, impossible where it is per-chunk.
- **Numbers that matter:** 256×256 colormaps; ≈15 climate rows to fill in for 27 biomes; the exact hexes above; blend radius 3×3 (Fast) / 5×5 (default); grass-block **side overlay** is a separate texture from the top and takes the same tint.
- **Risks / dependencies:** ⚠️ The commonly-quoted index formula (`adjRain = downfall × adjTemp`, `x = (1−adjTemp)×255`) is **not printed on minecraft.wiki** — the wiki gives only the axis description. Since the per-biome result hexes *are* published, **use the hex table directly and skip the colormap image entirely**; that sidesteps an unverified formula and removes a 256×256 texture from the load path. Second risk: the biome must reach the mesher without breaking meshing purity — `MeshJobInput` already carries a copied volume plus border, so the biome id has to be copied in alongside it, not looked up from a worker.

#### G9.10 — No stars · XS · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** **1500 generation attempts, seed 10842, producing ~780 actual stars**. No texture — plain white squares, side length **0.3–0.5**. They appear at tick **11576**, reach maximum brightness at **13219**, begin fading at **22782**, and are at minimum at tick **425**. Hidden by precipitation and by "Beautiful Skies" being off. The night sky itself is always **`#000000`**, and the sky fades to full transparency **7° above the horizon**. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Sky&action=raw]
- **What we have:** nothing. `sky.glsl` produces a scattering gradient and two glow lobes; the moon is a textured quad with 8 phases. Grepping the shaders for `star` returns no hits.
- **What must be built:** the sky is already written by the lighting pass wherever nothing was drawn (`TIMELINE.md` M25), so this costs **no pass and no geometry** — a hash of the view ray direction quantised to a grid, thresholded, multiplied by a brightness ramp driven by the same day fraction the sun direction already uses. Twenty lines in `sky.glsl`. Snap the sample grid the way the water reflection is snapped so the stars read as square pixels rather than as points, consistent with the rest of the art direction.
- **Numbers that matter:** ~780 visible; size 0.3–0.5 blocks at the sky distance; brightness ramp 11576→13219 in and 22782→425 out (Bedrock ticks, 24000/day); suppress under precipitation, which `Renderer::setPrecipitation` already knows.
- **Risks / dependencies:** must not brighten the horizon — the M25 constraint that the horizon stays **exactly** the fog colour outranks everything, so fade stars to zero over the bottom ~15° of the sky.

#### G9.11 — Particle catalogue · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** particles are **front-facing 2-D sprites** culled at a **32-block spherical radius** (except campfire smoke and fireworks, which use simulation distance), collide with solid blocks, are slowed by cobwebs, unaffected by entities, and drawn from `particles.png`. Many are **greyscale textures with colour applied afterwards**, colours often defined by Molang — e.g. basic smoke is `rgb = random1 × 0.5`, explosion/poof `random1 × 0.6 + 0.4`, redstone dust `r = (random1×0.2+0.8) × (random2×0.4+0.6)` with `g = b = 0`. Effect swirls (`mobspell_emitter`, `mobspell_ambient`, `mobspell_lingering`) take **the effect's own colour** applied to an 8-frame greyscale sheet, and with multiple effects each particle randomly picks one effect's colour (tipped arrows and lingering clouds merge instead). Effect colours include Poison `#87A363`, Regeneration `#CD5CAB`, Strength `#FFC700`, Swiftness `#33EBFF`, Night Vision `#C2FF66`, Slowness `#8BAFE0`, Nausea `#551D4A`. Overworld identifiers we do not have include `heart_particle`, `villager_happy`, `villager_angry`, `critical_hit_emitter`, `basic_crit_particle`, `magical_critical_hit_emitter`, `note_particle`, `enchanting_table_particle` (26 glyph textures), `snowflake_particle` `#DFE5ED`, `water_drip_particle` `#334DFF`, `lava_drip_particle`, `honey_drip_particle` `#947215`, `basic_bubble_particle`, `bubble_column_up/down_particle`, `water_wake_particle`, `rain_splash_particle`, `campfire_smoke_particle`, `campfire_tall_smoke_particle`, `redstone_wire_dust_particle`, `falling_dust`, `electric_spark_particle` `#FFE6FF`, `totem_particle`, `crop_growth_emitter`, `biome_tinted_leaves_particle`, `spore_blossom_shower_particle` `#528038`. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Particles&action=raw&section=1, &section=5, &section=7, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Effect_colors]
- **What we have:** **7 emitter kinds** — `spawnBlockBreak`, `spawnSplash`, `spawnFootstep`, `spawnSmoke`, `spawnFlame`, `spawnEat`, `spawnExplosion` (`Particles.hpp:70-92`) — plus `emitAmbient` (`Particles.cpp:193-260`) which drives torch/fire/furnace/lava smoke off a half-second cached emitter scan. Call sites: `Main.cpp:4198` (footstep), `:4629` (block break), `:4865` (eat), `:6035`/`:6070` (thrown potion, splash cloud — reusing `spawnEat`), `:6398` (explosion), `:6634` (lightning smoke), `:6833` (rain splash). Ceiling 3000; a particle carries no colour of its own, only sky light / block light / face shade, so it goes down the existing lit cutout path with no shader case.
- **What must be built:** the *system* is finished; this is emitters and call sites. Ranked by what a player will actually miss, given what already ships:
  1. **Effect swirls** — potions, brewing and 20+ effects shipped at M29i and produce no visual at all. Needs a per-effect colour and a greyscale sprite. **This is the biggest single hole**, because the feature exists and is invisible.
  2. **Heart / villager happy / villager angry** — villagers, trading and breeding all shipped at M29d.
  3. **Crit and magic-crit** — combat shipped at M20b/M29l; a hit currently has sound but no spark.
  4. **Note** — note blocks are in the redstone kit (M29h).
  5. **Water drips, bubbles, wake, rain splash on water** — the last one partially exists (`Main.cpp:6833`).
  6. **Falling dust, snowflake, crop growth, campfire smoke column, redstone dust.**
- **Numbers that matter:** 32-block cull radius (we have a 3000-particle ceiling but no documented radius cull); ~90 Bedrock identifiers vs our 7; the effect-colour hex table above is directly usable.
- **Risks / dependencies:** ⚠️ **A particle here has no colour channel** — the three vertex channels are already sky light, block light and face shade (`TIMELINE.md` M28). Everything coloured (swirls, hearts, redstone dust, drips) needs either a coloured texture layer per particle type or a fourth channel. The cheapest honest answer is a **small palette of pre-tinted texture layers**, since the game already resolves particles to texture layers. Also remember the recorded trap: **particles shrink as they die rather than fading**, because the cutout path discards below half alpha.

#### G9.12 — Screen overlays and the damage response · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the documented full-screen overlay set is suffocation, **on-fire (Bedrock draws it as a cubemap around the player; Java uses two intersecting planes across the bottom half of the screen)**, underwater ("a blue vignette"), freezing/powder snow, **pumpkin blur (Bedrock centres it with dark edges; Java stretches it to the screen edges)**, spyglass scope, darkness vignette (pulsing), and the Java-only nausea green vignette. Camera transformations: **damage tilt (Java tilts toward the damage source; Bedrock always tilts right)**, view bobbing, FOV change, and Bedrock's camera shake. The vignette itself is a Fancy-graphics feature — **Bedrock Simple has no vignette at all** — and Bedrock applies a **full vignette below Y = −11**. Fog collapses to pure black at **5 blocks** under Blindness and **15 blocks** under Darkness. Java exposes Damage Tilt, Distortion Effects, FOV Effects and Darkness Pulsing as 0–100% accessibility sliders. ⚠️ Bedrock does **not** currently expose a Distortion Effects slider — that is Java-only, with Bedrock arrival flagged as upcoming. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Screen_effects&action=raw, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Graphics_settings&action=raw, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Fog]
- **What we have:** none of them. `player.hurtFlash` exists and its only visual consequence is a 0.004 jitter on the heart row (`StatusBars.cpp:136`). Being on fire, drowning and wearing a carved pumpkin are all visually identical to standing still. Underwater fog exists and is good (`deferred.frag:195-255`) but there is no overlay on top of it.
- **What must be built:** the UI pass already has **no depth attachment** and sorts screen geometry farthest-first by triangle (`TIMELINE.md` M23d), so a full-screen textured quad is nearly free and needs no new pipeline. In order:
  1. **Damage vignette** — a red radial falloff driven by `hurtFlash`, which already exists and already decays. Two triangles.
  2. **Fire overlay** — the fire block's own animated texture layer across the bottom of the screen while burning; the animated-layer machinery is already in the renderer (`setAnimatedLayer`, `Renderer.hpp:158`).
  3. **Underwater blue vignette** — gated on the same `frame.eye.w <= 0` bit the fog already uses.
  4. **Pumpkin blur** — gated on the head armour slot; a carved pumpkin is already placeable and already an item.
  5. **Low-light vignette** — driven by the player's own block/sky light, matching Bedrock's Fancy behaviour.
- **Numbers that matter:** Blindness fog at 5 blocks, Darkness at 15 (neither effect exists here yet, but the potion system does); Bedrock's rain sky overlay is rgb(103,103,103) at 100% and thunder rgb(51,51,51) at 75% — worth comparing against our current staggered ramps; lightning flash rgb(204,204,255) at 45%.
- **Risks / dependencies:** ⚠️ **These are HUD quads and the world/HUD share one pipeline that writes depth** — `audit.md` §5.3 documents exactly this. Adding overlapping full-screen quads is the most likely way to *reproduce* that bug. Draw them in the UI pass (no depth attachment), never the forward pass.

#### G9.13 — Block selection outline follows a box, not the shape · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the **interaction box** is shown as a black outline around the block's edges, following the interaction shape rather than a unit cube — over 100 block classes define distinct shapes, so a fence outlines post-plus-arms and a stair outlines the stair. Drawn only when the block is inside interaction range: **Bedrock block reach 5 blocks** (keyboard/mouse and controller), 6 on touch and 12 in touch creative; Java 4.5 survival / 5 creative. Bedrock exposes an **"Outline Selection"** video option, default **ON** on Windows/console and **OFF** on mobile; turning it off replaces the wireframe with the legacy white block highlight. Java's High Contrast Block Outlines makes it cyan `#57FFE1` with a small black outline. Known quirk: shapes that exceed 1×1×1 (extended piston arm, opened shulker lid) do not draw the outline when the crosshair hits the protruding part (MC-158827). [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Hitbox&action=raw&section=8, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Interaction_range&action=raw]
- **What we have:** `makeBlockOutline(size)` (`BlockOutline.hpp:20`) builds a cage of thin solid bars around a box, rebuilt only when the size changes (`Main.cpp:6515-6517`) and moved by transform. The size is the **union** of `worldSelectionBoxes` (`Main.cpp:6462`). That is exactly right for a slab, a double chest and a carpet, and wrong for a fence, a wall, a pane, a torch and a stair — all of which get a box larger than the thing inside it. Note the *cracks* mesh does this correctly already (`BlockOutline.hpp:22-35`, built from `worldDrawnBoxes`), so the codebase already contains the better answer twelve lines away.
- **What must be built:** change `makeBlockOutline` to take the **box list** rather than a single extent and emit one cage per box, exactly as `makeBlockCracks` already walks `worldDrawnBoxes`. Rebuild when the *target cell* changes rather than when the size changes, since a list has no cheap equality test — that is once per targeted block, not per frame.
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock reach **5 blocks**; our raycast reach is in `Raycast.hpp`. The outline is drawn in the forward pass and therefore already inherits the depth-write behaviour of `audit.md` §5.3 — worth checking it is not being depth-rejected by water.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none; it is the same traversal the cracks already do. **This is the project's own bug shape #14 again** — the correct rule exists in one of the two places that need it.

#### G9.14 — Enchantment glint · S (shader) · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** ⚠️ **The wiki's `Enchantment glint` page is a `{{wip}}` stub with `{{info needed}}` on the animation itself.** What *is* verified: the glint is **hardcoded**, not driven by `.mcmeta` animation data; its rendering is tied to texture-atlas size (MC-276841); Java has had **separate item and armour/entity glint textures since 1.20-pre1**; and Java's accessibility options expose **Glint Speed default 50%** and **Glint Strength default 75%**. Bedrock resource packs can retexture it, but green/yellow/white glints render poorly. The scroll rates, the ±10° texture-matrix rotation and the exact texture paths are **not documented anywhere citable** — a web search returned only mutually inconsistent mod-forum numbers. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Enchantment_glint&action=raw, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Options&action=raw&section=21]
- **What we have:** nothing, and nothing to put it on — `Enchant*` appears only as a block row and an item name (`Block.hpp`, `Item.hpp`); there is no enchanting screen, no enchantment state on an item stack and no enchanted-book contents. The `glint` identifier in `triangle.frag:318-321` is the water specular's luminance term, unrelated.
- **What must be built (shader only, if the mechanic is deferred):** two additively-blended copies of one greyscale texture, scrolled at different rates with a rotated UV matrix, multiplied by a violet tint and by a strength constant. Drawn over the item sprite in the HUD pass and over the held-item mesh in the forward pass. Because Bedrock's constants are unciteable, **pick values by eye and expose them as two settings rows** mirroring Java's own two sliders — that turns an unverifiable number into a player choice, which is the honest resolution.
- **Numbers that matter:** the only two defensible numbers are Java's defaults, **speed 50% and strength 75%**. Do not assert any scroll rate as "the reference's".
- **Risks / dependencies:** the visible payoff is zero until items can actually be enchanted; sequence this **after** an enchanting mechanic, or build it against the existing enchanted-book item as a single hardcoded case to prove the shader.

#### G9.15 — Name tags and world-space text · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the `minecraft:name_tag_distance` attribute has **default 64 blocks, minimum 0, maximum 512**; the scoreboard `below_name_distance` attribute defaults to **10**. When `CustomNameVisible` is false the name shows only if the entity is **aimed at from ≤3 blocks in Survival/Adventure/Spectator, or ≤5 in Creative**. Name length caps at **50 characters [JE] / 30 [BE]**. Bedrock exposes `nameplateDepthTested` and `nameplateRenderDistance` per entity in its scripting API, which confirms the nameplate has a depth-test toggle. ⚠️ The 0.025 text scale, the `height + 0.5` offset and the alpha-0.25 background quad are **not on the wiki** — treat as unverified. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Attribute&action=raw&section=29, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Name_Tag&action=raw&section=6]
- **What we have:** no world-space text path at all. `ItemId::NameTag` exists (`Item.hpp:331`) as an item with nothing behind it. The HUD text primitives (`HudPrimitives.cpp`) are screen-space only and go through the UI pass.
- **What must be built:** a camera-facing quad batch in the forward pass sampling the same font atlas the HUD uses, plus a dark backing quad. The particle system already builds camera-facing quads on the CPU with two cross products for the whole set (`Particles.cpp`) — that is the pattern to copy, not a new billboarding path.
- **Numbers that matter:** 64-block cutoff; 30-character cap [BE]; ≤5-block aim-at reveal when the tag is not persistent.
- **Risks / dependencies:** this must be **depth-tested but not depth-writing**, which lands squarely on `audit.md` §5.3's shared-pipeline problem; it is a second consumer of that fix, not a reason to work around it.

#### G9.16 — Per-biome sky and fog colour · S · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** sky colour is derived from temperature — `T = clamp(temperature/3, −1, 1)`, then `skyColorHSV = (0.62222224 − 0.05×T, 0.5 + 0.1×T, 1.0)`. Resulting hexes: `#78A7FF` plains/swamp/beach, `#79A6FF` forest, `#7AA5FF` birch forest, `#7BA4FF` ocean/river, `#77A8FF` jungle, `#6EB1FF` desert/badlands, `#7DA3FF` taiga, `#7FA1FF` snowy plains, `#859DFF` jagged/frozen peaks, `#B9B9B9` pale garden (hardcoded, exempt from the formula). The night sky is always `#000000`. Sky and fog colour are **Gaussian-blurred over a 5×5×5 block region centred on the camera's block**. Bedrock's overworld air fog is `#ABD2FF` (Java `#C0D8FF`) and render-distance fog starts at **92% of render distance**; Bedrock weather fog appears at **23%** and is opaque at **70%** of render distance, colour `#666666`. Bedrock also **darkens brightness from Y=32 down to Y=−11, going pure black with a full vignette below Y=−11**. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Sky&action=raw, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Fog]
- **What we have:** one global sky, computed physically (`sky.glsl`), and one fog colour set per frame (`Renderer.hpp:173`). Neither varies with biome. Rain and thunder already flatten and darken both on staggered ramps (M27), which is the correct half of the behaviour.
- **What must be built:** the biome tint work in G9.9 already puts a per-column climate value in reach; the sky needs only the camera's own biome, so this is a single lookup and a lerp toward the temperature-derived hue, blurred over the neighbouring columns. **Critically, this must be applied as a tint on the existing scattering result, not as a replacement** — the M25 constraint that the horizon stays exactly the fog colour is absolute.
- **Numbers that matter:** the HSV formula above; 5×5×5 blur; fog onset at 92% of render distance.
- **Risks / dependencies:** depends on G9.9 landing the climate lookup; do not do it first.

#### G9.17 — Entity blob shadow, third person, view bobbing · S / M · P2–P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Fancy graphics draws a **static round shadow under every entity — 13-sided (tridecagonal) in Bedrock, circular in Java**; Simple graphics draws none. Camera perspective cycles **First Person / Third Person Back / Third Person Front** on F5, and the third-person camera collides against the **block visual box** (a distinct concept from the collision box: fences/mud/snow/soul sand use their interaction box; glass, glass panes, iron bars, copper bars/grates, powder snow and tinted glass have an **empty** visual box; everything else uses the collision box). View Bobbing and Camera Shake are separate toggles; Damage Tilt is a 0–100% slider defaulting to 100%. [https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Graphics_settings&action=raw, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Settings&action=raw&section=26, https://minecraft.wiki/index.php?title=Hitbox&action=raw&section=11]
- **What we have:** contact shadows off the depth buffer (`deferred.frag`, 8 taps, fading past 24 m) do most of the *contact* job but nothing at distance and nothing under a floating entity. `F5` is the diagnostics overlay (`Main.cpp:3245`). No bobbing, no third person, no player model on screen — which means **53 creature skins and a full joint rig exist and the player has never seen their own character**.
- **What must be built:** the blob shadow is a single downward-facing textured quad per entity, raycast to the ground, faded by height — it can ride the existing particle mesh path with no new pipeline. Third person needs a camera offset, a collision sweep against the visual box, and the player rendered as a creature (the rig already draws 57 species). View bobbing is a sine on the camera transform driven by the same distance accumulator the footsteps use (`Main.cpp:4152-4170`).
- **Numbers that matter:** Bedrock's entity shadow is 13-sided; Java's Entity Distance 100% = 160 blocks; FOV range 30–110°, Bedrock default **60°** (Java 70°).
- **Risks / dependencies:** third person is the one item here that is a *feature* rather than a rendering detail, and it changes input, collision and the HUD. Do the blob shadow and the bobbing first; they are hours, not days.

### 9.6 Errors and inconsistencies noticed while reading

| Location | Symptom | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| `Sounds.cpp:186-224` vs `:245-247`, `:274-276` | **`SoundMaterial::Coral` is never returned by `soundMaterialFor`.** The function tests leaves, logs, glass, sand, gravel, snow, wet, grass, carpet, then recurses through `shapedParent`, then falls back to Wood-or-Stone. There is no coral test anywhere. So `DigCoral` and `StepCoral` are **unreachable by construction**, not merely unwired — 10 staged recordings that no code path can select. | **certain** |
| `Sounds.hpp:139-151` vs `Sounds.cpp:271-273` | **`StepLadder` is unreachable for the same reason, one level worse**: `SoundMaterial` has no `Ladder` enumerator at all, so `stepSoundFor` cannot return `StepLadder` even in principle. Five staged recordings, zero possible callers. Ladders exist in the game (`SYSTEM_MEMORY.md` "Ladders, vines and the third table run"). This is the project's own bug shape #1 — a value derived somewhere other than the one table that owns it. | **certain** |
| `Main.cpp:4268-4269` | **Cave ambience can never play above y=40.** The condition is `sky <= 2 && player.position.y < 40.0f`. A sealed windowless room, a covered ravine or a surface mineshaft at y=70 satisfies the darkness test and is silently excluded. The reference's rule is darkness, not depth. Bug shape #4: a predicate written as "equals the specific case" where the general test was already right there. | **certain** (logic) / **likely** (observable) |
| `Sounds.cpp:359-369` | **`playGlobal` applies no pitch randomisation** while `play` (`:345-357`) applies ±8%. Every eat, burp, fall, hurt, bow-shot, thunder and rain retrigger is therefore bit-identical on every occurrence. The comment at `:353-355` states the reason the jitter exists — "most of what stops a repeated sound reading as a loop" — and the second function did not inherit it. Bug shape #14. | **certain** |
| `Sounds.cpp:371-389` | **`playVoice` hardcodes `volume = 0.85f`** and offers no volume parameter, so a creature 19 blocks away and one at your feet differ only by the linear rolloff over a hardcoded 20-block radius. Every other event lets the caller size it. | certain (state) / cosmetic |
| `Sounds.cpp:391-405` | **Music is picked with replacement**, so with 8 tracks there is a 12.5% chance each gap of hearing the same track twice running. One remembered handle fixes it. | certain |
| `Main.cpp:1003-1004` | **Volumes are pushed to the engine exactly once**, at startup. Nothing re-reads `settings.soundVolume` afterwards, so the setting is restart-only despite `AudioEngine::setMasterVolume` being explicitly designed to be safe to call live (`AudioEngine.hpp:68-71`). | certain |
| `Sounds.cpp:36` / `make-reference-sounds.ps1:111-115` | **The staging script's comment says "there are twenty-three of them precisely so it never repeats within a session"** and then lists **eight**. The comment describes the reference's 23 cave recordings; the table stages `cave1`–`cave8`. Harmless, but the comment asserts a property the data does not have. | certain |
| `Main.cpp:2109` + `:6515-6517` | **The block outline is rebuilt only when its *size* changes**, so two different blocks with the same union extent share a cage — correct today because the cage is a single box, and it becomes wrong the moment G9.13 makes the outline shape-aware. Worth noting now so the change is made in both places. | certain (as a latent trap) |
| `Sounds.hpp:227-230` | **`has()` exists to catch exactly the §9.1 failure and nothing calls it.** The stem list, the enum and the staging script are three places that must agree; the loader reports a total but never asserts per-event coverage. A startup probe over all 57 events plus 102 voice banks is ~10 lines and would have caught the three unreachable materials above. | certain |

## 10. Player mechanics, movement and interaction

**Scope:** Everything the player *does* in the Overworld — walking, sprinting, sneaking, jumping, falling, swimming, climbing, flying, breaking, placing, using, attacking, and the camera and controls that carry all of it — measured against Bedrock Edition. Nether/End movement (portals, elytra, ender pearls, chorus fruit teleport) is out of scope by instruction and is not counted as a gap anywhere below.

**Headline verdict:** The constants that decide how the game *feels on flat ground* are already Bedrock-correct and were clearly derived rather than guessed — walk 4.317, sprint 5.612, sneak 1.295, jump apex 1.25, gravity 32 m/s², terminal 78.4 m/s, eye heights 1.62/1.27, reach 5/3/5, water speeds, 15 s of air, the 1.6 s meal and the 0.5 s damage-immunity overwrite rule all match. The damage is concentrated in three places instead. ✅ ~~**The break-time formula is Java-shaped, not Bedrock's** — it is missing the `speedMultiplier = 1` reset that doubles every wrong-tier mine, the round-up-to-whole-ticks step, the ÷5 in-water and ÷5 off-ground penalties, and Haste/Mining Fatigue/Efficiency entirely.~~ **The break formula was rebuilt on 2026-08-18 and is now Bedrock's exactly** — the reset, the `ceil`, both ÷5s and the Haste/Mining Fatigue scale are all in, and `canHarvest` tests tool kind as well as tier; **only Efficiency remains, and it is absent because enchanting is (G6.x)**. See G10.1 — and note it has never been played. **Combat is paced by an attacker-side 0.45 s swing timer** where Bedrock has none at all and limits the rate with a target-side immunity window that our creatures do not have. And **sprint-jumping does nothing here**: the +0.2 b/t launch impulse is absent, so the reference's standard travel technique costs four times the hunger for zero extra speed and clears ~3.1 blocks instead of ~4.22. Below that sit a large set of absent-but-cheap items — crawling, scaffolding, cobwebs, the off-hand, middle-click block pick, entity-intersection placement, shield blocking, melee criticals — and a completely empty camera-feel budget: no sprint FOV, no head-bob, no hurt tilt, no third person, no first-person hand.

**Completeness estimate:** Roughly **70% of Bedrock's Overworld player surface**. Of the ~95 comparable constants and rules in §10.1, about 48 match, **21 differ on value or model**, and 26 are absent. Three correct `constexpr` helpers (`miningSpeedScale`, `jumpScale`, `fallSpeedScale`) are written, commented and **have zero callers**, so three status effects are silently inert.

---

### 10.1 Constant-by-constant comparison

Bedrock is 20 ticks/second, so blocks/second ÷ 20 = blocks/tick. Where a figure is documented only for Java it is tagged **`[JE]`**. Where I derived a number from our code rather than reading it, it is marked *(derived)*.

| Eye height, sneaking | 1.27 (−0.35) | 1.27 — `Player.hpp:27` | matches | |
| Swim/crawl pose | 0.6 × 0.6 visual, 0.625 collision height | absent — `Player.hpp:206` `height()` returns only 1.8 or 1.5 | **absent** | No third pose exists, so no crawling and no swim silhouette |
| Step height | **0.5625 (9/16)** — official BE entity property | 0.6 — `Player.hpp:36` | **differs** | 0.6 is `[JE]`'s value. 0.0375 blocks; a feel nuance, not a bug |

### 10.4 Gap detail

#### G10.1 — Break-time formula is Java-shaped · M · P0 — ✅ **closed 2026-08-18**

> ✅ **All six items below are done except item 6, which has nothing to be done to.** The formula now
> lives in `game/src/item/Mining.hpp` (`breakTicksFor`) rather than `Tool.cpp`, and it steps through the
> wiki branch in order: `isBestTool ? multiplier : 1` → **the `canHarvest` reset** → `effects::miningSpeedScale`
> → **÷5 submerged** → **÷5 airborne** → `speed / hardness / (canHarvest ? 30 : 100)` → instant if `≥ 1` →
> **`ceil` to whole ticks**.
>
> - Item 1 (the reset) and item 5 (`ceil`, and instant as `damage ≥ 1`) are in.
> - Item 2 is in and was **much larger than this gap estimated**: `canHarvest` is now kind **and** tier, and
>   correcting the underlying table moved **291 block ids' harvest requirement** — 290 tighter, one looser
>   (mangrove leaves, which want shears or a sword and were demanding a hoe). Iron, gold, diamond, emerald,
>   lapis and copper *blocks* had been **punchable by hand for a full drop**, and so were **152 stair, slab
>   and wall ids** that inherited the same hole through `shapedParent`. **860 ids now refuse the wrong tool
>   kind.** A separate 100 ids had silently defaulted to hardness 1.0 — 16 concretes, 16 terracottas, the
>   whole wool family, deepslate variants and prismarine among them.
> - Item 3 is in, and it took the `BreakContext` struct this gap recommended rather than four overloads.
> - Item 4 is in: `effects::miningSpeedScale` finally has callers.
> - **Item 6 is not applicable** — this game has no copper or gold tool tier and is not getting one here.
>
> The numbered figures below are now the *reference* column and we match them: wooden pickaxe on iron ore
> is **300 ticks**, and stone by hand while submerged and airborne is **the ÷25 case**, both pinned by
> `static_assert`. The old "ours" column is what was replaced.
>
> ⚠ **Not played.** Every claim here is a compile-time assert or a reviewer's reading. The one thing an
> assert cannot check is *feel* — whether 15 s on iron ore with the wrong pickaxe reads as correct
> punishment or as a bug — and that is exactly what a playtest is for.
>
> One thing this gap asked for is **not** done: `RESEARCH.md` §10.1 still records the *Java* flavour of the
> formula, and that file belongs to someone else.

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the wiki gives the branch verbatim — https://minecraft.wiki/w/Breaking

  ```
  if isBestTool:  speedMultiplier = toolMultiplier
      if not canHarvest:  speedMultiplier = 1          # BE-only reset
      elif efficiency:    speedMultiplier += eff^2 + 1
  else:               speedMultiplier = 1
  if haste/conduit:   speedMultiplier *= 0.2*L + 1
  if miningFatigue:   speedMultiplier *= 0.3^L
  if inWater and not aquaAffinity: speedMultiplier /= 5
  if not onGround:                 speedMultiplier /= 5
  damage = speedMultiplier / hardness
  damage /= canHarvest ? 30 : 100
  if haste/conduit:   damage *= 1.2^L                  # BE-only second term
  if miningFatigue:   damage *= 0.7^L                  # BE-only second term
  if damage >= 1: instant
  ticks = ceil(1 / damage);  seconds = ticks / 20
  ```
  Tool multipliers: none 1, wood 2, stone 4, copper 5, iron 6, diamond 8, netherite 9, gold 12. Shears 2 (wool 5, leaves 15, cobweb 15); sword 1.5 (cobweb 15, bamboo 30). Efficiency adds `L² + 1`. Net Haste in BE is **×1.44** at I and **×2.016** at II; net Mining Fatigue is **0.21^L**.
- **What we had on 2026-08-17:** `Tool.cpp:880-897` —
  ```
  speed   = (wanted != None && tool.kind == wanted) ? tool.speed : 1.0
  penalty = tool.tier >= harvestTier(block) ? 1.5 : 5.0
  return hardness * penalty / max(0.1, speed)
  ```
  Algebraically this equals Bedrock's `hardness × 30 / speedMultiplier` and `hardness × 100 / speedMultiplier` — so **the correct-tool case is already exactly right**. Four things are missing and one is wrong.
- **What must be built:** ✅ **All six closed 2026-08-18/19 — re-verified against `item/Mining.hpp` on 2026-08-19 06:07, and §0.5 Tier 2 already ticks this row. Kept as the record of what was built; do not build it again.**
  1. ✅ ~~Add the **`speedMultiplier = 1` reset** when the block cannot be harvested. Today a wooden pickaxe keeps its ×2 against iron ore.~~ — `Mining.hpp` `breakTicksFor`: `if (!harvests) { speed = 1.0f; }`
  2. ~~Gate `canHarvest` on tool **kind as well as tier**.~~ **Done 2026-08-18, see the closed entry below** — `canHarvest` (`Mining.hpp:2363`) tests kind *and* tier. The range this cited, `Tool.cpp:899-909`, is past the end of a file that is now **77 lines**: `Tool.cpp` no longer holds any mining logic.
  3. Add the **÷5 in water** (no Aqua Affinity) and **÷5 off the ground** penalties. Both need `player.inWater` / `player.onGround` threaded into `breakSeconds` — that is a signature change, so do it once with a small `BreakContext` struct rather than four overloads.
  4. Call the already-correct `effects::miningSpeedScale` (`Effects.hpp:260`) — it implements both Haste terms and both Mining Fatigue terms and has zero callers.
  5. Round the result up to whole ticks and re-derive instant-break as `damage >= 1` rather than `hardness <= 0`.
  6. Add the copper (5) and gold (12) multipliers when those tiers exist.
- **Numbers that matter:** wooden pickaxe on iron ore — ours **7.5 s (150 ticks)**, Bedrock **15.0 s (300 ticks)**. Diamond pickaxe on stone — both **0.28 s (6 ticks)** once rounding is added (ours currently 0.28125 s). Mining stone by hand while swimming and airborne: Bedrock 187.5 s, ours 7.5 s. Haste II with an iron pickaxe on stone: Bedrock 0.15 s (3 ticks), ours 0.375 s.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `breakSeconds` is `constexpr`-friendly and probably has callers in tooltip/HUD code that will not have a player context; give those an overload that assumes grounded, dry and unaffected. `RESEARCH.md` §10.1 records the *Java* flavour of this formula and should be corrected in the same pass.

#### G10.2 — Combat paced by an attacker cooldown instead of target immunity · S · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** **there is no attack cooldown and no charge meter.** Attack rate is bounded entirely by the target's **10-tick (0.5 s) damage immunity**, and during that window a larger hit applies only the *difference* while a smaller one is ignored — the same overwrite rule we already implement for the player. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Damage and https://minecraft.wiki/w/Melee_attack
- **What we have:** `kSwingSeconds = 0.45` at `Main.cpp:112-114` gates the *attacker*. `Creatures::strike` (`Creature.cpp:5112-5155`) applies damage unconditionally; `hurtTimer = 0.35 s` is cosmetic only, so creatures have **no immunity window at all**.
- **What must be built:** move the limit to the target. Give each creature `lastDamage` and `immunitySeconds` mirroring `Player::damagePlayer` (`Player.cpp:955-982`) — that function is already correct and commented, so the cleanest change is to lift its body into one shared free function both call, which is exactly the "a rule that did not travel" shape. Then delete `kSwingSeconds`, or reduce it to a purely visual swing-animation timer with no gameplay effect.
- **Numbers that matter:** immunity **10 ticks = 0.5 s** (ours for the player: `Survival.hpp:35` = 0.5 — already right). Attacker cooldown: **0 ticks**. Cosmetic hurt flash 0.35 s can stay.
- **Risks / dependencies:** arrows, fire, lava, cactus and TNT all currently damage creatures through the same path, so adding immunity will *reduce* total damage from stacked sources — that is the correct Bedrock outcome, but it changes mob-farm and TNT numbers. Playtest required for whether melee now feels too fast.

#### G10.3 — No sprint-jump impulse · S · P0

- **Bedrock behaviour:** jumping while sprinting adds **+0.2 blocks/tick (= +4 b/s)** of horizontal velocity in the facing direction on the launch tick. Sustained sprint-jumping averages **7.127 b/s (0.35635 b/t)**, versus 5.612 for flat sprinting — a 27% gain, which is why it is the reference's standard travel method. A flat sprint-jump clears a **4-block gap** (measured maxima around 4.22 blocks). https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation and https://minecraft.wiki/w/Jumping
- **What we have:** the jump branch in `Player.cpp` sets `velocity.y = kJumpVelocity` and nothing else. Airborne horizontal speed is preserved (the target is `max(top, |current|)`), so the sprint speed carries — but nothing is added. Sprint-jumping therefore travels at exactly sprint speed while paying `kSprintJumpExhaustion = 0.2` per jump instead of `0.1`/m, i.e. **4× the hunger for zero benefit**.
- **What must be built:** on the jump tick, when `player.sprinting && onGround`, add 4.0 m/s along the horizontal facing direction (not the movement input — Bedrock uses yaw). Clamp so repeated jumps do not compound past the sprint-jump ceiling; Bedrock's own drag does this naturally, ours needs an explicit cap around 7.13 b/s. Optionally add the **~10-tick jump cooldown** at the same time, since without drag our re-jump is instant and would otherwise overshoot.
- **Numbers that matter:** impulse **+0.2 b/t = +4.0 b/s**; sustained sprint-jump **7.127 b/s = 0.35635 b/t**; airtime 12 ticks = 0.60 s; gap cleared ~4.22 blocks (community measurements dispute 4 vs 4.225 vs 5 — build against **4**). Our current derived distance: 0.559 s × 5.612 = **3.14 blocks**.
- **Risks / dependencies:** interacts with G10.17 (vertical drag). Getting the exact 4.22 without Bedrock's drag model will need one tuning pass against a measured gap in-game — **playtest required**.

#### G10.4 — Three dead status-effect helpers · XS · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** Haste/Mining Fatigue on mining (see G10.1); Jump Boost adds **+0.1 b/t per level** to jump velocity and removes **1 block** from fall-damage distance per level; Slow Falling caps descent and negates fall damage.
- **What we have:** `effects::miningSpeedScale` (`Effects.hpp:260`), `effects::jumpScale` (`Effects.hpp:312`) and `effects::fallSpeedScale` (`Effects.hpp:364`) are written, commented and correct — and **grep finds zero callers for all three**. `effects::moveSpeedScale` *is* wired, which is what disguises this.
- **What must be built:** three call sites. `jumpScale` at the `velocity.y = kJumpVelocity` line in `Player.cpp`; `fallSpeedScale` in the gravity integration; `miningSpeedScale` inside `breakSeconds` as part of G10.1. Then add a startup probe or `static_assert` proving each is reachable, per the project's own "a `default:` that returns a real value hides every missing entry" lesson.
- **Numbers that matter:** Jump Boost I: 0.42 → 0.52 b/t, apex 1.25 → ~1.90 blocks; fall-damage threshold 3 → 4 blocks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none — this is the cheapest P1 in the fragment.

#### G10.5 — Slime block: friction, sneak fall damage, stale fall distance · XS · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** slime blocks have **slipperiness 0.8** and additionally scale walking speed to ×0.4 on top; they **always negate fall damage**, and sneaking cancels only the *bounce*, not the negation. Max bounce height is 57.625 blocks. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Slime_Block
- **What we have:** `Block.hpp:6320` lists ice 0.98 and blue ice 0.989 and nothing else, so slime falls through to 0.6. `Player.cpp:~845` skips the bounce when sneaking — **and with it the fall-damage negation**, so sneak-landing on slime hurts. The bounce also does not reset `fallDistance` (`Player.cpp:~853` shows the bed branch does), so a bounce can carry stale distance into the next landing.
- **What must be built:** add slime to the `slipperiness` table at 0.8; negate fall damage on slime **before** the sneak check; reset `fallDistance` on the slime bounce as the bed branch already does.
- **Numbers that matter:** slipperiness 0.8; walk-on scale ×0.4 → effective 0.32 friction behaviour; bounce coefficient — ours 0.8 (`Player.hpp:47`), Bedrock's is effectively elastic up to 57.6 blocks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none.

#### G10.6 — Placement does not check creatures · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** since 1.19, a block cannot be placed where it would intersect an entity's hitbox, with a small set of documented exceptions (lily pads can be placed inside entities; end crystals require no intersecting entities). Note: `/w/Block_placement` is a 404 on the wiki, so there is **no single authoritative statement** of the general rule — it is inferred from the per-block exception notes and from patch behaviour, and should be confirmed by measurement rather than treated as certain.
- **What we have:** `Main.cpp:~5511` calls `playerOverlapsBlock(player, placeCell)` (`Player.hpp:213`) and nothing else. Creatures, dropped items and projectiles are all ignored.
- **What must be built:** an AABB query against the creature list for the candidate cell, using the block's actual collision shape rather than a unit cube (so slabs and stairs behave). Exempt non-colliding blocks (torches, plants, rails) and the documented exceptions.
- **Numbers that matter:** none — this is a predicate, not a constant.
- **Risks / dependencies:** needs a spatial query on `Creatures`; if none exists, a linear scan bounded to the chunk is fine at our entity counts. Watch the cost — this runs on every placement attempt, at up to 5.6/s with `kPlaceRepeatSeconds`.

#### G10.7 — Block pick (middle click) · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** middle mouse button picks the aimed block into the hotbar; in creative it also supplies the item. Unassigned on controller by default. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Controls
- **What we have:** nothing. `engine::MouseButton` in `engine/include/engine/platform/Window.hpp` declares **only `Left` and `Right`**, so the button never reaches the game.
- **What must be built:** add `MouseButton::Middle` to the engine enum and its platform mapping (this is an engine change — it exposes a mechanism, not a game concept, so it does not violate the layering rule); then, on press, map the aimed `BlockId` to its `ItemId` and either select an existing hotbar slot holding it or overwrite the selected slot in creative.
- **Numbers that matter:** none.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the block→item mapping must handle blocks whose item differs (grass block, snow layer, double slabs).

#### G10.8 — Placement ignores the cursor position inside the clicked face · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** orientation is decided by the clicked **face**, the **cursor's position within that face** (the threshold is exactly **0.5**), and the player's yaw. That sub-face position is what places a top slab or an upside-down stair when you click the upper half of a *side* face. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Stairs and https://minecraft.wiki/w/Slab
- **What we have:** `RaycastHit` (`Raycast.hpp:10-17`) carries the cell and the entry direction but **no hit point**. `Main.cpp:5490-5640` therefore derives stairs and slabs from `clickedAbove` / `clickedBelow`, which only exist for the ±Y faces. Aiming at the top half of a wall gives a bottom slab.
- **What must be built:** have the raycast return the exact intersection point (it already computes the crossing to step the DDA, so this is nearly free), then compare the relevant component against 0.5 in the slab/stair/trapdoor branches.
- **Numbers that matter:** threshold **0.5** exactly.
- **Risks / dependencies:** `RaycastHit` is used in many places; adding a field is additive and safe. Everything downstream keeps working.

#### G10.9 — Ladder descent speed and missing scaffolding · S · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** climbables (ladders, vines) move **2.35 b/s up (0.1175 b/t)** and **3.0 b/s down (0.15 b/t)**. Scaffolding is the one entry with explicit per-edition rows: **BE 1.2 b/s up and 2.94 b/s down** (`[JE]` 2.352 / 3.000). You jump to ascend scaffolding and sneak to descend; it never causes fall damage. BE-only extras: holding jump on a ladder climbs faster, and a waterlogged ladder is unclimbable. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Transportation, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Ladder, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Scaffolding
- **What we have:** `Player.cpp:799-800` hardcodes `kClimbSpeed = 2.4` (good) and `kSlideSpeed = 1.4` (**2.1× too slow**). `isClimbable` (`Block.hpp:3337-3339`) covers ladders and vines only.
- **What must be built:** raise the descent constant to 3.0; add scaffolding as a third climbable with its own pair (1.2 / 2.94) and jump-to-ascend / sneak-to-descend handling; keep fall-damage negation.
- **Numbers that matter:** 2.35 / 3.0 for ladders and vines; **1.2 / 2.94** for scaffolding in BE. A 30-block shaft: 10.0 s at our 1.4, **10.0 s → 4.3 s** once corrected.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the constants should move out of the function body into `player_constants` so they are greppable, since a hardcoded literal inside a branch is exactly how the 1.4 stayed wrong.

#### G10.10 — Camera feel: sprint FOV, view bobbing, hurt tilt · M · P1

- **Bedrock behaviour:** sprinting widens the field of view (Bedrock does not publish the magnitude; community measurement puts it near +10%, and Java's is a 1.1× multiplier eased over ~0.1 s — **treat the number as unverified**). View Bobbing is a documented setting and **defaults on**. Taking damage produces a red vignette plus a camera tilt that is not toggleable. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Options and https://minecraft.wiki/w/Screen_effects — both of these were reached through search summaries rather than a clean primary read, so mark the *magnitudes* as worth checking.
- **What we have:** FOV is a fixed 70 with F3/F4 stepping (`Main.cpp:123-126`), not persisted to `Settings`. `player.hurtFlash` exists (`Player.hpp:153`) but the only consumer is a 0.004 jitter on the health bar (`StatusBars.cpp:136`). Grep finds no bobbing, no tilt, no third-person and **no first-person hand model at all**.
- **What must be built:** ease the vertical FOV toward `fov × 1.1` while `player.sprinting`, over ~0.1 s in and ~0.15 s out; add a sinusoidal camera offset driven by the existing footstep distance accumulator (`kStepDistance = 2.1` at `Main.cpp`, already tracking distance travelled — reuse it rather than adding a second clock); add a roll/pitch impulse driven by `hurtFlash`, and a red screen tint. Expose bobbing and FOV as persisted settings.
- **Numbers that matter:** FOV 70 → ~77 while sprinting (unverified); bob period = one footstep = 2.1 blocks; hurt flash duration `survival::kHurtFlashSeconds` (already exists).
- **Risks / dependencies:** all three are pure feel and **must be playtested** — no amount of research substitutes for the user judging bob amplitude.

#### G10.11 — Crawling and the swim pose · L · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the swimming pose is **0.6 × 0.6**; crawling gives a collision box **0.625** blocks tall that fits a **0.375**-block gap, and you enter it by swimming into a 1-block space. Crawling has existed in Bedrock only since **1.20.30** — it is a recent parity addition, not an old feature. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Crawling
- **What we have:** `Player::height()` (`Player.hpp:206`) returns 1.8 or 1.5 and nothing else, so no third pose is representable.
- **What must be built:** a `Pose` enum (Standing / Sneaking / Swimming / Crawling) replacing the boolean, with height, eye height and collision box derived from one table; entry when submerged-and-moving or when standing up is blocked; exit blocked while a ceiling is present.
- **Numbers that matter:** swim 0.6 × 0.6; crawl collision 0.625 tall; minimum gap 0.375; swim eye height ~0.4.
- **Risks / dependencies:** touches collision, the camera, the sneak ledge guard and the step-up retry. This is the largest single change in the fragment and should not be started before G10.1–G10.5.

#### G10.12 — Controls: rebinding, sensitivity, Ctrl+Q, double-tap-W, pause menu · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** every key is rebindable; mouse sensitivity is a slider; **Ctrl+Q drops the whole stack** and holding Q drops singles rapidly; sprint is Ctrl **or double-tap W**; sneak on the keyboard is hold-only (there is no toggle — MCPE-74082), while the controller's RS click toggles it. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Controls
- **What we have:** every binding is an `engine::Key::` literal inside `Main.cpp`. `Settings.hpp` has six `controller_*` entries and no mouse sensitivity, no bindings and no persisted FOV. Q drops one (`Main.cpp:~4468`); there is no Ctrl+Q and no double-tap-W. `Main.cpp:3390`'s own comment records that no pause menu exists.
- **What must be built:** a binding table mapping an `Action` enum to a key, loaded from `Settings`, with `Main.cpp` querying actions instead of keys. That is a mechanical but wide edit. The three small wins — Ctrl+Q, double-tap-W (reuse `kDoubleTapSeconds = 0.3`), and a mouse-sensitivity multiplier — are each XS and can land first.
- **Numbers that matter:** double-tap window 0.3 s (already ours, matches the fly toggle).
- **Risks / dependencies:** the rebinding table is the kind of "configuration hook" the architecture rules warn about — but here there is a real second case (the pad already has its own map), so it qualifies.

#### G10.13 — Shield blocking and melee critical hits · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the shield is raised by **holding sneak** (not the use button, unlike Java), takes 5 ticks (0.25 s) to raise, blocks within a ±90° semicylinder with pitch ignored, has 336 durability, and is disabled for **5 s (100 ticks)** by an axe hit. Critical hits multiply damage by **1.5** when falling; **Bedrock permits crits while sprinting** where Java forbids them, and applies the multiplier *after* enchantments. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Shield, https://minecraft.wiki/w/Critical_hit
- **What we have:** the shield is craftable (`Recipe.cpp:630`, `Item.hpp:310`) and completely inert. No melee crit exists; arrows have their own crit roll at `Projectile.cpp:236`.
- **What must be built:** a `blocking` flag on the player set by sneak-while-holding-shield, a directional test in `damagePlayer`, a disable timer, and a `×1.5` multiplier in the melee path gated on `velocity.y < 0 && !onGround` (with no sprint exclusion, which is the Bedrock difference).
- **Numbers that matter:** raise 5 ticks = 0.25 s; arc ±90°; disable 100 ticks = 5 s; crit ×1.5.
- **Risks / dependencies:** binding blocking to sneak collides with the ledge guard and sneak-place; that interaction is exactly what Bedrock lives with, but it needs a playtest.

#### G10.14 — Off-hand · L · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** the off-hand accepts a **restricted set only** — shield, arrows, tipped arrows, firework rockets, totem of undying, filled and explorer maps, nautilus shell — and **has no keybind at all**: you place items there by dragging in the inventory. Java's F swap does not exist in Bedrock.
- **What we have:** nothing anywhere in `game/src`.
- **What must be built:** one inventory slot with an allow-list, an HUD indicator, and consumption hooks in the arrow, totem and shield paths.
- **Numbers that matter:** none.
- **Risks / dependencies:** touches inventory serialisation (a save-format bump), the HUD and the shield work in G10.13. Defer until after G10.13.

#### G10.15 — Cobweb, powder snow, sweet berries, bubble columns · M · P2

- **Bedrock behaviour:** cobweb ~25% speed with entities falling at 0.078 b/s and no fall damage; sweet berry bush ~34% speed plus 1♥ per 0.5 s while moving and no fall damage; powder snow sinks you, freezes after **7 s** then deals 1♥ per 2 s; bubble columns push **14 b/s up / 6 b/s down in Bedrock** (`[JE]` 11 / 4.9).
- **What we have:** all four blocks exist in `Block.hpp`; none has a movement rule.
- **What must be built:** one hook — "what does the block I am standing in do to my motion?" — called once from the movement integration, rather than four separate special cases. The `isSticky` / `slipperiness` pair is the existing precedent.
- **Numbers that matter:** as above; note the bubble column numbers are among the few where BE and JE are both published and differ substantially.
- **Risks / dependencies:** the shared hook is the whole value here; four independent branches would be the "a rule that did not travel" failure again.

#### G10.16 — Third-person views · M · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** F5 (or D-pad up) cycles first person → third person behind → third person in front; the camera sits about 4 blocks back. https://minecraft.wiki/w/Third-person_view
- **What we have:** nothing, and there is no player model to look at.
- **What must be built:** a camera-offset mode plus a player model. The model is the real cost.
- **Numbers that matter:** camera distance ~4 blocks.
- **Risks / dependencies:** depends on a player model existing; that is animation work, not player-mechanics work.

#### G10.17 — Vertical drag, creative vertical fly speed, step height · XS · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** vertical velocity is multiplied by **0.98 per tick**, so terminal velocity is approached asymptotically and never quite reached. Creative **vertical** flight is **7.49 b/s**, not the horizontal 11.0. Step height is **0.5625 (9/16)** per the official entity property `minecraft:variable_max_auto_step`, against Java's 0.6.
- **What we have:** no vertical drag — a hard clamp at `kTerminalVelocity` 78.4 (`Player.hpp:80`); `kFlySpeed` 11.0 is reused for the vertical axis; `kStepHeight` 0.6 (`Player.hpp:36`).
- **What must be built:** three constant/one-line changes. The drag one is the only real work: multiply `velocity.y` by `pow(0.98, dt/0.05)` each step and drop the clamp to a safety net.
- **Numbers that matter:** drag 0.98/tick; a 23.5-block drop 1.21 s here vs ~1.35 s there landing at 38.8 vs 32.0 m/s *(derived)*; a 100-block drop 2.5 s vs ~3.05 s, 78.4 vs ~55 m/s. Vertical fly 7.49 b/s = 0.3745 b/t. Step 0.5625.
- **Risks / dependencies:** drag interacts with G10.3's sprint-jump tuning and with jump airtime (0.559 s → ~0.60 s, which is the *correct* direction). Do them together.

#### G10.18 — Per-food eat durations, crossbow, Depth Strider, Dolphin's Grace · S · P3

- **Bedrock behaviour:** most food is 32 ticks = **1.6 s**, but dried kelp is **16 ticks = 0.8 s** and honey bottle is **40 ticks = 2.0 s**. Crossbow draw is **25 ticks = 1.25 s**, reduced 5 ticks per Quick Charge level. Depth Strider multiplies swim speed ~×1.33/level (III sprint-swim 5.305 b/s); Dolphin's Grace gives a flat **9.80 b/s**.
- **What we have:** one global `kEatSeconds = 1.6` (`Survival.hpp:233`); no crossbow; neither enchantment.
- **What must be built:** move eat duration into the per-food table; the rest are new items/enchantments and belong to their own fragments.
- **Numbers that matter:** 16 / 32 / 40 ticks = 0.8 / 1.6 / 2.0 s; crossbow 25 ticks = 1.25 s.
- **Risks / dependencies:** none.

### 10.5 Errors and inconsistencies noticed while reading

All of the following were **read in the code**, not inferred, unless the entry says otherwise.

- `Player.cpp:~845` · The slime bounce is skipped while sneaking, and the fall-damage negation is inside the same branch — so **sneaking onto a slime block takes full fall damage**. Bedrock negates it regardless of sneak; sneak cancels only the bounce. · **certain**
- `Player.cpp:~845` vs `~853` · The bed branch resets `fallDistance`; the slime branch does not. A bounce can therefore carry stale fall distance into the next landing. This is the "a rule that did not travel" shape — two adjacent branches, one guarded. · **likely**
- `Effects.hpp:260, 312, 364` · `miningSpeedScale`, `jumpScale` and `fallSpeedScale` are written, commented, correct, and have **zero callers**. Haste, Mining Fatigue, Jump Boost and Slow Falling are therefore all silently inert. `moveSpeedScale` *is* called, which is what makes this invisible. · **certain**
- ✅ **Fixed — verified 2026-08-19 in `Mining.hpp` `breakTicksFor`, which now reads `if (!harvests) { speed = 1.0f; }`. Left as history:** `Mining.hpp` (was `Tool.cpp:889`) · ~~`speed` takes the tool's multiplier whenever the tool's *kind* matches, even when the tier cannot harvest the block.~~ Bedrock explicitly resets `speedMultiplier` to 1 in that case, so every wrong-tier mine here is exactly half the time it should be. · **certain**
- ✅ ~~`Tool.cpp:899-909` · `yieldsDrop` compares tier only (with a shears special case), never tool **kind**. An iron shovel therefore harvests stone — both the drop and the 1.5× rate. Bedrock's `canHarvest` requires the right tool type *and* tier.~~ · **fixed 2026-08-18** — `canHarvest` now lives in `Mining.hpp` and tests kind and tier; `yieldsDrop` is a one-line forward to it.
- `Block.hpp:6320-6325` · The `slipperiness` table has ice and blue ice and no slime block, so slime falls through to the 0.6 default instead of 0.8. · **certain**
- `Fluid.hpp:139` · `kPlayerSuffocateGrace = 1.0` has no callers. `kDrownInterval` and `kDrownDamage` immediately below are used only by creatures, not the player, which is easy to misread as the player's drowning path. · **certain**
- `Main.cpp:112-114` · `kSwingSeconds = 0.45` is a Java-shaped attacker-side cooldown in a Bedrock-referenced game. Combined with creatures having no immunity window (`Creature.cpp:5112-5125`, where `hurtTimer` is cosmetic), the rate limit sits on the wrong side of the exchange and stacked damage sources can over-apply. · **likely**
- `Player.cpp:799-800` · `kClimbSpeed` and `kSlideSpeed` are `constexpr` **inside a branch body**, not in `player_constants` with every other movement number. That is why the descent value has been 2.1× wrong without being noticed — it is not where anyone auditing constants would look. · **certain**
- `Main.cpp:123-126` · FOV is adjustable at runtime (F3/F4) but is **not** in `Settings.hpp`, so it resets to 70 on every launch. Every other tunable in that area persists. · **certain**
- `Main.cpp:117, ~4637` · `kBreakRepeatSeconds = 0.22` is applied only to instant breaks. Bedrock's 6-tick (0.30 s) gate applies between all block breaks except sub-tick ones. · **certain**
- `engine/include/engine/platform/Window.hpp` · `MouseButton` declares only `Left` and `Right`. Middle click cannot reach the game at all, which forecloses block pick without an engine change. · **certain**
- `RESEARCH.md` §10.1 · The recorded mining formula is the **Java** branch. Since Bedrock is the stated reference and §10.1 is the owner of that number, it will keep re-seeding the wrong implementation. *(Inferred from comparing the doc against the wiki, not from a code read.)* · **likely**
- `Main.cpp:82-84` · Not an error — a correctness win worth protecting. Block reach is 5 in **both** creative and survival, which is right for Bedrock and would look like a bug to anyone who knows Java's 4.5/5 split. Leave it. · **certain**

**Judgements I cannot make without playing** (I did not build or run the game, by instruction): whether the missing sprint-jump actually reads as sluggish or merely as "different"; whether the 0.45 s swing rhythm feels wrong in the hand; whether ladder descent at 1.4 is noticeable or merely slow; whether the step-up camera ease at half-per-tick is too soft; whether treading water bobs convincingly; and every magnitude in G10.10 (bob amplitude, sprint FOV, hurt tilt) — those are tuned by eye, not by citation.
